title: The World That Forgot to Listen
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: There is a kind of silence that is not quiet.

It is the silence of a mother calling her child's name in a crowded street and nobody turning to look. The silence of an old man weeping on a bus while every person around him stares at a small glowing screen. The silence of a billion voices speaking at the same moment — shouting, performing, arguing, confessing — and none of it landing anywhere. Words travelling at the speed of light and arriving nowhere.
That was the world the year this story begins.

People had never been more able to reach each other. You could send a message to someone on the other side of the earth and it would arrive before your next breath. You could see the face of a stranger ten thousand miles away. You could watch a child go hungry in real time, from the comfort of a warm room, while eating your dinner.
And yet.

A ten-year-old boy sat in the rubble of what had been his home and held up a handwritten sign: *PLEASE HELP US.* He held it up to a small camera his neighbour had given him before fleeing. Six million people saw his face that week.
Forty-one pressed a button to say they cared.
One sent a laughing face.
Nobody came.

A teenage girl in a comfortable city watched the boy's face between two advertisements — one for a perfume, one for a car — and felt something crack open in her chest. She stared at him for a long moment. Then she looked away. Not because she was cruel. She was not cruel. She looked away because that same screen had already shown her nine other children in nine other ruins that same afternoon, and her heart, which was a good heart, simply could not hold that much. No heart can. So she did what the world had quietly trained her to do without her knowing it had trained her at all.
She scrolled past.
This is not a story about bad people.

There were very few truly bad people in this world. There were mostly just overwhelmed ones. Frightened ones. People who had been shown so much suffering for so long that some quiet part of them had learned to feel nothing, because feeling everything was a kind of madness. People who had been told so many times that everything wrong with the world was someone else's fault that they had stopped asking the only question that could change anything:
*What can I do?*
Not: *Who is to blame?*
Not: *Why isn't someone fixing this?*
Just: *What can I do?*
This question had almost disappeared from the world.

The people in power had discovered, some time ago, that a frightened and angry population is easier to control than a calm and questioning one. Keep people afraid of each other, keep them convinced that the person across the street or across the border is the source of their suffering, and they will never look up long enough to notice who is actually deciding their lives. So they fed the fear. Every year, a little more. Every election, a little louder. Every crisis, a little more pointed in its blame.
It worked.

Neighbours who had shared meals for twenty years stopped speaking because of things a stranger on a screen had said. Families broke apart over beliefs that none of them had held five years earlier. Communities that had survived floods and famines and foreign occupation together fell into bitterness over words — over the particular words people used, the particular prayers they said, the particular leaders they trusted — while the floods came back, bigger than before, and nobody could agree on what to do.

A grandmother in one country could not talk to her granddaughter without it ending in tears. They loved each other completely. They could no longer find each other across the distance of what they believed.

A man lost his job. His anger was real. His pain was real. But the people who told him who to blame for it were the same people who had taken the job. He never found that out. He was too angry to look.

A child grew up hearing, every day, that the children across the border were different from her in ways that mattered. She believed it. She had never met one of those children. Neither had the person who told her.

This is how the world breaks. Not with bombs, though there were bombs. Not with floods, though there were floods. With the small, daily, ordinary decision to stop trying to understand the person standing in front of you.
Into this world, in a city that the news had stopped covering because the suffering there had gone on too long to still be interesting, something was about to begin.
It would not begin with a great leader rising to power.
It would not begin with an army or a revolution or a law.
It would begin with a girl on a rooftop, alone, asking a question nobody around her was asking anymore.
Her name was Tali.
She was fourteen years old. She was the most important person alive. Not because she was the strongest or the most gifted or the most certain.
Because she was still asking.

title: How Tali Came Into the World
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: Her father had been working abroad when the war began.

He had gone eight months earlier — there was no work at home, and a cousin knew a contractor building roads in another country who needed workers. The wages were better than anything at home. Not comfortable — a third went to the transfer service that moved the money across the border, another third to rent and food in the expensive city where he worked. What remained was less than the figures on paper suggested, but it was real money arriving each month, and at home real money was scarce. He had planned to return after six months. Then the contract extended. Then another month. Then another. His wife was four months pregnant when he left. He had calculated it carefully. He had been wrong.
His last visit was nine months before the war began.

They had two weeks together. Long enough to remember what it felt like to be in the same room. Long enough to talk until late, to make plans that felt real for the first time since he had left, to say the things that were easier to say in person than through a screen. He went back. She stayed. And some weeks later she called him and she was laughing before she had even said hello.
She was pregnant.
When the call ended he sat in the dark for a long time.

Happy — he was happy, he knew that. The kind of happy that sits in the chest and doesn't know what to do with itself. He was going to be a father. There was a person coming who did not exist yet and who would be his.
But underneath the happiness, already, was the other thing.

He knew what the city was like. He had left because there was no work, and there was no work because the city was slowly being swallowed by something he could not name and could not fix. He knew what the streets looked like now compared to how they had looked when he was a boy. He knew what kind of world his child was being born into.

He sat with both feelings — the joy and the fear — and did not try to choose between them. They were both true. That was the hardest part. Not that he was afraid, but that the fear did not cancel the happiness, and the happiness did not cancel the fear.
He was going to be a father.
He wanted, more than he had ever wanted anything, to be there.

Weeks after that she went to the clinic for the scan. She held the image up to the camera that evening — a small blurred shape, white against black, unmistakably a person — and he looked at his child on a small screen and did not say anything for a long time.
*A girl,* his wife said.
He hadn't known what he'd been hoping for. He knew now. This.

They talked for three hours that night. About names — they went through a long list, dismissing each one for reasons that were sometimes practical and sometimes entirely made up, until they found the one that felt true. They talked about what she would be like. What her voice would sound like. Whether she would have his stubbornness or her mother's patience, and they agreed it would probably be both, which would either make her extraordinary or impossible, most likely both.

He wrote the name down on a piece of paper that night and pinned it above his bed. It was the first thing he saw each morning and the last thing before sleep. The name of someone he hadn't met yet. Someone he was already certain about.
His wife told him the due date the same night they chose the name. He wrote it down beneath the name on the piece of paper above his bed. A name and a date.
He submitted his leave request the next morning.
It was rejected.

He submitted it again. Rejected. He wrote a letter to the site manager explaining the situation — his wife, the pregnancy, the date, the distance. Rejected. He asked a colleague who had done this before how to appeal. He appealed. He waited. He submitted again with more documentation, more explanation, more of himself laid out on paper for strangers to approve or deny.
Rejected. Rejected. Pending. Rejected.

Each time he told his wife he was still trying. Each time she said she knew he would get there. He did not tell her how many times they had said no. He did not want her carrying that on top of everything else.
Then one morning, four months into the waiting, the approval came through.

He booked the ticket the same day. Did not wait until the afternoon, did not sleep on it — walked to the booking office on his lunch break with the approval letter in his hand and bought the ticket and stood outside on the pavement afterward holding the confirmation and feeling something loosen in his chest that had been tight for months.

He counted the days on the calendar that night. Circled the date he would land. Drew a line between that date and the due date — three weeks of overlap, enough time to be there, to be ready, to hold his daughter before she was a day old.
He packed his bag that same week. Checked the ticket so many times the paper went soft at the folds.
There was no reason he couldn't travel. No ban, no restriction. He was days away from boarding. He was nearly home.
Then the bombs started falling and the borders closed overnight.

It happened fast. It always happens fast. One morning the city was alive. By evening the bridges were on fire. By midnight the borders were sealed and the phones were dead and every road out of the country was closed or watched or too dangerous to try. Her father stood in a foreign airport staring at a departures board that had gone blank, with a ticket that was now worthless and no way to know if his wife was alive.
He stood there for a long time.
Then he sat down on the floor of the airport and tried to think.
He was on the outside. She was on the inside. And between them was a war that did not care about the child coming.

He tried the phones until the lines went dead. He tried every number he had — her phone, her sister's phone, the neighbour's phone, a number he found written in an old letter that he wasn't even sure was still connected. Nothing.
He could not sleep. He lay in a chair in the airport the first night because he could not make himself leave, as if leaving the airport meant accepting that he was not going to board a plane.
In the morning he went to the embassy and stood in a queue for four hours and was told there was nothing they could do.

He went back to his room. He sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the piece of paper above it — the name, the date — and imagined her. That was all he could do. Imagine. Was she safe? Was she inside somewhere? Was the baby coming? Was anyone with her? He had no answers. He just sat there with the questions, in a room that still had her name on the wall, in a city that was not his, waiting for news that did not come.

He could not get to her. He could not send word. He could not do anything except wait in a foreign city and not know — not know if she was safe, not know if the baby had come, not know if either of them were alive. Every morning he woke up hoping that day would bring some news. Every night he went to sleep having heard nothing. He told himself no news was not bad news. He told himself they were alive. He told himself this the way a person tells themselves something they cannot afford not to believe.
He waited. And he prayed.

He was not a religious man. He had never been one — had drifted past faith the way most people drift past things that don't seem necessary until suddenly they are. But on the second day he walked into a mosque because the door was open and he did not know where else to go. He sat in the back and said nothing and felt, for a moment, slightly less alone.
On the fourth day he lit a candle in a church. On the sixth he stood for a long time outside a temple, watching people go in and out, and then went in himself and sat quietly in the cool of it.

He was not sure who he was talking to. He was not sure it mattered. The last time he had heard her voice she was pregnant, and that was still how he held her in his mind — his wife, his unborn daughter, somewhere on the other side of a war. He would walk into every house of every god on earth if there was any chance at all that one of them was listening.

Nine days of waking up and checking for word that wasn't there. Nine days of the name on the wall and the date that had already passed. Nine days of not knowing whether he was a father or whether he was something else — something he did not have a word for and did not want to find one.
He just wanted them to be alive.
On the ninth day after the borders closed, Tali was born.

Not in a hospital. The hospital had been hit on the third day. In the back room of a building that was still partly standing, by candlelight, helped by the woman from the floor above who had trained as a midwife twenty years earlier and had not forgotten how. There was dust in the air from the shelling. There was no clean water. There was a woman who had spent nine days alone and terrified, who had eaten whatever she could find, who had slept in the basement when the bombing was close and crept back upstairs when it stopped, who had talked to her unborn child in the dark because it was the only voice she had.

The baby came in the early hours of the morning. She came out fighting — not in any mystical sense, but in the plain sense that she was loud and strong and entirely unwilling to be ignored. The midwife held her up in the candlelight and said:
*She came out screaming. That means she knows what she wants.*
Her mother held her daughter and named her Tali.
In one language it meant dew — the small drops of water that form on the grass before sunrise, before anyone is awake to see them, the first sign that the night is ending.
In another it meant rising.
Both were true.
Tali grew up running.

Her earliest memory was not a place but a movement — her mother's arms, the smell of smoke, the sound of feet on broken ground, moving. Always moving. They never stayed anywhere long enough to grow roots. A building in one street until it became unsafe. A basement in another until the water rose. A half-destroyed school where forty families sheltered together for six months, sharing what they had, keeping each other alive through the simple stubborn act of not leaving each other.
Her mother was the most capable person Tali had ever seen.

She had been a schoolteacher before the war. Gentle. Patient. The kind of teacher children remembered for the rest of their lives. The war had not made her cruel. It had burned away everything that wasn't necessary and left behind the part of her that would simply not stop. She could make a meal from almost nothing. She could calm a crying child who wasn't hers. She could look at a street and know, from the quality of the silence, whether it was safe to cross. She could walk into a group of desperate strangers and within an hour know who needed comfort and who needed something to do and who needed simply to be seen by another human being.
She called this paying attention.
*Most suffering,* she told Tali once, when Tali was old enough to understand, *is invisible. Not because people hide it. Because nobody looks.*
Tali looked.

By the time she was six, she could take a broken thing apart and put it back together. Not because she had been taught — she had been taught almost nothing, because there was no school, no teacher, no normal childhood to speak of. But she had her mother's instinct for paying attention. She would find a broken object — a radio, a lamp, a clock — lay all its pieces on the ground, and study them the way her mother studied streets. Then she would put them back together. She was almost always right. When she was wrong she tried again.

Her mother wept the first time she heard a voice come crackling out of a radio Tali had fixed. Tali didn't understand the tears. To her it was straightforward. The thing was broken. The pieces were there. You just had to look long enough to understand how they fit.
By nine, she had applied this same thinking to people.

She knew every family sheltering within reach. She knew who had medicine and who needed it. Who had grain and who had cooking oil. Who could speak the language of the aid workers and could help families understand what they were being told. Who had a skill — stitching wounds, delivering babies, fixing engines — that nobody around them knew about because nobody had thought to ask. She moved through the ruins every morning like a thread weaving through broken beads, carrying information, making connections, asking nothing in return.
The adults called her useful. They ruffled her hair and thanked her and went back to their own survival.

Tali thought of it differently. It wasn't charity. The needs were there. The resources were there. All that was missing was someone paying enough attention to see both at the same time and draw a line between them.

*Why does nobody do this?* she wondered. She was nine, and she could already see things that seemed obvious to her that the adults around her had stopped seeing. Not because they were less intelligent. Because they were too exhausted, too frightened, too deep inside their own pain to look up.
She filed the question away. She was collecting questions the way other children collected stones.

At ten the city got worse. Not more bombs — just more desperation. The random cruelties of people who had been frightened too long. They lost their last stable shelter in a single afternoon and moved twice in one month. Her mother grew quieter. Not broken — she did not break — but quieter, in the way of someone spending carefully from a reserve that was running low.
Tali watched her the way she watched broken things. Trying to understand all the pieces. Trying to know what held her together.
She never fully found out. Some things are not meant to be taken apart.
Tali was eleven the night her mother shook her awake and said: *we are leaving now.*

The bombing had shifted direction in the night. Her mother had heard it in her sleep and known, the way she always knew — not by thinking, but by the feeling in her body that had kept them alive for eleven years.
They walked out.
They walked for three days.

Tali's mother held her hand. She held it crossing roads and through checkpoints and sleeping on the ground at night, curled around each other for warmth, her mother's arm over her like a wing. She held it the whole way. Tali understood, in the way children understand things without words, that her mother was holding her hand not only to keep her close but to keep herself from falling apart. So Tali held back. As hard as she could.
The border crossing was the worst thing she had ever seen, and she had seen bad things.

Thousands of people in an open area the size of several football fields, fenced, with processing stations at the far end that could handle perhaps one hundred people an hour. They had arrived with thousands more behind them and thousands already in front. The sun was brutal. There was one water point and a queue at it two hundred people long. Children were crying — not all of them, but enough that it became a kind of constant sound, a layer underneath everything else.
Her mother locked her fingers through Tali's and did not let go.

For two hours they moved with the crowd — forward a few metres, stop, forward again, the pressure from behind building as more people arrived and the only direction was toward the stations at the far end. Her mother used her body as a shield, turning sideways in the crush, keeping Tali on her protected side.
Then somebody screamed.

Tali never found out why. A scuffle somewhere in the crowd, a gunshot from somewhere outside the fence, a rumour that moved faster than truth — it didn't matter. What mattered was that several thousand frightened people moved at the same instant, all in different directions, and the crowd stopped being a crowd and became a force.
Her mother's hand was torn from hers.

Not slowly. Not with warning. One moment it was there, the next moment there was a wall of bodies between them and the wall was moving and Tali was moving with it and there was nothing — no grip, no voice she could hear over the noise, nothing.
She was swept twenty metres before the surge broke.

She stood still. The crowd heaved around her. She breathed — *stop, breathe, think, move* — and turned in a full circle, looking. Her mother's face was not there. She pushed back against the flow, calling, checking every face she passed. She did this for two hours. Methodically. The way she had searched ruined buildings for useful things — every corner, every shadow, nothing skipped.
Her mother was gone.
What had happened to her, Tali did not know. She would not know for years.

An official found her eventually — a young woman with the hollow eyes of someone who had seen too much that day and had more still to come. She asked Tali where her family was. Tali told her. The woman took her by the shoulder to a low building at the edge of the processing area and put her in a room with thirty-nine other people and closed the door.
The room smelled of sweat and fear and the particular exhaustion of people who have been waiting too long.
Tali sat against the wall and looked at what she had.

The bag her mother had handed her two hours earlier. Inside: a change of clothes, three photographs — one of her parents together before the war, one of the street where they had lived, one she had never been able to identify, a courtyard somewhere, a woman laughing — and her mother's small book, the one she read from every night before sleep, its spine cracked from use, its pages soft as cloth.
That was everything.
She looked at the room. Forty people, one guard, one door, one window on the east wall with a latch that someone had repaired badly with a piece of wire.
She looked at the window for a long time.

She was eleven years old. She was exhausted and her feet were bleeding from three days of walking and she wanted her mother so badly it felt like a physical injury, a hole in her chest where the wanting lived.
She was also the daughter of a woman who had kept moving through eleven years of war without stopping.
She watched the guard's pattern for one hour. She waited for the room to go still. She waited for 4 a.m., when the body's need for sleep overrides almost everything else, including vigilance.
Then she went through the window.

Six feet down. She hit the ground on her bad foot and went down hard, bit the inside of her cheek to keep quiet, tasted blood. She lay still for thirty seconds, listening. No shout. No running feet. She got up, picked up the bag, and moved.

The facility was set in flat open land. She could see a road, its lights a pale smear on the horizon, perhaps two kilometres away. She walked toward it in the dark, staying low, her ankle a steady fire with every step. She crossed a field of something dry and crackling, a drainage ditch she nearly fell into, a stretch of gravel that seemed designed to be as loud as possible.
The sky was turning from black to grey when she reached the road.
She did not flag down a car. She had been alive long enough to know what happened to girls who flagged down cars alone on dark roads. She walked alongside the road instead, in the scrub, invisible.

An hour later a truck slowed beside her. The driver was a woman — older, grey-haired, with the weathered face of someone who spent her life on roads and had seen most things. She looked at Tali for a long moment through the window. Said nothing. Jerked her head once toward the cab.
Tali read her face. Her mother had taught her to read faces and she trusted what she read now.
She got in.
The woman drove for forty minutes without a word. She stopped at the edge of a city, pointed once toward the centre, and waited. Tali got out. The truck pulled away.
She stood on the pavement alone.

Eleven years old. A bag with three photographs and a book. One good foot and one that was swelling inside her shoe. The smell of a city she had never been in, full of people who had no reason to care that she existed.
She straightened her back — her mother's gesture, the one she made before she walked into anything difficult — and walked toward the centre.
By the end of that day she had found food, a place to sleep, and a girl named Sara.
Not safety. Not comfort. Not her mother.
But enough to keep going.
That had always been enough.
The girl's name was Sara. She was fifteen — four years older than Tali — and she had been on this side of the border for eight months and knew things Tali needed to know.

Not because Sara was kind, exactly. She was watchful and careful and not given to warmth. But she recognised in Tali the particular alertness of a child who has been surviving for a long time and decided that useful was better than alone.
Sara did not teach her anything at first.

That was not how it worked. Sara had survived eight months in this city by being careful about who she trusted and how much, and a girl who had appeared from nowhere with a bad ankle and a worn bag was not automatically worth trusting. She showed Tali the building. She showed her the rooftop. That was all.
What changed it was the phone.

Sara had a phone — old, cracked across one corner, the kind of phone that was worth nothing except that it was the only way she had of receiving messages from her family, who were still on the other side of the border and sent word when they could. One morning it stopped turning on entirely.
Sara sat with it for a long time, pressing the button, willing it to respond. It didn't.
Tali was on the rooftop. She had seen Sara's face when she came up the stairs and recognised the particular expression of someone whose one connection to something they love has just gone silent.
She said nothing. She did not offer. She waited.
After a while Sara came and sat near her and held out the phone without speaking.

Tali looked at it. She had no tools — she had nothing. She asked Sara if there was a pin, a hairgrip, anything thin and metal. Sara found a hairgrip. Tali straightened it, used it to open the back of the phone, looked at what was inside, and found a connection that had worked loose from its housing — probably from being dropped, probably more than once. She pressed it back into place with the tip of the hairgrip, careful and slow.
The phone turned on.
Sara stared at it. Then she looked at Tali.
*"Where did you learn that?"*
*"I just look at things until I understand them,"* Tali said.
Sara was quiet for a moment. *"That's useful."*

It was the closest Sara came to a compliment. After that, slowly, over days and then weeks, she began to share what she knew about the city — not all at once, not as a gift, but in the way that trust actually moves between people who have learned to be careful with it. A piece of information here. A warning there. Which market stalls were run by people who would call the authorities if they saw an undocumented child. Which parts of the city were dangerous for a girl alone after dark. Which women could be trusted with a real problem.
Tali listened and remembered all of it.
They found the building together.

Sara knew about it — a place at the edge of the district, technically owned by a company that had gone out of business three years earlier. Nobody collected rent. Nobody did repairs. A loose collection of people lived there because it was shelter and shelter was what they needed.
Sara had a room on the second floor. She showed Tali the rooftop — accessible through a hatch at the top of the stairs, flat, with a low wall on three sides. Nobody used it.
*"You can sleep up here,"* Sara said. *"Nobody will bother you up here."*

This was partly true and partly advice. Up here, a girl alone was harder to reach than a girl alone in a ground-floor room. Tali understood what Sara was not quite saying and was grateful for the not-quite-saying of it.
She slept on the rooftop.

She ate by being useful to women — this was the rule she made for herself, quietly, without saying it aloud. The woman in the yellow building gave bread. A mother on the first floor had a sick child and no sleep and Tali could sit with the child and tell stories while the mother rested, and the mother paid in food without either of them making it transactional. An older woman two streets away did alterations and tailoring and needed someone with small steady hands for the fine work, and paid in meals and in the unsentimental kindness of a woman who had seen enough of the world to know that a girl surviving alone deserved respect rather than pity.

She stayed away from men she didn't know. This was not paranoia. It was information, given to her by Sara in the first week, confirmed by everything she observed in the months that followed. The city had enough good people in it to survive on. She chose carefully who those people were.
She was not safe. She knew this. But she was managing, and managing was something she had been doing her whole life.
The laptop came from Sara.

They were at the market when Sara spotted it on a table of secondhand electronics — cracked along one side, priced at almost nothing because the seller had tried it and it wouldn't turn on. Sara had no interest in it. Tali stood in front of it for thirty seconds and then looked at Sara.
*"How much do you have?"*
*"That doesn't work,"* Sara said.
*"I know. How much do you have?"*
Sara bought it with the understanding that if Tali got it working, Sara got first use.

It took eleven days. The problem was a corroded connection she found by eliminating everything else — not guessing, observing. She had no soldering iron. She found one eventually at a stall in the market run by a man who repaired phone chargers and small appliances, who let her use his bench for an hour in exchange for helping him sort a box of tangled cables. He watched her work without comment. When she finished he said nothing, but the next time she passed his stall he nodded at her.
On the eleventh day the screen lit up.
Sara used it first, as agreed. Then Tali used it.

Getting online was its own problem. The building had no connection. A bakery two streets away had wifi — the password on a chalkboard for customers — and she went there most mornings, sat in the corner with the laptop, ordered nothing, and downloaded everything she could before they noticed her. Articles, books, pages of news, entire threads of argument — saved offline, to be read later on the rooftop where nobody could ask her to leave. The bakery owner tolerated her for three weeks before asking her to buy something or go. She went. She found a laundromat on the next street that advertised free wifi for customers and didn't check whether you actually had washing in the machines. She used that instead.

She had never had access to the whole world before. The whole world was louder than she had expected. Angrier. More afraid. She had grown up in a war and she had not expected to find, in the peaceful countries on the other side of the screen, so much fury — so much hatred aimed at strangers, so much careful deliberate effort to make people fear each other.

She read for weeks. Every language she knew and two more she taught herself. News and arguments and histories and stories — especially stories, because stories were where people told the truth about themselves when they thought no one important was listening.
And the more she read, the larger a question grew inside her.

She had spent years moving between broken people in broken places, carrying what one person had to the person who needed it. Drawing lines between needs and resources. It had always seemed obvious: the need is there, the resource is there, someone has to draw the line.
Why did so few people draw it?

The world had more food than it needed to feed everyone and people starved. It had more empty houses than homeless people and people slept in doorways. It had enough of almost everything and distributed almost none of it fairly — and nobody seemed able to explain why this was simply the law of things rather than a problem that could be fixed.

One night she sat on the rooftop with the cracked screen on her knees and the city below her and looked up at a sky full of stars that had been watching humans for longer than humans had been asking questions.
She asked out loud, because the question had grown too large to keep inside:
*"Why is it so easy to hurt someone you've never met, and so hard to help them?"*
No answer came. The stars said nothing. They never do.

But the question did not leave. It pressed against her ribs like something alive, like something that had been waiting a long time to be asked properly and was not going to let go now that it finally had been.

Three years had passed since she arrived in the city. She had turned twelve, then thirteen, then fourteen on the rooftop with no ceremony and no one who knew the date. Sara had left at eighteen — not dramatically, not with a goodbye speech, just one morning her room was empty and her few things were gone. She had found work in another city, or a way across another border, or something else entirely. Tali did not know. That was the nature of the lives they had been living — people arrived and people left and you learned not to hold too tightly.

She had kept going. The alterations woman still gave her work when there was work. The market stall man still let her use his bench occasionally. She had learned the city the way she had learned every place she had ever lived — its moods, its dangers, its small unexpected kindnesses. She was not comfortable. She was not safe in any permanent sense. But she was still here, which was the only measure that had ever mattered.
She was fourteen years old and she had a question she could not put down.
She was about to find out what it would cost her to answer it.

title: The Night Everything Changed
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: It happened the way most important things happen — without announcement, without ceremony, without any of the signs you would expect if you had been taught that important things arrive with thunder and light.
Tali was asleep on her mattress on the rooftop.

She had been awake late, as she often was, reading everything the cracked machine could show her. She had been reading about loneliness — there were studies, written by scientists in quiet universities, saying that loneliness had become one of the great illnesses of the age. Not the loneliness of being physically alone. The loneliness of feeling that nobody truly knows you. That you could disappear and the world would continue without a crease. That the things you feel most deeply, you have never said aloud to anyone, because there is nobody to say them to.
The scientists had numbers. Charts. Long careful sentences.
Tali had read their words and thought: *I know. I have known this since I was four years old. Why are you surprised?*
She fell asleep with the screen still glowing.
And something came.

She could not, afterward, say exactly what it was. She had no word for it that felt fully honest. Not a dream — she had had many dreams and knew what they felt like, and this was different. Not a vision, because she was not the kind of person who believed in visions. It was more like — a moment of absolute clarity. As if someone had cleaned a window she hadn't known was dirty, and now she could see through it properly for the first time.
She saw the world.

Not from above, not like a map. She saw it the way you see a face when you are close enough to notice the lines around the eyes, the tension in the jaw, the fear the person is trying to hide behind their expression. She saw the world's face.
And the world was in pain.

Not the pain of disaster — though there was disaster. The deeper pain. The pain of people who had forgotten how to reach each other. Who had been so hurt, so many times, by people they had tried to trust, that they had quietly stopped trying. Who sat in rooms full of other lonely people, all of them starving for the same thing, none of them able to ask for it.

She felt this — all of it — not as an idea but as a physical weight in her chest. The grief of the man on the bus that nobody looked at. The shame of the woman who had wanted to help the boy with the sign and hadn't known how. The fear of the child who had been taught to hate a face she had never seen.
She felt it all at once.
And then — in that same moment of clarity — she felt something else.

She felt how close it all was. How thin the wall was between all that loneliness and all that longing. How the grief of one person and the grief of the person beside them were so nearly identical that if either of them spoke first, everything might change.

She felt the connections that were not being made. The hands that were not being held. The words that were not being said. The million small moments every day, everywhere in the world, where one person could have looked at another and said: *I see you. I know. Me too.* And didn't.
She woke up.
The stars were still out. The city below was quiet. The broken machine lay beside her, its battery dead.
She sat up and stayed still for a long time.

She was not the same as she had been when she lay down. She could feel that. Something had shifted inside her the way ground shifts after rain — settled into a new arrangement, deeper and less likely to crack.
She knew three things she had not quite known before.
Not new things. Old things, suddenly visible.

**The first:** She could feel what the people around her were carrying underneath what they were showing. Not magic — she was careful with herself about this. It was what happened when you paid close attention for long enough. Her mother had had it. She had been watching her mother do it since she could remember. She had done a version of it herself since she was nine, moving through the camp knowing who needed what before they asked. The clarity she felt that night was not a gift arriving. It was a practice arriving at legibility — years of attention finally able to name itself.
She would use it more deliberately now.

**The second:** She could see, with uncomfortable clarity, when what someone was saying was not what they meant. Not the obvious lies. The deeper ones — the fears renamed, the wounds disguised as positions, the distance between what was being performed and what was actually there. She had noticed this her whole life without knowing how to use it. Now she understood: the gap between what was said and what was real was not an obstacle. It was a door. And the fear behind the performance was not the enemy. It was the wound that needed meeting.
**The third — and hardest:** She could see where the connections were missing.

This one she had been doing since she was nine years old. The family with medicine and the family who needed it. The person with a skill and the person who needed it. She had always thought of this as observation — noticing what was there. That night she understood it differently: it was also imagination. The ability to see not just what existed but what could exist. Not the wall. The door in the wall. Not the gap. The bridge.
She had been building bridges her whole life without a word for it.
Now she had words.
Now she would teach them.
She sat on the rooftop until the sky began to lighten.
Then she went downstairs, knocked on the door of the man on the second floor — the man who had said something ugly to her the week before, who she had avoided since — and asked if he needed anything.
He opened the door ready for a fight. He had been expecting one.
She asked again, quietly. She could feel the layer below his face now — the fear, the shame, the loneliness that had come out as cruelty because cruelty was the only language he had for pain.
He stared at her for a moment.
Then he told her. His sister was sick. He had no money. He had been shouting at everyone for a week because he didn't know what else to do.

Tali sat with him for an hour. She didn't fix the sister — she couldn't. But she knew a woman three streets over who had medicines she wasn't using. She knew a man on the fourth floor who had once been a doctor and might know what to do. She drew the lines between what existed and what was needed.
She asked for nothing in return.
She went back to the rooftop and sat down.
This, she understood, was going to be her life.

Not a life of grand gestures. Not speeches or marches or declarations. A life of paying attention, of sitting with people long enough to find out what they actually needed, and of drawing lines between those needs and the people who could answer them.
She looked out at the city.

She was fourteen years old. She had nothing — no money, no family nearby, no position, no power. She had a broken machine, a soldering iron, and three things she could feel and see and do that most people had forgotten.
It was, she thought, enough to start.

title: The First People
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: She did not go looking for them. They found her.
Or — more accurately — the need found them, and she happened to be in the right place to see it.
The first was Fatima.

Fatima was seventy-two years old, walked with a cane, and had lived in the building longer than anyone. She had been an engineer — had helped design the pipes and channels that brought water to this part of the city, forty years ago, when there was still a city worth designing for. She had watched her life's work get buried — first by a corrupt government that sold the water rights, then by the company that built over the old system without understanding what it had destroyed.
Now the district had water for a few hours a day, if it came at all. People queued at a single tap in the courtyard. Children got sick.

Fatima knew where the old pipes were. She had always known. She had the drawings in a folder under her bed, yellowed with age. She had tried, for years, to interest someone in them. Nobody had listened. She was old and she walked with a cane and the people with power were not in the habit of listening to old women who walked with canes.

Tali knocked on her door one afternoon because she had felt, passing it, a frustration so deep it was almost grief. Not anger. Something older. The particular pain of a person who has something to give and has been repeatedly told that nobody wants it.
She knocked. Fatima opened the door with the expression of someone who expected to be disappointed.
Tali said: *"You know how to fix the water, don't you?"*
Fatima stared at her for a long time.
Then she opened the door wider and said: *"Come in."*
The second was Carlos.

Carlos was nineteen, strong, and magnificently cynical. He had grown up in this city and watched it get worse every year and had decided that the only honest response to this was to expect nothing and be surprised by nothing. He fixed pipes for cash when there was work and went hungry when there wasn't and trusted nobody over the age of thirty.

Tali found him in the courtyard one afternoon, replacing a valve that had nothing wrong with it except that the man who owned the building wanted to charge residents for a repair that had already been made. She stood beside him and watched.
*"You know that's not broken,"* she said.
He looked at her. *"I know."*
*"So why are you fixing it?"*
*"Because I get paid whether it needs fixing or not."*

She felt the layer underneath — not greed, which would have been simple. Something more complicated. A person who had been told so many times that this is how the world works, that it has started to feel like physics. Inevitable. Not changeable. Just the way things are.

She said: *"There's something that actually needs fixing. The old water mains under the street. Fatima on the third floor knows where they are. If we could reach them, the whole district would have water every day."*
Carlos stared at her. *"Who's going to pay for that?"*
*"Nobody. That's the point."*
He laughed. Then he saw she wasn't laughing. He thought about it for a while.
*"What's in it for you?"* he asked.
*"The water comes back,"* she said.
He was quiet for a long moment. Then: *"Tell me more."*
The third was James.

James had lost the use of both legs in a war that had ended officially but continued unofficially in the way that wars always do — in the bodies of the men and women who carried them home. He lived in the basement with a collection of radios, a very large dog named Wallace, and a talent for communication that the military had trained and then wasted.

He had built a small network of people who talked to each other on old radio frequencies — not for any particular purpose, just because it was something to do and because he had found that people who couldn't reach each other were people who felt alone, and alone was the worst thing he knew how to feel.
Tali found him because Fatima knew he was there. She knocked on his door with Wallace barking on the other side.
When he opened it she said: *"I need someone who knows how to get many people moving in the same direction without telling them what to do."*
James looked at her for a moment. Then he said: *"How old are you?"*
*"Fourteen."*
*"That's very young to be organising things."*
*"I know. Do you want to help or not?"*
He let her in.

These three — an old engineer, a cynical young plumber, a man with no legs and a gift for connection — were not heroes. They were not exceptional people in the way that stories usually require. They were ordinary people with specific things to offer, who had been waiting without knowing it for someone to ask.
Tali asked.
Not because she had a plan. Because she could see what each of them had, and she could see what was needed, and the line between them was obvious if you were paying attention.
They sat on the rooftop that first evening — Fatima with her drawings, Carlos with his tools, James with Wallace asleep across his lap — and Tali explained what she had seen.
Not a vision. Not a prophecy. Just what she had observed.
The water was there. Under the street. All it needed was someone to clear the path to it.
Fatima said: *"I've been trying to tell people this for twenty years."*
Tali said: *"I know. This time it will be different."*
*"Because this time, instead of asking permission, we're just going to do it."*
Carlos laughed his cynical laugh. James's mouth moved in what might have been a smile. Fatima looked at Tali for a long time with the particular expression of someone deciding whether to hope again.
She decided yes.
They started the next morning.

title: Water
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: It took three weeks.

Three weeks of evenings spent underground — in a tunnel that ran beneath the street, that James had known about for years and Fatima had partly designed and Carlos could navigate by feel in the dark. Three weeks of digging and cutting and failing and trying again. Three weeks of Tali moving between them carrying tools, carrying information, sitting with each of them when they were ready to give up and asking the question that she had found, through experiment, worked better than any encouragement:
*"What do you need right now to keep going?"*
Not: *"You can do it."* Which was a comfort but not a plan.
Not: *"Think of the goal."* Which was true but not useful when your hands were bleeding and the tunnel smelled of old water and you hadn't slept properly in a week.
Just: *What do you need right now?*
Sometimes the answer was practical. A different tool. Another pair of hands. More light.
Sometimes the answer was: *I need someone to sit here with me for ten minutes.*
Tali sat.
On the twenty-second day, at half past eleven at night, Carlos put down his tool and said very quietly: *"I think that's it."*
They listened.
From somewhere deep in the old pipe, they heard water moving.

Fatima put her hand on the pipe and felt it — forty years of silence ending in a shudder against her palm. She didn't speak. She didn't need to. Tali could feel what was happening in the old woman's chest and chose not to look away from it. Some feelings are too large and too earned to be polite about.
The water came back to the district three days later.

Not with any announcement. Not with a ceremony or a photograph or a politician taking credit. One morning the taps ran, and the people who had been queueing at the single courtyard tap looked at each other in silence for a moment before someone started crying and then several other people started crying, because clean water from a tap is one of those things that you only understand the value of once you have lived without it.
Nobody knew who had done it.
Tali preferred it that way.

Word spread. Not loudly — quietly, the way important things spread. The way a smell travels on the wind. Someone would say to someone else: *there's a girl in the old building, she fixed the water, she might be able to help.* And that person would come, and Tali would listen to what they needed, and she would look for the line between what existed and what was needed, and sometimes she could draw it and sometimes she couldn't, but she always tried.
The man whose sister was sick found a doctor.
A family who had been living in one room found two more rooms in the building that had been sealed off and forgotten.

An argument between two families about a shared wall that had been going on for six years ended in a single afternoon when Tali sat with both of them separately, asked each of them what they were actually afraid of, and discovered that they were afraid of exactly the same thing. She put them in the same room and let them find that out for themselves.

She didn't solve everything. Many things she couldn't solve. She was fourteen and she had no money and no power and no way to stop a war or feed a city or find a mother who had vanished into a crowd three years ago. Her father was a photograph in a bag and her mother's voice saying his name in the dark. Not a person she knew. A shape of a person — the outline of someone who had chosen her name, who had pinned it above a bed in a foreign city and looked at it every morning, who might or might not still be alive somewhere in the world but who had, at least, been real. Had wanted her. Had known she was coming.
But she solved what she could. She drew the lines she could see. And slowly — so slowly that you couldn't measure it day to day, only month to month — the building became a different kind of place.
People spoke to each other. Not always. Not perfectly. But more than before.
People knew each other's names.

And in the space that this created — in the ordinary warmth of a group of people who had decided, without making any great announcement about it, to try looking out for each other — something began to grow that Tali did not have a name for yet.
She would find the name later.
For now, she only knew that the rooftop, which had been the loneliest place she had ever lived, was becoming something else.

title: Doubt
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: Thirty days after the night everything changed, Tali could not sleep.
She sat on the rooftop in the dark with her arms around her knees and asked herself the question she had been avoiding for a month:
*What if I am wrong?*
Not about the water — the water was real. Not about the man whose sister was sick, or the sealed rooms, or the argument about the wall. Those were real.

But about the larger thing. The thing she had felt that night when the clarity came. The sense of purpose. The conviction that she could feel other people's pain, see through the surface of their lies to the fear underneath, draw lines between things that seemed separate.

What if that was just — her? Just her own loneliness, mistaken for a mission? Just a child who had grown up without enough people looking after her, deciding to look after everyone else because it was the only way she knew how to feel less alone?
What if she was not the answer to anything?
What if she was just a fourteen-year-old girl on a rooftop with a cracked machine and a soldering iron, telling herself a story to survive?
She sat with this for a long time.
The cat that had adopted the rooftop came and sat beside her. It said nothing. Cats are like that. They will sit with you in the dark without pretending the dark isn't dark.
In the morning, Fatima found her still sitting there.
Fatima lowered herself carefully onto the plastic chair she had carried up from her flat and said: *"Tell me."*
Tali told her. All of it. The doubt. The fear of being wrong. The fear that everything she had done was smaller than it seemed and wouldn't last and wouldn't matter.
Fatima was quiet for a while.

Then she said: *"When I was thirty years old, I designed a water system. It served fifty thousand people. I gave three years of my life to it — my marriage, my sleep, my health. Then the government sold the rights to a private company and the company buried everything I had built. For thirty years I thought: what was the point? I might as well have done nothing."*
She paused.
*"Then a fourteen-year-old knocked on my door and asked if I knew how to fix the water."*
Tali looked at her.
*"Nothing I built was wasted,"* Fatima said. *"It was just waiting. Waiting for someone who still believed it was possible."*
She stood up, slowly, using her cane.
*"Doubt is not the enemy,"* she said. *"The enemy is stopping. Keep going. The doubt will come with you. That is fine. Doubt and keep going. It is the only honest way to do anything."*
She went back downstairs.
Tali sat for another hour. Then she went downstairs too.
She knocked on a door. She listened. She drew a line between what existed and what was needed.
She kept going.

title: The Others
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: They came, as the people who matter always come — not with fanfare, not on a schedule, but because the need was real and the need found them.

**David** was a pastor who had spent twenty years preaching to a congregation that listened on Sundays and forgot on Mondays. He had not lost his faith. He had lost his belief that his faith was doing anything. There is a difference, and it is a painful one.

He had been told about Tali by a man he had never met, who had been told by a woman he had never met, who had been told by someone who had drunk water from a tap in a building where water had not flowed for years.
He arrived with a Bible in one pocket and a phone in the other and a look on his face of someone who has made a decision and is not entirely sure it was the right one.
He sat with Tali for an afternoon. She asked him what he actually believed — not the official version, but the real one, underneath.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said: *"I believe that every person on earth matters. And I believe we have built a world that acts like they don't. And I don't know how to fix the gap between those two things."*
Tali said: *"I don't either. But I think the fixing starts with one person at a time."*
He thought about this. *"That's very slow."*
*"The problems are very large."*
*"So we just — help the person in front of us? And trust that it adds up?"*
*"I don't know if it adds up. I know it's the only thing that doesn't make things worse."*

He came back the next day. And the day after. He brought food, because his congregation gave generously when they understood who they were giving to. He brought his hands, which were large and useful. He brought his voice, which was the kind of voice that made people feel less afraid.

**Ananda** had walked away from everything — her career, her city, her old life — after spending ten years helping a company understand how people behaved, and then watching that company use the information to keep people frightened and addicted and spending money. She had been good at her job. She had been good at her job in the way that a person can be good at something that is slowly killing something inside them.
She arrived carrying nothing but a small bag and the particular stillness of someone who has stopped trying to perform being fine.

She had one skill that Tali needed: she understood, better than almost anyone alive, why people did the things they did. Not in a manipulative way — she was done with manipulation. In the way of someone who has looked very honestly at human beings for a long time and has arrived at compassion rather than contempt.
She could sit with someone and ask one question and find the thing underneath all the other things. The real wound. The one that everything else was growing from.
Tali could feel it. Ananda could name it. Together, they were more useful than either alone.

**Soraya** came from a country where women with ideas were considered a problem. She had spent fifteen years proving, with careful research and patient argument, that kindness was not weakness — that communities where people genuinely cared for each other were stronger, healthier, and more resilient than communities built on fear and competition. She had published papers that serious people had read and then failed to act on.
She was done with papers.

She wanted to do something that actually worked. She had heard — from someone who had heard from someone — about a building where people had started looking out for each other. About a girl who asked three questions and drew lines between people.
She came to see for herself.
She stayed.

**Li Wei** could not come in person. His land was sick — a river that fed his village had been poisoned by a factory upstream, and the poisoning had been allowed to continue because the people who owned the factory had more influence with the government than the people who drank the water. His daughter was ill. He had been told, by doctors and officials alike, that there was nothing to be done.
He sent a letter instead. It arrived through a chain of hands that Tali would never fully be able to trace.

The letter said: *I have proof of what is being done to us. I don't know what to do with it. I heard that you draw lines between what is and what is needed. The line I need drawn is between this proof and the people who should be made to see it. If you can draw that line, my daughter might live. I am not asking for a miracle. I am asking for someone to try.*
Tali read the letter three times.
Then she showed it to the others.
They started working on it that evening.

There were more. A young woman who had built tools to make people angry and wanted, now, to build tools that did the opposite. An old soldier who had spent years fighting and wanted to spend whatever time remained building. A scientist who had spent two decades measuring the damage being done to the natural world and was desperate to stop measuring and start repairing.
They were all different. Different countries, different beliefs, different languages, different ways of seeing the world and different wounds and different things they were good at.
But they all had one thing in common.
They were still asking: *What can I do?*
In a world that had largely stopped asking, this made them extraordinary.

The night they all sat together on the rooftop for the first time — seven of them, plus Wallace the dog — nobody made a speech. There was no ceremony. Fatima had brought bread. Carlos had found something to drink. James had carried his radio up in case it was useful.

Tali looked at all of them and felt — not for the first time, but more strongly than before — the strange and fragile thing that happens when people who have been carrying something alone discover that others have been carrying the same thing.
Relief.
Not the relief of a problem solved. The relief of no longer being alone with it.
*"What are we?"* David asked. Not critically — genuinely.
Tali thought about it.
*"We are people who draw lines,"* she said. *"Between what is broken and what could fix it. Between what someone has and what someone needs. Between people who should know each other and don't."*
*"That sounds simple,"* Carlos said.
*"It is simple. Simple is not the same as easy."*
He considered this. *"What do we call ourselves?"*
*"Nothing,"* Tali said. *"Names become walls. We are just people who do this. Anyone can do this. That is the whole point."*
They sat with that for a while.
Wallace put his head in Tali's lap. She scratched behind his ears.
The city hummed below them, indifferent and enormous and full of people who were, most of them, trying their best in the only ways they knew how.

*There is enough,* Tali thought. Not enough money, not enough time, not enough of what the world called power. But enough human beings who still cared. Enough skill, enough knowledge, enough love, scattered and unconnected and waiting.
All it needed was someone to draw the lines.

title: The Three Questions
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: Over the months that followed, people began to come to the rooftop with problems.

Not the kind of problems that governments are supposed to solve — though many of those were present too, lurking in the background like bad weather. Smaller problems. Immediate ones. The man who had not spoken to his brother in six years. The family whose landlord was threatening to throw them out. The young woman who had been given information at a medical appointment that she hadn't understood and was now terrified. The group of neighbours who wanted to plant vegetables in the empty lot down the street but couldn't agree on how to divide the space.
Tali listened to all of them.

She had developed, over time, a way of listening that she had never formally named but that the others had begun to notice and, quietly, to copy. It involved three questions — not always asked aloud, sometimes just held in the mind while the person was talking.
The first was: **What is the real pain?**

Not the argument. Not the complaint. Not the version of events the person has rehearsed so many times it has become a performance. Underneath all of that — what is the actual hurt? What did they lose? What are they afraid of? What do they need that nobody is giving them?

People rarely lead with the real pain. They lead with the surface — the money argument, the unfair decision, the thing someone said. The surface is real too, but it is a door, not a room. The room is behind it. Most people never get asked to open it.
Ask. Then be quiet. The answer, when it comes, is almost never what you expected.
The second was: **Who is not being seen?**

In any conflict, any problem, any room — there is always someone missing from the conversation. Not absent by accident. Absent because nobody thought to ask them. Because they are quiet, or powerless, or on the wrong side of the argument, or simply overlooked in the way that certain people are always overlooked.
That person almost always holds something important. A piece of information. A different angle. The thing that, once known, changes the whole shape of the problem.
Find them. Not to fix them or speak for them. Just to ask: *what do you see from where you are standing?*
Then listen.
The third was: **What can be done right now, with what we actually have?**

Not what could be done if circumstances were different. Not what should be done in a just world. What could be done today, with these hands, these people, this much time, this much money — which was often very little — and this particular, specific, limited set of things that existed and could be used.

This question was the hardest. It required letting go of the perfect solution in order to find the real one. It required a particular kind of honesty — looking clearly at what was actually available, rather than mourning what wasn't.

But it was also, in Tali's experience, the question that most often produced something. Not a solution — usually not a clean solution. But movement. A small shift. A door that hadn't been open before, now slightly open.

She began to teach these questions to the people who came. Not as a system, not as a method with a name and a set of rules. Just: *here is how I try to think about it. Try it yourself. See if it helps.*

Some people found it useful immediately. Others struggled. A few came back weeks later and said: *I tried the thing with the questions. It didn't work.* Tali asked them to describe what had happened, and usually it turned out that it had worked in ways they hadn't recognised, or that they had asked the questions but not been willing to hear the answers.

*"The questions are not hard,"* she told one man who had come back frustrated. *"The answers are hard. Because the answers usually ask something of us. They tell us something we need to do that we would prefer not to do. It is easier to say the method failed than to do the thing the method showed us."*
He thought about this for a long time. Then he went home and called his brother.

His brother picked up. They talked for two hours — badly at first, with long silences and old resentments surfacing like objects from the bottom of a stirred river. Then better. Not resolved. Not healed. But open, in a way it had not been open for six years.
The man came back the following week. He climbed to the rooftop, set a bag of fruit down beside Tali without a word, and sat for a while looking out at the city.
Tali didn't ask how the call had gone. She could tell.
Some things don't need words.

The three questions spread the way things spread in communities — not through announcement, but through use. Someone would try them and find them helpful and mention them to someone else. That person would try them and adapt them slightly for their own situation and pass them on in that adapted form.
Tali did not mind the adaptations. She had never thought she owned the questions. Nobody owns a question.

What she noticed — and what the others noticed, each in their own way — was that the questions had a consistent effect. Not a magical one. Not a transformative one in the grand sense. A practical one.
They slowed people down.
They made people look at the person in front of them more carefully.
They made people ask: *what does this person actually need?* rather than *what do I think they should want?*

And from that slowing down, from that looking more carefully, from that asking — small things happened. Small, real, lasting things. A dispute resolved. A need met. A person who had been invisible made visible. A wall with a door in it that nobody had found before.
Small things, multiplied across enough people and enough days, become the world.

title: What the Powerful Do
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: They had been quiet long enough to be noticed.

The water returning to the district had been noticed. The resolved disputes had been noticed. The growing number of people passing through the old building with problems and leaving with something — not always a solution, but a direction — had been noticed.
And some of what had been noticed did not like what it saw.

A working community is a threat to people who profit from a broken one. People who have clean water from a communal system do not pay extra for water from a private one. People who have each other do not need to buy the many things that are sold to fill the hole left by loneliness. People who ask *what can we do?* instead of *who is to blame?* are much harder to direct. Much harder to use.

The first sign was small. An official arrived one morning with papers claiming the building needed an inspection, and the inspection could not be done until certain fees were paid, and until the inspection was done the building's residents could not legally make alterations to the water system.

Fatima read the papers carefully. She had been dealing with officials for fifty years. She pointed out, politely, that the alterations in question had been made to pipes that existed before any of the laws cited in the papers, and that there was no provision in any of those laws for what they had done.
The official went away.
He came back a week later with different papers.
Fatima called a lawyer she had known for forty years, who came and read the papers and sent the official away again.
*"They'll keep coming,"* the lawyer said quietly, before he left.
*"I know,"* Fatima said.
*"What will you do?"*
*"Keep going."*
The second sign was louder.

A man with a website and a large following published an article claiming that the building was being used for activities that he described with words that were technically not accusations but were intended to function as accusations. He had no evidence for any of it — the article was built entirely out of suggestions and implications and the particular kind of language that is designed to make people afraid without saying anything that can be legally disproved.
Thousands of people shared it.

Some of the people who came to the rooftop stopped coming. Not because they believed the article — most of them didn't. But because it was easier not to be involved in something that had become complicated.
Carlos, who had a gift for a particular kind of cheerful fury, wanted to respond publicly.
Tali said no.
*"Why not?"* he demanded. *"The man is lying."*
*"I know."*
*"We should say so."*
*"If we respond, the story becomes the argument. The water disappears. The people we've helped disappear. All anyone sees is two sides shouting at each other. We've seen how that ends."*
*"So we just let him lie?"*
*"We keep doing the work. The work is the answer. The work is the only answer that matters."*
Carlos didn't like this. But he accepted it.
They kept working.
The third sign came in the form of a visit.
A man in a good suit came to the building one evening and asked to speak with Tali. He was polite. He was well-dressed. He had the particular manner of someone who is accustomed to being listened to.

He explained, calmly, that certain people — he did not name them — were concerned about the, he paused here to choose his word, *influence* that was growing around this building and this girl. He explained that these people were not hostile, but that they believed it would be in everyone's interest if this influence were directed more — another pause — *constructively.*
He had, he said, a proposal.

The proposal involved money — a significant amount — and a platform, and access to people in positions of power who could help. In exchange, Tali would work within certain structures, would coordinate her activities with certain organisations, would take guidance on — another pause — *messaging.*
Tali listened to all of it.
Then she asked: *"What problem are you trying to solve?"*
He was surprised by the question. He had expected acceptance or refusal, not redirection.
*"I'm sorry?"*
*"What is the actual problem you're trying to fix? Not the organisational concern. The human one. What is hurting that you want to help?"*
He was silent for a moment. He had not expected this.
Tali waited.

And she felt — with the clarity that had been sharpening in her for months — the layer beneath his manner. Beneath the suit, beneath the polite confidence, beneath the practiced language of people who were used to managing things: genuine unease. A man who had spent his career making large things work and had begun to wonder whether the large things were pointed in the right direction.
Not a villain. A person.

She said, more gently: *"If you want to help, help. You don't need to manage it. You don't need to own it. Come and sit with us. Learn the three questions. Go home and use them in the place where you actually live. That is what we do. That is all we do."*
He was quiet for a long time.
Then he stood up, thanked her, and left.
She did not know what he would do with what she had said.
That was not her part. Her part was to draw the line. What others did with it was theirs.

title: What Happens When You Stop
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: It started with her hands.

She noticed it one morning when she was fixing a lock on the door of the family on the first floor — the Osman family, mother and three children, who had been in the building for four months and whom Tali had slowly come to know the way she knew everyone, through small exchanges and careful observation. She was turning a screwdriver and her hand shook. Not violently. Just a tremor, there and gone. She finished the job. She said nothing.

The next day her hands shook again. And she was cold in a way that had nothing to do with the weather, which was warm. And there was a pain behind her eyes that had been there for a week without her fully admitting it.

She had been ignoring her body for a long time. She had learned this the way she had learned most things — from necessity. In the years of running and surviving there was no space to be unwell, and so she had developed the habit of pushing symptoms to the back of her mind and continuing. The habit had served her. It had also, apparently, accumulated a debt.
She was on the rooftop that afternoon when her legs went.

Not dramatically. She sat down suddenly on the concrete because standing had become too much, and then she lay down because sitting was too much, and then she was looking at the sky and the sky was doing something strange, tilting slightly, and she thought with the last clear part of her mind: *this is what happens when you stop.*
She did not know how long she was there before Fatima found her.

Fatima had come up to the rooftop to check on her — she did this occasionally, without making anything of it, in the way of someone who has decided to keep an eye on a person without being asked. She found Tali flat on the concrete, eyes open, not quite conscious.
She did not panic. She was seventy-four years old and had seen worse.
She got down on one knee — her bad knee, which cost her — and put her hand on Tali's forehead.
*"You have a fever,"* she said. *"A serious one. How long?"*
Tali tried to say *I don't know.* What came out was not words.
Fatima sat down beside her on the concrete and said, to nobody in particular: *"Stubborn child."*
Then she called down to the Osman family below.
What happened next was something Tali had never experienced before and would not know how to describe for a long time afterward.
People took care of her.

Not abstractly. Not from a distance. The Osman mother — whose name was Hana, and who had three children and more competence than the situation she had been handed — came upstairs with water and a cloth and the particular efficiency of a woman who had nursed children through fevers in worse conditions than this. She assessed Tali the way Tali assessed broken things: quickly, without drama, looking for what was actually wrong rather than reacting to the surface.
*"When did she last eat a proper meal?"* Hana asked Fatima.
Fatima thought about it. *"I don't know. I don't think she does either."*
Hana's expression said several things at once without words. She went downstairs and came back with food.

Carlos appeared at the top of the stairs at some point — she heard his voice before she saw him, arguing with someone she couldn't identify about something she couldn't follow. Then he was there, and he sat against the low wall and stayed, not doing anything in particular, just present in the way that Carlos expressed concern, which was never directly.

James sent a message through the network asking if anyone had medical training. A woman two streets away responded. She arrived within an hour, examined Tali, and said the words Tali had been hiding from herself for weeks: malnourished, exhausted, mildly dehydrated, a fever that was the body's announcement that it had been running on nothing for too long and had finally filed a formal complaint.
*"Rest,"* the woman said. *"Real rest. Not lying down while your mind works. Rest."*
*"There are things—"* Tali started.
*"There are always things,"* the woman said. *"They will wait. You will be no use to anyone if you break."*
She slept for most of three days.

She woke in intervals to find different people on the rooftop — always someone there, never making a fuss about it, just present. Hana's youngest child had apparently decided the rooftop was interesting and needed to be explored, and Hana had let her, and so Tali woke at one point to find a three-year-old sitting beside her mattress examining the soldering iron with intense concentration.
*"Don't touch that,"* Tali said. Her voice came out as a croak.
The child looked at her. *"Why?"*
*"It gets very hot. It will hurt you."*
The child considered this with the seriousness that three-year-olds bring to important information. Then she put the soldering iron down and picked up a bolt instead.
*"That one is fine,"* Tali said. And went back to sleep.
On the fourth day she sat up and ate a full meal for the first time in longer than she could honestly say.
Fatima sat with her while she ate. Neither of them spoke for a while.
Then Fatima said: *"You know what the real pain is, don't you. The one you never ask yourself about."*
Tali looked at her.
*"You ask everyone else. You never ask yourself. What do you need, Tali? Not what does the building need, not what does the district need. You."*
Tali was quiet for a long time.

She had not been asked this before. She had not asked it of herself. It had not seemed relevant — there was always something more urgent, always someone whose need was more immediate, always the next broken thing waiting.
She thought about it honestly, for the first time.

What she needed was ordinary. Unremarkable. The kind of thing that billions of people had and barely noticed: enough to eat. Enough sleep. Someone who knew her name and would notice if she disappeared.
Not a mother. She couldn't have that. Not yet. Maybe not ever.
But something.
*"I don't want to need things,"* she said finally. *"It makes you vulnerable."*
*"Yes,"* Fatima said. *"That's what being alive is."*
They sat with that for a while.
Below them the city went about its business, indifferent and enormous. On the rooftop, a three-year-old was building something out of bolts and pieces of wire that only she understood the purpose of.
*"What is she making?"* Tali asked.
Fatima looked. *"I have no idea. But she's been at it for two hours."*

Tali watched the child work. The total concentration. The complete unselfconsciousness. The absolute conviction that what she was building mattered, regardless of whether it would ever make sense to anyone else.
Something loosened in Tali's chest.

She was fourteen years old. She had been surviving since she was born. She had spent three years in this city asking everyone around her what they needed and drawing lines between their needs and the people who could meet them.
She had not once asked what she needed.
She was asking now.
The answer, when it came, was quieter than she expected:
*To still be here. To keep going. To not do it alone.*
