She looked at Fatima. At the child with the bolts. At the rooftop that had been only a place to sleep and had become, without her quite noticing, something else.
She was not alone.
She had not been alone for a long time.
She had just been too busy to notice.

title: What Spreads
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: The three questions spread the way a fire spreads in dry grass — not because anyone carried them deliberately, but because the conditions were right and the spark was real.

David took them back to his congregation. He stopped preaching at people and started asking them. What is the real pain in this community? Who is not being seen? What can we do this week, with what we actually have? His congregation shrank at first — some people come to church to be told what to believe, and questions make them uncomfortable. Then it grew again, because the people who stayed started doing things, and the things they did brought other people who also wanted to do things.

Ananda took them into her work with people who were struggling — people who had lost their way, who were in the long slow process of deciding whether to stay in the world. She found that the questions did something the usual approaches did not: they turned the person's attention outward, briefly, from their own pain. Not to ignore the pain — to find a place where the pain could be made useful. A person who is needed by someone else has a reason to keep going. She started teaching the questions to others who did the same work she did.

Soraya refined them into something she could teach in a day to groups of strangers. She travelled with nothing but a notebook and a change of clothes, sitting in community halls and school rooms and the back rooms of places of worship, in languages she spoke and languages she didn't, with a translator beside her or sometimes without. She found that the questions crossed languages easily, because the human realities they pointed to did not change between languages.

Carlos fixed things. He went on fixing things. But now he noticed, while he worked, who was not being seen. He found himself having conversations with people he would previously have treated as simply the problem to be solved, and discovering that they were not simple. He did not become softer, exactly. He became more useful. Which for Carlos was the same thing.

James stayed on his radio, but his network grew, and the things the network carried changed. Less complaint, more information. More: *does anyone know someone who can do this?* More: *there is a family in this street who need that, does anyone have that?* He became, without particularly intending to, a kind of living library of who had what and who needed it. He could not have said when this happened. It happened the way most things happen — gradually, and then as if it had always been true.

Fatima drew blueprints. She was always drawing blueprints. New ones, now — plans for what could be, rather than records of what had been. She was seventy-two years old and she drew blueprints with the urgency of someone who knows they have a limited number of mornings left and intends to use each one.
And Tali?

Tali kept doing what she had always done. She listened. She asked the three questions, silently or aloud. She drew lines between what was broken and what could fix it, between what someone had and what someone else needed, between people who should know each other and didn't.

She did not become famous. She did not try to. She had seen, very clearly, what happened when one person became the face of a thing — how the thing stopped being about the work and started being about the person, how people came to follow rather than to act, how the whole fragile mechanism of people helping each other got reduced to watching someone else do it.
She did not want followers.
She wanted more people asking the three questions.

She wanted the questions in every language, in every house, in every place where people were trying to understand each other or failing to. She wanted them so common, so ordinary, so unremarkable, that no one would remember where they had come from.
Let the questions spread, she thought. Let the questions be everyone's.
Let my name, in time, mean nothing.
Let the work mean everything.

title: What This Book Is For
part: PART ONE: THE WORLD BEFORE TALI
paragraphs: You have reached the end of this part of the story.
It is not the end of the story. The story continues — in the next volume, and the one after that, and in the lives of the people you have read about, which are still being lived.
But this is the place to stop and say what this book is actually for.
Not to entertain you, though I hope it has.
Not to inspire you, though I hope it has done that too.
This book is a set of instructions.
Simple instructions, for a complicated world.
**The First Question: What is the real pain?**
The next time you are in a conflict — with a family member, a neighbour, a colleague, a stranger — stop before you defend your position or attack theirs.
Ask yourself: what is the real pain underneath this? Not the words. Not the stated disagreement. The pain that is driving it.
Then ask them: *what is it that you actually need?*
Not sarcastically. Not as a tactic. As a real question.
And then listen to the answer.

This is harder than it sounds. The answer is sometimes something you can help with. Sometimes it is something you cannot help with but can acknowledge. Sometimes it will change the way you see the whole situation. It will almost never be what you expected.
**The Second Question: Who is not being seen?**
Look around whatever situation you are in. At the meeting. On the street. In your family. In your community.
Who is silent? Who is absent? Whose perspective is missing from this conversation?
Find that person. Not to fix them or save them. To ask them: *what do you see, from where you are standing, that we might be missing?*
They almost always know something that nobody else knows, because nobody else has been standing where they are standing.
**The Third Question: What can I do right now, with what I have?**
Not when things are better. Not when you have more time, more money, more certainty.
Right now. With these hands. In this place.

Something small. A check-in message to someone who is struggling. An hour of time offered to a neighbour who needs practical help. A conversation you have been avoiding because you are not sure how it will go.
Small things, done consistently, by enough people, across enough time, are how the world changes.
This is not a comfortable truth. We would prefer the large gesture, the single decisive action, the one conversation that fixes everything. These rarely happen and rarely last.
The small thing, done today, and again tomorrow, and again the day after — this lasts.
**The One Thing to Remember**
You do not have to be extraordinary.
You do not have to be brave in the dramatic sense. You do not have to stand up in front of crowds or walk into danger or sacrifice anything large.
You have to be willing to look.
At the person in front of you. At what they actually need. At what you actually have that could be useful.
And then do something.
Anything.
The world does not need more people waiting to be ready.
It needs more people beginning.
*Begin.*
*You already have everything you need.*

*The questions are:*
*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now?*

*Ask them today.*
*Ask them tomorrow.*
*Keep asking.*

*That is the whole book.*
*That is the whole work.*
*That is enough.*
**END OF PART ONE**
*Part Two: The Gathering Storm — in which what they have built is tested, and tested again, and what survives the testing turns out to be stronger than anyone expected.*

title: What Gets Noticed
paragraphs: There is a moment in the life of any real thing when it stops being invisible.
Not because it has changed. Because it has grown large enough that the people who benefit from invisibility can no longer pretend not to see it.
For Tali and the people on the rooftop, that moment came on a Wednesday morning in March, twelve months after the water came back.
A journalist arrived.

She was young — perhaps twenty-five, not long out of university — and she had the look of someone who had chosen her profession because she still believed that the truth, properly told, could change something. This belief had not yet been beaten out of her. She was, in that sense, dangerous.

Her name was Nadia. She had heard about the building through the chain of people who had heard about the building — the chain that had, by now, stretched across three cities and two countries and one international border that was not supposed to be crossable but apparently was, for the right information.
She had a recorder and a notebook and a list of questions.
Tali sat with her for an afternoon.

She answered every question honestly. She said what they did and how they did it and why. She said what had worked and what had failed. She said that she was fourteen — now fifteen — and that she had no special qualifications and no funding and no plan beyond the three questions and the work each day.
Nadia wrote all of this down.
Then she asked: *"What do you want people to take from this?"*
Tali thought for a long time.

*"I want them to go home and ask their neighbour what they need. That's it. Not to write about us. Not to come here. To go home and look at the person who lives closest to them — the one they have walked past a hundred times without really seeing — and ask what they need."*
Nadia looked up from her notebook. *"That's a very small request for someone who has done what you've done."*

*"The small things are the only things that last,"* Tali said. *"Grand gestures fade. Movements become institutions. Institutions become the thing they were built to replace. But a person who has learned to ask the right questions — that person carries it with them forever. That doesn't fade."*

The article Nadia wrote was read by a significant number of people. Not millions. Tens of thousands. But they were, in many cases, the right tens of thousands — people who were already trying to do something and needed a shape for what they were doing. People who were sitting with the same questions Tali had been sitting with and had not found anyone else who was asking them.
They wrote to the address Nadia included at the end of the article.
The letters came from forty-one countries.

title: Li Wei's Daughter
paragraphs: Three months after the article, they finally drew the line for Li Wei.

His daughter's name was Mei. She was eight years old. She had been sick for two years — not dramatically sick, not the kind of sick that arrives suddenly and demands immediate action, but the slow grinding kind. Low energy. Recurring infections. The particular pallor of a child whose body is fighting something it should not have to fight.

The river that ran through Li Wei's village had been poisoned — slowly, steadily, for years — by a factory upstream that processed chemicals and discharged waste into the water when the inspectors were not watching, and sometimes when they were. The inspectors had been watching less frequently in recent years, because the factory's owners had developed a relationship with the people who decided how frequently inspectors watched.

Li Wei had proof of this. He had been collecting it for years — photographs, water samples tested at his own expense, records of the discharge dates cross-referenced with the inspection schedules, testimonies from other farmers written down in careful detail. He had a folder three centimetres thick.

He had sent copies to the regional government. To the national government. To three newspapers. To an environmental organisation. To a law firm that advertised itself as specialists in exactly this kind of case.
Nothing had happened.

Not because no one read what he sent. Some of them did. But the factory employed two thousand people and contributed significantly to the regional economy and had lawyers on retainer who were very skilled at turning a clear situation into a complicated one. And Li Wei was one farmer. One farmer, however determined, is a manageable problem.
What Li Wei needed was not more proof. He had proof. He needed the proof to reach people who could not be managed.

Soraya found them. She had spent three months, since receiving Li Wei's letter, mapping the networks of people who had both the will and the position to make the right kind of noise. Not politicians — politicians could be managed. Journalists with specific audiences. Scientists whose names carried weight in the right circles. Lawyers in other countries whose firms had no connection to the factory's lawyers and no reason to be careful.
She assembled twenty-three of them.

Ananda translated the materials — not the language, but the human reality of them. She took Li Wei's careful factual documentation and wove through it the story of Mei. Not manipulatively. Honestly. This is the child. This is what is happening to her. This is what the documents show. These are the same thing. Do not let them be separated in your mind.
James sent it through his network with a subject line that simply said: *A child is sick. Here is why. Here is the proof. What can you do?*
The twenty-three people did what they could do.

Not all of it was decisive. Some of it was slow. One of the journalists wrote a piece that was quietly buried by an editor who had his own relationships to protect. Two of the lawyers sent letters that went unanswered for months. The environmental organisation published the data on a website that was read mainly by people who already knew the problem existed.
But three things landed.

A scientist in another country replicated Li Wei's water tests independently and published the results in a journal that was read by people who made decisions about international trade agreements. The factory exported goods. The goods had to meet certain standards. Suddenly there were people with power over the factory's future who had a reason to care about what went into the river.

A lawyer in a third country filed a civil suit on behalf of the village — not in Li Wei's country, where it would have been managed away, but in the country where the factory's parent company was registered. The suit was complicated and slow and expensive. A small crowdfunding campaign, sent through James's network, raised enough to keep it alive.

And one of the journalists — a woman who had been covering environmental stories for twenty years and had the particular doggedness of someone who has been frustrated by this exact problem a hundred times and has not yet stopped — found the inspection records. The real ones. The ones that showed when inspections had been scheduled and when they had been mysteriously rescheduled and what the inspectors had written in their reports and what had been changed in the reports before they were filed.
She published them.
The factory's owners tried to bury this too. They were experienced at burying things.
This time, too many people were watching.

The discharge stopped. It stopped first because the trade agreement pressure made it economically necessary, and then — more slowly, more genuinely — because the factory's workers, many of whom lived near the same river and drank the same water, had read the reports and had their own thoughts about it.

Mei did not recover overnight. Her body had been carrying this for two years and two years cannot be undone in a week. But the water cleared. Slowly. Month by month. And with it, gradually, her colour came back.
Li Wei sent a letter. It was not long.
*She ran across the field today. The whole field. Without stopping.*
*Thank you for drawing the line.*
Tali read it on the rooftop, alone, in the early morning. She read it twice. Then she folded it carefully and put it in her pocket, where she kept the things that mattered.
Then she went downstairs to start the day.

title: The Man in the Good Suit Returns
paragraphs: He came back four months after his first visit.

This time he did not wear the suit. He wore ordinary clothes — the kind that suggested he had thought about what to wear and decided that wearing less impressive things was, in this context, the more honest choice. Tali noticed this. She noticed most things.
He sat down across from her on the rooftop and said: *"I tried the questions."*
She waited.

*"I went home after I left here. I have a team at work — twelve people. I have managed them for six years. I thought I knew what they needed. I asked the first question. About the real pain." He paused.* "I did not know what any of them were carrying. Not one of them. I have sat in rooms with these people for six years and I had no idea."
*"What did you find?"* Tali asked.

*"Three of them are afraid of losing their jobs. Two of them are caring for sick parents and have never mentioned it. One of them has been trying to solve a problem for eighteen months that two other team members could solve immediately — nobody knew, because nobody asked." He stopped. "I have been managing output for six years. I have not managed people once."*
He was quiet for a moment.

*"I asked the second question. Who is not being seen. There is a woman on my team who has been there longer than anyone. She has never been promoted. Nobody — including me — had ever asked her why she hadn't applied for promotion. I asked her."*
*"What did she say?"*

*"She said nobody had ever suggested she was the kind of person who got promoted. She said she had accepted this as a fact." He looked at his hands. "It is not a fact. It was an assumption that everyone shared because nobody questioned it."*
*"And the third question?"*

*"That one is harder. What can I do right now, with what I have." He looked at her. "I have quite a lot of what the world calls power. I have never thought about what to do with it that is actually useful. I have thought about how to increase it. I have thought about how to protect it. I have not thought about what it is for."*
Tali said nothing. Sometimes the most useful thing is silence.

*"I would like,"* he said carefully, *"to learn how to think about that. I'm not asking to join something or fund something or put my name on something. I am asking if you would talk to me, occasionally, about how to use what I have more honestly."*
Tali looked at him for a long time with the seeing that had been sharpening in her for two years now.

What she saw: a man at the midpoint of his life who had been successful by every measure he had been taught to use, and had arrived at a place of deep unease that success by those measures could not touch. Not a bad man. A man who had been swimming in one direction for so long that he had forgotten to ask where he was going.
She said: *"Come on Thursdays. We all eat together on Thursdays. Bring something to contribute to the meal. Then stay and listen. Not to learn — to participate. There's a difference."*
He nodded.
He came the following Thursday. He brought bread — good bread, the kind that takes time to make, which told Tali something about how he had spent his week.
He sat at the edge of the group and listened.
He came back the Thursday after that, and the one after that.

He did not transform. Transformation is a story we tell about change because gradual change is harder to narrate. What happened was slower and more real: he began, degree by degree, to see differently. To ask differently. To use the considerable things he had access to in directions that were pointed at what was needed rather than at what was safe.
He never became a different person. He became a more honest version of the person he had always been. That is the most that can be asked of anyone.

title: The Weight That Stays
paragraphs: A year after the water came back, a woman arrived on the rooftop who changed what Tali understood about the three questions.
Her name was Mira. She was in her fifties. She climbed the stairs slowly, sat down on the concrete without asking permission, and said nothing for a long time.
Tali waited. She had learned that waiting was often more useful than asking.
Eventually Mira said: *"My son died eight months ago. He was seventeen. He survived the war. He did not survive what came after it."*
She said it the way people say things they have said many times — not because it gets easier with repetition, but because they have learned to say the words without the words destroying them.

Tali did not ask what had happened. She did not ask the three questions. There was no wound to diagnose here, no forgotten person to find, no line to draw. There was only a woman who had lost her child, and the particular gravity of that loss, which does not respond to questions.
She sat with her.
That was all. She sat and did not look away and did not try to fix it.

Mira came back the following week. And the week after. She never said much. She drank tea and sat and after a while went home. The others on the rooftop learned, without being told, to let her be — not to ignore her, but not to press.

After three months she started talking. Not about her son — about small things. The city. The food. What she had done before the war, which was cook. One Thursday she brought a pot of something she had made and put it down in the middle of the rooftop and said nothing. They ate it. It was the best thing anyone had eaten on that rooftop.
She came back the next Thursday with something else.

Tali watched this happen and understood something the three questions had not fully shown her: not every problem has a solution. Some things cannot be fixed. The only thing you can offer, in those cases, is presence. A place where the person does not have to pretend that the unfixable thing did not happen.
That is not nothing.
It is, in many cases, everything.
She thought about this for weeks.

The three questions pointed toward repair. Ask what the wound is, find who is unseen, do what can be done. The whole logic of the questions was the logic of a person who believes that things can be made better if approached honestly.
But Mira's wound was not approachable. It could not be made better. Her son was gone and would not come back and no question asked honestly would change that.
What the questions could not do — what no question could do — was undo. They could not restore. They could not reach back through time and return what had been taken.

Tali had built her practice around connection. But the deepest wound was not disconnection. The deepest wound was loss. And loss was not a disconnection that could be reconnected. It was an absence that remained an absence.

The questions worked in the presence of absence. They did not make the absence smaller. They made the person carrying it less alone with it. That was different. That was enough. But it was important to be clear about what it was and what it was not.
She added something to her notebook that evening. Not a fifth question. A clarification:

*The questions are for when something can be done. When nothing can be done, put down the questions. Sit down. Stay. That is the whole practice for that situation. Do not mistake presence for passivity. Presence is the hardest thing.*

title: The Girl Who Didn't Know Her Own Name
paragraphs: Eight months after the article, a girl arrived on the rooftop who changed the way Tali understood what she was doing.

Her name was — she said she didn't have one. This was not true in the literal sense; she had a name on paper. But she said she didn't have one because the name she had been given belonged to a version of herself that she was trying to leave behind.

She was sixteen. She had grown up in a city Tali had never visited, in a family that had been kind to her in the ways it knew how to be kind and harmful to her in the ways it didn't know were harmful. She had done what a great many sixteen-year-olds with access to the internet did: she had gone looking for herself online, in the communities and conversations and spaces where people like her might be found.

She had found communities that understood part of her. She had also found communities that understood part of her and then used that understanding to draw her further and further from everything else. Communities that were very skilled at locating the wound — the real pain, as Tali would have said — and then explaining the wound in a way that required an enemy.

She had spent two years inside one of those communities. She had said things she was ashamed of. She had believed things she no longer believed. She had lost friends. She had hurt people. Not with violence — with the particular cruelty of a young person who has been handed a comprehensive explanation of the world and is wielding it without fully understanding what it does.

She had found her way out slowly and at some cost, and she had read the article about the rooftop, and she had travelled for three days on very little money to get here, and now she was sitting in front of Tali with the expression of someone who does not know whether to expect judgment or pity and is bracing for both.
Tali said: *"What do you need?"*
Not: *"What did you do?"* Not: *"Why did you believe those things?"* Not: *"How could you?"*
Just: *"What do you need?"*
The girl stared at her. *"I don't know."*
*"That's all right. We can start there."*

They talked for three hours. Tali asked the questions and listened and asked more questions. She felt, in the girl across from her, a tangle so dense it was hard to find the thread. Shame and anger and genuine grief and a need to belong that had been so strong and so unmet for so long that she had accepted a belonging that required her to be less than she was.
Tali did not absolve her. That was not hers to give. The people the girl had hurt were not on this rooftop.

But she also did not condemn her. Because condemnation was not what was needed. What was needed was exactly what the girl had not found in the community that had taken her in: someone who was willing to see her fully — all of it, the damage and the potential and the wound underneath both — and not look away.
She stayed for two weeks.

She was useful in practical ways — she was good with her hands, she helped Carlos with several repair jobs, she helped James with the radio network in ways that his older equipment couldn't manage. She was also, more importantly, useful in a way she hadn't expected: several people who came to the rooftop during those two weeks had been through similar experiences to hers, and the things she said to them — not as advice, but as someone who had been there — reached those people in ways that nothing Tali or the others said could have reached.
She left with a name she had given herself. She chose it carefully, consulted the people on the rooftop who had become, briefly, the nearest thing to a community she had trusted in years.
She chose the word for *beginning* in a language that was not her own, because she said she wanted to be reminded every time someone called her name that she was not finished yet.
She was not the last person to arrive broken and leave carrying something.
She was not the most broken, or the most changed.
She was simply one person who came looking and was looked at in return.
That is all. That is everything.

title: What Tali Understood, Finally
paragraphs: Two years after the night everything changed, Tali sat on the rooftop on a morning in early summer and understood something she had been circling for a long time.

She had been trying to understand what they were doing. Not in the practical sense — she knew what they were doing. She was trying to understand what it *was*. What to call it. Whether it was enough to call it anything.

She had resisted every name people tried to give it. Movement. Organisation. Community. Philosophy. Those words all described things that had leaders and structures and eventually, in her experience, walls.

She had resisted calling it a method, because methods suggested that the same approach worked for every situation, and it didn't. The three questions were not a method. They were more like a direction. Point yourself at the real pain. Look for who isn't being seen. Act with what you have.

She had resisted calling it a belief, because belief suggested something you held, and what they were doing felt more like something that held them — something that kept choosing them as much as they chose it.
She sat with this for a long time.
And what she arrived at, finally, on that summer morning, was this:
It was not a thing at all.
It was a practice.

Like breathing — not dramatic, not requiring a name or a monument, simply necessary. The practice of paying attention to the person in front of you. The practice of asking what they actually need rather than deciding for them. The practice of looking for who isn't in the room. The practice of acting with what you have instead of waiting for better conditions.

These were not new. Every tradition that had ever tried to make human beings better at being human had arrived at some version of them. The details were different. The clothing was different. The names given to the force that called people toward this practice were wildly different.
But the practice itself — *look, listen, act, keep going* — was as old as the first time one human being sat with another who was suffering and did not walk away.
They had not invented anything.
They had remembered something.
That was all. That was sufficient.

She looked out over the city. It was not healed. It was damaged and complicated and full of people who were doing their best in ways that sometimes made things better and sometimes made them worse. The water ran in the pipes. The questions were travelling. Mei was running in a field somewhere she had never seen. Her mother was out there somewhere. That had to be enough.
Tali was sixteen years old.
She was a person who paid attention, and looked for what was needed, and drew lines between what was broken and what could fix it.

She did not know yet what the next years held. She did not know what would be asked of her. She did not know how many things would fail, how many times she would doubt, how many nights she would sit on this rooftop wondering if the work was worth the cost.
She knew she would keep going.
Not from certainty. Not from faith in any particular direction. From the plain, stubborn, unglamorous knowledge that stopping was worse.
From the memory of a woman who had kept running with her daughter on her back through a city that was falling, because the alternative was to stop running.

From the feeling, which she had learned to trust, that when you are doing something real — something that meets a real need, something that sees a real person, something that acts with real hands on a real problem — you are in the right place.
Even if the right place is hard.
Especially then.
From below, someone called her name — one of the neighbours, probably, needing something fixed.
She stood up. Stretched. Looked at the city one more time.
Then she went down to breakfast.

title: A Letter to the Reader
paragraphs: You are the reason this book exists.
Not you specifically — though yes, you specifically. You, reading this now, in whatever country, in whatever language, at whatever hour and in whatever circumstance brought this book into your hands.
We live in a world that is very skilled at making people feel small.
Small in the face of large problems. Small in the face of powerful systems. Small in the face of a hatred that seems too old and too deep to be touched by anything one person could do.
This book is an argument against that feeling. Not a denial of it — the problems are large and the systems are powerful and the hatred is old. But an argument that the smallness is a lie.
You are not small.

You are connected to every other person alive by chains of need and gift that are so intricate and so old that no government has ever been able to fully map them or fully break them. The woman who fed your grandparent during a hard year. The teacher who said the right thing to the child who became a person who helped the person who eventually helped you. The stranger on a road somewhere who stopped and asked if you were all right.

These chains are not visible. They are not measured. They do not appear in any ledger. But they are the actual substance of human civilisation — more real, more durable, more important than any of the structures built on top of them.
You are part of these chains.

Every time you look at someone — really look, past the surface — and ask what they need, you strengthen them. Every time you find the person in the room who isn't being seen and give them your attention, you strengthen them. Every time you act with what you have instead of waiting for better conditions, you strengthen them.

You will not see most of what your actions cause. The chains are too long and too indirect. A thing you do today may matter to someone you will never meet, in a time you will not live to see. This is not a reason to do nothing. It is precisely the reason to do something.
This is what Tali learned on the rooftop.
Not in one revelation, not in one night of clarity, but slowly, through the ordinary work of paying attention and acting and failing and continuing.

She learned that connection is not a resource that runs out when you give it. It multiplies. The more you see other people clearly, the more capable you become of seeing them. The more you act to help, the more you notice what needs helping. The more you look for the person not being seen, the more you find them everywhere.
This is the quiet miracle at the centre of this story.
Not that one girl on a rooftop changed the world. She didn't change the world. The world is still complicated and damaged and full of people hurting each other.
But she changed what was possible in her reach. And the people in her reach changed what was possible in their reach. And those people changed what was possible in theirs.
This is how it works.
This has always been how it works.
Go home.
Or stay where you are — you may already be home.
Look at the person nearest to you.
Ask what they need.
Listen.
Then act.
That is the whole instruction.
Everything else is detail.

*The story of Tali continues in Part Three: The Long Work — in which everything that has been built is tested by the things that cannot be fixed, and the people who built it discover what they are actually made of.*
**THE END OF PART TWO**

*The only condition: use it to help.*

title: The Man Who Wanted to Own It
paragraphs: He was not the first person to arrive wanting to own something that belonged to nobody.
He was a younger man, with the particular energy of someone who has recently discovered a cause and has not yet learned the difference between enthusiasm and possession.

His name was Rafi. He was twenty-six. He had read about the rooftop in an article that had been shared widely, and he had come to the city specifically to find it, and he had spent three days asking around before someone pointed him to the building.
He arrived with a notebook and a phone and the expression of someone who expects to be impressed.
Tali was fixing a pipe joint on the second floor when he found her. He stood in the doorway and said: *"You're Tali? The one who started all this?"*
*"I live here,"* she said. *"Hand me that wrench."*
He handed it to her, confused. She tightened the joint, checked it, stood up.
*"I've been following what you're doing,"* he said. *"It's extraordinary. The three questions, the water system, Li Wei's river, the way it's spreading — I want to help you scale it."*

Tali looked at him. She felt, with the clarity that had been sharpening in her for two years, what was underneath his words. Not malice. Genuine excitement. And underneath the excitement — something she recognised because she had felt versions of it herself in darker moments — the need to matter. To be part of something that meant something.
*"Scale it how?"* she said.

He opened his notebook. He had plans — detailed ones, actually well-thought-out ones. A website. A training programme. A network of certified facilitators who would teach the three questions in structured workshops. A funding model. Partnerships with organisations in twelve countries.
He talked for twenty minutes. He was articulate and passionate and clearly intelligent.
Tali listened to all of it.
Then she said: *"What happens to the person who can't afford the workshop?"*
He paused. *"We could offer scholarships—"*
*"What happens to the question when it gets a certificate attached to it?"*
Another pause.
*"What happens when the organisation that funds you decides it wants a say in what the questions are?"*
He was quiet now.

*"The questions work,"* Tali said, *"because they belong to nobody. The moment they belong to someone — to a brand, to an organisation, to a methodology with your name on it — they stop being questions and start being a product. Products need customers. Customers need to be sold to. And the people who most need these questions are the ones who can't be sold to."*
Rafi sat down on the step. He looked at his notebook for a long moment.
*"So what do I do?"* he said. *"I want to help. I have skills. I have time. I have connections you don't have."*

*"Use them where you are,"* Tali said. *"Go home. Find the person nearest to you who isn't being seen. Ask what they need. Do that every day. Tell other people how to do it. Don't build an organisation around it. Don't put your name on it. Just do it."*
He looked at her with the expression of someone who came expecting to find something large and is being handed something small.
*"That feels insufficient,"* he said.
*"It always does,"* she said. *"That's not a reason to make it bigger. That's a reason to trust it more."*
He left without his notebook. He had put it down on the step and walked away without picking it up.
Tali picked it up and looked at the plans inside. They were good plans. Some of them were genuinely good.
She left it on the step for whoever needed paper.

title: The Night the Water Stopped Again
paragraphs: Fourteen months after they had restored it, the water stopped.

Not from neglect. Not from corruption — though corruption had tried several times and been blocked each time by Fatima's institutional memory and Carlos's stubbornness and James's network, which had developed an almost supernatural ability to make noise in exactly the right direction at exactly the right moment.

This time it stopped because of a pipe that was simply old. Forty years old, the original metal fatigued past the point of repair, the joint that held it to the new system finally giving way in the night with a sound that woke two families on the ground floor and flooded the basement to Fatima's knees before anyone could shut the valve.

Tali was on the rooftop when she heard the shouting below. She was down the stairs and in the basement in three minutes, water cold around her ankles, Fatima standing in the middle of it holding a torch and pointing at the break with the expression of someone who is furious and focused and not wasting a moment on feelings.
*"There,"* Fatima said. *"The T-joint. The weld failed. We need a replacement section, forty millimetres, galvanised."*
*"At three in the morning?"*
*"Carlos knows a supplier who opens at five. James can reach him."*

This was the thing about the people they had gathered over the two years: they did not panic. They had all, in different ways, survived things that had required them to keep functioning when functioning was difficult. A burst pipe in the night was manageable. They had tools and knowledge and each other.
By 5:30 a.m. Carlos was back with the pipe section. By 7 a.m. the joint was replaced. By 8 a.m. the water was running again.

The families on the ground floor had lost some stored food to the flooding. Hana organised a collection from the other residents — not formally, not with a meeting, just by knocking on doors and asking. By noon the affected families had more food than they had lost.
Tali sat on the rooftop afterward and thought about what had just happened.
A crisis. A real one. And it had been handled — not by her, not by any single person, but by all of them, each doing the thing they were best at, none of them waiting for permission.

That was it. That was what two years of asking the three questions had actually built. Not a system. Not an organisation. A group of people who knew each other well enough to act together without being told to.
She wrote one line in her notebook that morning:
*"The goal was never to fix the water. The goal was to become the kind of people who could fix the water. Those are different goals. Only the second one lasts."*

title: What Fatima Said Before She Went to Hospital
paragraphs: Fatima had been getting slower for months.

Not dramatically — she had always moved at her own pace, which was deliberate and unhurried and gave no impression of haste even when haste was happening. But Tali noticed, because Tali noticed most things about the people she spent time with, that the pace had shifted. That Fatima was sitting more than she used to. That the cane was doing more work than before.
She said nothing. This was Fatima's way. She would say what needed saying when it needed saying.
What needed saying came on a Tuesday evening in October.

Fatima came up to the rooftop, which she did less often now, and sat down beside Tali and looked at the city for a while. The light was going. The sounds of the evening — cooking smells, a child somewhere, the particular hum of a city shifting from work to rest — drifted up around them.
*"I am going to need to go to hospital,"* Fatima said. *"Not tomorrow. But soon."*
Tali looked at her.
*"My heart,"* Fatima said. *"It has been making a case for retirement that I am finding harder to argue with."*
She said it the way she said most things — flatly, without performance, as a fact to be dealt with rather than a drama to be experienced.
Tali felt the weight of it land. She let it land without trying to move it.
*"What do you need?"* she asked.
Fatima looked at her with something that might have been amusement. *"You ask everyone that."*
*"It's the right question."*

*"It is,"* Fatima agreed. She was quiet for a moment. *"I need someone to look after the blueprints. I need to know the work will continue. I need—"* she stopped. Started again. *"I need to know that what I built will still be here after I am not."*

Tali looked at her. Felt the layer underneath — not fear of dying, Fatima was past fear of dying. Something older and more specific. The fear of having been irrelevant. Of having spent a life building things that got buried.
*"The water runs,"* Tali said. *"Every day. Because of you. That will not stop."*
Fatima was quiet.
*"And the blueprints will be looked after,"* Tali said. *"And the work will continue. Not because you made it — because you showed us how. We know how now. That doesn't disappear when you do."*
Fatima looked at the city for a long time.
*"Good,"* she said finally. *"That is what I needed to hear."*

She went to hospital three weeks later. She came back six weeks after that, slower still, the cane doing even more work, but present — sitting on the rooftop on Tuesday evenings, drawing blueprints of things that did not yet exist but might.
She was still drawing them the last time Tali saw her that year.

title: The Mother
paragraphs: A letter arrived.

It came the way things arrived for Tali — through chains of hands, passed from person to person across borders that did not officially allow such passing, arriving finally in the hands of James who gave it to Carlos who left it on the rooftop with a look that said he knew it was important without knowing why.
It was written in her mother's handwriting.

Tali recognised it immediately — the particular slant of the letters, the way her mother pressed harder on certain words as if underlining them from inside the ink. She had learned to read from this handwriting. She had spent eleven years watching it by candlelight and in the grey half-dark of basements and under the open sky on nights when there was nothing else to look at.
She sat down on the concrete and held the letter for a long time before opening it.

Inside: three pages. Dense, careful. Her mother's voice, unmistakably — that particular way she had of saying serious things in plain language, without decoration, as if she respected the truth too much to dress it up.
Her mother was alive.

She had been in a detention facility for fourteen months after the border crossing — not the same facility Tali had escaped from, a different one, further along the border, one of the ones the news sometimes mentioned and usually forgot. She had been released when a policy changed. She had spent the time since then trying to trace Tali through every channel available to her, which were few and slow.
She had found her through James's radio network. Someone had mentioned a girl on a rooftop in a city. The description had been enough.

The letter did not say: *I am coming.* Tali's mother was too precise with words for promises she could not yet keep. It said: *I am trying. The border is difficult. There are things I need to arrange. I will not stop trying.*
And at the end, in smaller writing, slightly different pressure, as if added after the rest was done:

*I heard what you have been doing. Someone told me about the water and the questions and the people on the rooftop. I was not surprised. You were always the one who paid attention. You learned it from watching me. But you went further than I did. You always go further.*
*I am proud of you.*
*I am coming.*

Tali sat on the rooftop with the letter in her hands until the light went completely and the city lit up below her, its thousand separate lights each marking a place where someone was trying to live a life.
She did not cry. She sat with what she felt the way she had learned to sit with difficult things — not pushing it away, not drowning in it, just letting it be true.
Her mother was alive.
That was enough for tonight.
Tomorrow there would be work. There was always work.
But tonight, her mother was alive and was trying and was proud.
She folded the letter back along its original creases and put it in the bag with the photograph and the book.
Then she sat for a while longer in the dark, just breathing, just being a girl on a rooftop who had just received the best news of her life and did not quite know yet what to do with it.

title: What Tali Knew at Sixteen
paragraphs: On the morning of her sixteenth birthday — a date she knew only approximately, her mother having told her the month but never being entirely certain of the day — Tali sat on the rooftop as the sun came up and took stock.

Not of achievements. She was suspicious of achievements, which had a way of becoming walls — things you defended rather than built on. Not of failures either. She had made peace with failure the way you make peace with rain. It came. You got wet. You dried off and continued.
She took stock of what she knew.

She knew that most human suffering was not inevitable. It was the product of disconnection — people with resources not knowing people with needs, people in pain not knowing they were not alone in it, people with answers not knowing where the questions were. The suffering was real. The disconnection was fixable. Not all at once, not everywhere, not by her. But fixable, one connection at a time, by anyone willing to pay attention.

She knew that the three questions worked not because they were clever but because they were honest. They pointed at what was actually there instead of at what people wanted to see. And honesty, in a world that had largely given up on it, had a kind of power that was almost embarrassing in its simplicity.

She knew that help given without strings was the most destabilising force she had encountered. It confused people. It made them suspicious first, then uncertain, then — in many cases — quietly, permanently changed. Because it demonstrated, by simply existing, that not everything was a transaction. That some things were offered because they were needed, full stop.

She knew that she could not save her mother. She could not reach across borders and cut through bureaucracy and make the letter into an arrival. She could only do what was in front of her, and trust that her mother was doing the same on her side, and that at some point the distance between them would close.

She knew that Fatima's heart was not reliable and that Carlos would eventually leave for something that paid and that James had good days and bad days that had nothing to do with anything Tali could fix. She knew that the rooftop was not permanent. Nothing was permanent. That was not a reason not to build.

She knew that the work would outlast her understanding of it. Things she had started would go in directions she had not anticipated and could not control. Some of those directions would be wrong. Others would be better than anything she could have planned. Both were fine. The work was not hers. It moved through her. She was one set of hands among many.
She knew, finally, that she was sixteen years old and had been surviving since she was born, and that surviving was not the same as living, and that she was only beginning to learn the difference.

Living, she suspected, had something to do with the letter in the bag. With Fatima drawing blueprints on Tuesday evenings. With Hana's daughter examining the soldering iron with total seriousness. With Carlos's bad jokes and James's dog and Mira's cooking on Thursday evenings and the three questions that kept travelling, hand to hand, city to city, language to language, changing slightly with each telling the way good things do.
Living was this.
She hadn't known that before.
She was starting to know it now.

title: The Open Road
paragraphs: Three months after the letter, another one arrived.
Shorter. Just one page. The handwriting slightly more hurried than before, which Tali had learned to read as urgency rather than carelessness.
*I have a date. I have a way. I will be there in six weeks if the border holds.*
*Keep the rooftop.*
Tali read it twice. Then she went downstairs and told Fatima, who was sitting in her room drawing, and Fatima looked up from the blueprints and said: *"Good. She should see what you have built."*
Then Tali told Hana, who hugged her without asking permission, which Tali had learned over two years to accept rather than sidestep.
She told Carlos, who said: *"About time."* Then: *"Is she any good at plumbing?"*
She told James, who said nothing but whose dog wagged its tail as if it understood the significance.

She did not tell anyone else. She had learned not to bank on things that had not happened yet. The border might not hold. Six weeks was a long time. Her mother was trying. She was always trying. But trying and arriving were different things and Tali knew the difference better than most.

She went back to the rooftop and sat in the place she had sat for four years now — the spot near the low wall on the eastern side where the sun hit first in the morning and last in the evening, where she had asked the question that would not leave her, where she had received the news that her mother was alive, where she had been sick and been cared for and come back to herself.
The city spread below her, indifferent and enormous and full of people trying.

She had six weeks of work ahead of her. There was the water joint on the third floor that had been slow to drain. There was the family in the next building who had asked about the three questions and needed someone to sit with them through the first attempts. There was a letter from a teacher in a country she had never been to who wanted to know if she could come and talk to her students, which she couldn't, but she could write something, which she would.
There was Fatima's heart, which required watching.
There was Mira, who was coming on Thursday with food.
There was the photograph in the bag and the book and the letter folded along its original creases.
There was the work, which was never finished, which was the point of it.
She had six weeks.
She picked up her tools and started.
**END OF PART THREE**
*Tali continues in Part Four: The Arrival — in which what has been waited for comes, and turns out to be both exactly what was expected and nothing like it at all.*

title: Six Weeks
paragraphs: The first week was ordinary.

The water joint on the third floor was replaced. The family in the next building — a couple in their forties and a teenage son who sat in corners and said nothing — came up to the rooftop on a Wednesday evening and Tali sat with them for two hours, asking the questions, listening, finding nothing dramatic and nothing simple. The mother had a conflict with a neighbour that had been going on for three years. The father had lost his job six months ago and had told nobody. The son said nothing all evening and then, on the way out, stopped and said quietly to Tali: *"Does it get easier? Being in a place where you don't know anyone?"*
She looked at him. He was perhaps fourteen. He had the specific wariness of someone who has been moved too many times and has learned not to get attached.
*"It gets different,"* she said. *"That's not the same as easier. But different is something."*
He thought about this. Then he went downstairs with his parents.
He came back the following Wednesday on his own.
The second week something unexpected happened.

Nadia — the journalist who had written the article — sent a message through James's network asking if she could come back. Not to write another article. She had left journalism. She wanted to learn the three questions properly, not as a subject but as a practice. She was in the city already, had been for a week, had been trying to find the courage to ask.
Tali replied: *"Come on Thursday. Bring nothing. Be ready to be uncomfortable."*

Nadia came on Thursday. She sat through the evening, watching, listening, occasionally being included in conversations in the way that Thursday evenings worked — nobody was a guest, nobody was an observer, everyone was simply there and was asked what they needed and what they saw and what they could do.
Afterward she sat with Tali on the rooftop.
*"I spent three years,"* she said, *"writing about what was wrong. Getting very good at describing damage. I could describe damage brilliantly. I never once fixed any of it."*
*"You told people it existed,"* Tali said.
*"Is that enough?"*
*"I don't know. Was the damage still there after you described it?"*
*"Then describing it wasn't sufficient. But it might have been necessary. Some people needed to know it was there before they could do anything about it."*
Nadia was quiet for a while. *"That feels like a generous interpretation."*
*"It's an honest one,"* Tali said. *"What would you do differently now?"*
Nadia thought about it for a long time. *"I'd stay longer. I'd learn people's names. I'd go back."*

*"Then do that,"* Tali said. *"You don't need to stop writing. Just write differently. Write the way you'd want someone to write about you — not as a problem, not as a victim, not as a symbol. As a person who is trying."*

Nadia came back the following Thursday. And the one after. She began to write again — differently, as she had said she would. The pieces she wrote were slower and less dramatic than her previous work. They were also more true.
The third week a boy from the neighbourhood was caught stealing from a market stall.

Not a significant theft — a piece of fruit, the kind of thing that hunger rather than malice explains. The stallholder wanted him arrested. The boy was twelve. His family, when found, turned out to live three streets from the building — a mother alone, working two jobs, a boy who was home alone most of the day with nothing to do and not enough to eat.
Tali did not solve this by herself. She asked the three questions, separately, to the stallholder and to the boy's mother and to the boy himself.

The stallholder's real pain was not the fruit. It was that theft from his stall had increased over three months and he felt powerless and disrespected and afraid that his livelihood was slipping away.
The forgotten person was the boy's mother, who had never been asked what she needed — who had been talked about, assessed, judged, and occasionally given things, but never simply asked.

The third point: the stallholder needed someone to watch the stall during his lunch break, which was when most theft occurred. The boy had time, needed structure, and was twelve years old — the precise age at which being given responsibility either ruins a person or saves them.
It took three conversations and one afternoon.
The boy watched the stall during lunch. The stallholder paid him in food. The theft stopped. The boy's mother had one less thing to worry about. Nobody signed anything. Nobody made a programme of it.
It just worked.
The stallholder came to Tali a week later and said: *"How did you know that would work?"*
*"I didn't,"* she said. *"I just asked what was actually needed. The rest was obvious once I stopped trying to be clever about it."*
The fourth week nothing happened that was worth recording.
This is also important.

Not every week contains a lesson or a resolution or a moment of change. Some weeks are just work — the slow, undramatic maintenance of a thing that exists and needs to be kept existing. Pipes checked. Questions asked. People seen. Food shared on Thursday.

Tali had learned to value these weeks. Early on she had found them frustrating — had felt, in the absence of visible progress, that nothing was happening. She understood now that the quiet weeks were when the roots went deeper. When the thing being built became more itself, more solid, more capable of surviving the weeks that were not quiet.
She worked. She waited. She asked the questions and listened to the answers.
The fifth week the teenage boy — the one from the family next door, who had asked if it got easier — came back and brought a friend.

The friend was also perhaps fourteen. He sat in the corner the way the first boy had sat the first time he came. He said nothing all evening. On the way out he stopped and asked Tali the same question the first boy had asked:
*"Does it get easier? Being in a place where you don't know anyone?"*
*"It gets different,"* Tali said. Same answer.
He thought about it. *"The other one said you'd say that."*
*"Did it help, when he told you?"*
*"A little."*
*"Good. That's how it works. Someone tells you, and it helps a little. Then you tell someone, and it helps them a little. The little things add up."*
He nodded slowly, with the seriousness of someone receiving information they intend to use.
He came back the following week.

The sixth week, on a Thursday evening, while Mira's food was being passed around and James was arguing with Carlos about something nobody else could follow and Fatima was drawing on a corner of the table and Nadia was talking to Hana's daughter who had opinions about everything and expressed them loudly —
The door at the bottom of the stairs opened.
Footsteps on the stairs.

Tali was sitting with her back to the staircase. She heard the footsteps and knew them before she turned around. Not because she had heard them before — she had not, not in any memory she could access. But because the body knows certain things that the mind has not yet processed, and her body had been waiting for these footsteps for sixteen years.
She turned around.
Her mother stood at the top of the stairs.

Older. Thinner. The particular look of someone who has been through something long and has come out the other side still standing, which is different from coming out undamaged. She was looking at Tali with an expression that had too many things in it to name.
The rooftop went quiet.
Tali stood up.
They looked at each other across the distance of five years and a border and everything that had happened in between.
Then her mother crossed the rooftop and held her.
Tali let herself be held.

She was sixteen years old and she had been surviving since the night she was born and she had not been held like this since she was eleven years old at a border crossing with thousands of people around her, and she had forgotten — she had made herself forget, because remembering was too costly — what it felt like to be held by the person who had always held her.
It felt like the ground.
She held on.

Around them, the people of the rooftop — who were not subtle people, but were kind ones — found things to look at in other directions and kept the noise going and did not make anything of the moment except to give it space.
After a while her mother stepped back and looked at her.
*"You got taller,"* she said.
*"You got thinner,"* Tali said.
*"I'm working on it."*

They stood looking at each other. Tali felt the layer underneath her mother — the guilt, which was there, and the exhaustion, which was deep, and the love, which was older than both and had survived everything.
*"Are you hungry?"* Tali said.
Her mother laughed. A real laugh, surprised out of her. *"Yes."*
*"Then sit down. There's food."*

Her mother sat. Mira put a plate in front of her without asking. Carlos moved along the wall to make space. James's dog investigated her shoes with great thoroughness. Fatima looked up from her blueprints, assessed the situation, and went back to drawing.
Life on the rooftop resumed.
Not as if nothing had happened. As if everything had happened and there was room for it.

title: After
paragraphs: The morning after her mother arrived, Tali woke before dawn.

She lay on her mattress on the rooftop — her mother was sleeping on borrowed bedding nearby, the first time in five years they had been close enough to hear each other breathe — and looked at the sky.
The stars were still out. The city below was quiet in the particular way of the hour before anything starts.
She thought about the question she had asked those two years ago, sitting in this same spot, looking at this same sky:
*Why is it so easy to hurt someone you've never met, and so hard to help them?*
She had an answer now. Not a complete one — she suspected the complete answer would take a lifetime, and even then might stay partial. But something.

It was easy to hurt strangers because hurting required no knowledge of them. You could hurt someone with an idea of them — with the version of them that fear had constructed in your mind. The hurt required no contact, no presence, no understanding.

Helping was harder because helping required you to actually see the person. To ask what they needed rather than deciding for them. To be present rather than distant. To risk being wrong, being refused, being insufficient. To do the work of connection rather than the easier work of distance.

Most people chose distance not because they were cruel but because connection was frightening. You might be rejected. You might be changed. You might find out that the person you had been afraid of was also afraid, and that the fear between you was more similar than either of you had admitted, and that would require you to do something about it.
Distance was safer.
Connection was better.
She had spent two years demonstrating this, one rooftop at a time, one question at a time, one person sat with in the dark at a time.
It was not enough. It would never be enough. The world was enormous and the hurt in it was deep and the people who profited from the hurt were powerful and patient and well-funded.
But it was something.
Something, multiplied across enough people and enough days, was how the world actually moved.
Her mother woke at dawn and sat up and looked at the city coming into the light.
*"Tell me everything,"* she said. *"From the beginning."*
Tali told her.
It took most of the morning.

title: What the Book Is For
paragraphs: You have reached the end of this part of the story.

There is more. There is always more — the work continues, the questions keep travelling, the world keeps breaking and being repaired and breaking again. But this is where this volume stops, because this is where the beginning ends.
The beginning: a girl born in a war, raised in rubble, separated from her mother at a border, alone in a city that didn't want her, asking a question that wouldn't let go.
The beginning ends here, on a rooftop at dawn, with her mother beside her, telling the whole story from the start.
Now it is your turn.

Not to have the same story — you have your own. Not to ask the same question — you have your own questions. Not to build a rooftop community or fix a water system or draw lines between Li Wei's stolen river and the people who could help.
To ask the three questions. Today. About the situation in front of you.
**What is the real pain?**
Not the argument. Not the surface. The actual wound underneath it all. Ask it of the situation. Ask it of the person in front of you. Ask it of yourself.
**Who is not being seen?**
Look around whatever room or street or conversation you are in. Find the person nobody is looking at. Ask them what they see from where they are standing. Listen to the answer.
**What can I do right now, with what I have?**

Not when things are better. Not when you are more ready. Now. With these hands. In this place. Something small. Something real. Something that meets an actual need rather than performing the idea of help.
That is all.
That is the whole book.
The rest is yours.

*The story of Tali continues.*
*So does yours.*
*Both of them matter.*
*Begin.*
**THE END OF PART FOUR**
*(Tali — Part Five: The Questions Travel — follows in the next volume.)*
