title: What Happened When Nobody Was Looking
paragraphs: The questions did not spread the way fire spreads.

Fire is fast and visible and leaves destruction behind it. The questions spread the way seeds spread — carried by wind and birds and the pockets of travellers, landing in soil that was sometimes ready and sometimes not, taking root quietly in the dark before anyone knew they were there.

Tali did not track this. She had no way to track it and no desire to. The moment you start measuring a thing like this you change it — it becomes a project with metrics rather than a practice with roots.
But things came back to her.

A letter from a woman in a country she had never visited who ran a small school in a neighbourhood where two ethnic groups had been killing each other's children for thirty years. The woman had tried the three questions with two mothers — one from each group — who had both lost sons. She had not tried to make them forgive each other. She had only asked: what is the real pain? And then listened while two women, in the same room for the first time, discovered that their pain was identical. Not similar. Identical. The same hollow, the same weight, the same impossible mornings.

They did not become friends. The letter was careful to say this — the woman who wrote it understood that the story would be ruined by a false ending. They did not forgive. They did not reconcile. They sat in the same room and recognised each other's grief and that was what happened.

Three months later they were running a small joint kitchen together. Not because of the grief. Because one of them had a working oven and the other had flour, and a child was hungry, and neither of them was willing to let a child go hungry in front of them.

*I thought you should know,* the letter said. *I don't know if this is what you intended. I don't think you intended anything specific. I think you just gave us a direction to look. We did the rest ourselves.*
Tali read it on the rooftop, her mother sitting nearby shelling something for Thursday's meal. She read it twice, then folded it and put it with the others.
*"Good news?"* her mother asked.
*"Two women who lost sons to the same war are running a kitchen together.*"
Her mother was quiet for a moment. Then: *"That's the whole story, isn't it. In one sentence."*
*"I think so,"* Tali said.

A teacher in a secondary school in a large city had been trying for four years to reduce the violence between two groups of boys — not gangs exactly, just the particular clusters that form when young men have no other way to establish identity and belonging. He had tried programmes. He had tried mediation. He had tried punishment and reward and every combination of both.
Then someone had shown him the three questions and suggested he try asking them — not to the groups, but to the individual boys, one at a time, in private.
He did this for three months.

What he found: the real pain, in almost every case, was invisible at home. Fathers absent or present in the wrong way. Mothers exhausted. Younger siblings to set an example for, older siblings who had set the wrong one. A fear of being nobody — of passing through life without anyone noticing. The violence was not the thing. The violence was what the thing looked like when it had nowhere else to go.

The forgotten person, in almost every case, was the boy himself. Seen only as a problem. Never asked what he needed. Never treated as someone whose interior life might be complicated and worth knowing.

The teacher could not fix the absent fathers or the exhausted mothers. But he could see the boys. He could ask them every week: what do you need right now? He could treat the answer as real rather than inconvenient.

The violence did not stop. This is important to say — it did not stop cleanly or completely or in a way that would make a good news story. But it diminished. Slowly. In the way that things diminish when the pressure underneath them finds a different outlet.

Two of the boys started coming in early on Fridays to help set up the classroom. Nobody knew why. The teacher did not ask. He made tea and they worked alongside him in comfortable silence and he asked them, occasionally, what they needed, and they told him things, occasionally, that surprised him.

He wrote to Tali about this. His letter ended: *I don't know if what I'm doing counts as using your questions correctly. It doesn't feel like a method. It feels like paying attention. Is that the same thing?*
Tali wrote back: *Yes. That's exactly the same thing.*
A woman who worked in a hospital in a poor country wrote about what happened when she began asking dying patients: *who is not being seen in your life?*
She had expected practical answers. People to call. Debts to settle. Things to say before it was too late.
Sometimes that was what she got.
But more often people named someone they had hurt and never apologised to. Someone they had loved and never told. Someone they had watched suffer at a distance and had not moved toward.

The woman began connecting them. She called people on behalf of patients who could not call themselves. She carried messages. She sat with people while they made calls they had been not-making for decades.

She wrote: *I don't know what I expected dying to look like up close. I did not expect it to look mostly like regret about connection not made. But that is almost always what it looks like. The same regrets, in different languages, in every room. I wish I had told them. I wish I had gone. I wish I had asked.*
*Your questions are just a way of not waiting until it is too late.*
*That is all they are.*
*That is everything they are.*
Tali read this on the rooftop and was quiet for a long time.
Her mother looked up. *"What is it?"*
*"Someone figured out what the questions are actually for,"* Tali said.
*"What are they for?"*
*"Not waiting until it's too late."*
Her mother looked at her for a long moment.
*"I know,"* she said. *"I nearly did. Wait too long."*
They sat with that.

Below them the city went about its business, indifferent and enormous and full of people who had not yet asked the questions and some who had and most who were somewhere in between, trying to figure out how to be less alone in a world that kept offering them reasons to stay separate.

title: The Boy on the Stairs
paragraphs: The teenage boy — the one who had come back with his friend, the one who had asked if it got easier — had been coming to the rooftop for four months when he stopped coming.
Not with any announcement. He simply was not there one Thursday. And then not the following Thursday. And then the one after.
His friend still came. Tali asked him carefully, not pressing: *"Is he all right?"*
The friend was quiet for a moment. *"His father came back."*
*"Is that bad?"*
The friend looked at her. The look said everything.
Tali sat with this for a week.

She understood what not good meant when a father came back. She had spent years in places where people lived too close together with too little to lose, and she knew what the inside of those situations looked and sounded like. She was not naive about it.
She also knew what she could and could not do.

She could not make the father leave. She could not make him be different. She had no authority, no legal standing, no official role. She was sixteen and she lived on a rooftop and none of the formal systems that were supposed to handle situations like this had ever, in her experience, handled them well.
What she had was the mother.

She had met the mother twice — a quiet woman, tired in the specific way of someone managing a dangerous situation alone, who had come to the rooftop once and sat at the edge of the group and eaten Mira's food and left early and not come back. She had the look of someone who had learned not to draw attention to herself.
Tali found her in the building next door on a Tuesday morning.
The woman opened the door and immediately looked past Tali into the corridor — checking, automatically, before she could stop herself.
Tali noticed this. She said nothing about it.
*"I'm Tali. Your son used to come on Thursdays."*
*"I know who you are."*
*"I'm not here about him. I'm here about you. Can I come in for a few minutes?"*
The woman looked at her for a long moment. Then stepped back.

The kitchen was very clean. The kind of clean that takes effort to maintain, that becomes its own kind of control when other things cannot be controlled. Tali sat at the table. The woman stood by the sink with her arms crossed — not hostile, just containing herself.
Tali asked: *"What do you need?"*
The woman stared at her. *"What?"*
*"Not what should happen. Not what the right answer is. What do you actually need, right now, today?"*
A long silence.
Then the woman sat down.

She talked for an hour. About the situation — carefully, not all of it, the parts she could say out loud. About what it had cost her and what it had cost her son. About the times she had nearly done something and hadn't. About the specific mechanics of how a person becomes trapped in a situation they could see clearly from the outside and could not seem to leave from the inside. About the exhaustion of managing it alone, of making sure her son knew it wasn't normal while also pretending, for survival reasons, that it was manageable.

Tali listened. She did not offer solutions. She did not tell the woman what to do. She did not say any of the things that are said in these situations that make the person saying them feel helpful and leave the person being helped feeling more alone.
She listened. She did not look away. She did not make it smaller than it was.

When the woman stopped talking she looked at Tali with the particular expression of someone who has just put something down that they have been carrying a long time — not relief exactly, because the thing was still there, but the temporary respite of having set it down in front of another person who had not flinched.
*"I still don't know what to do,"* she said.
*"I know,"* Tali said. *"I can't tell you what to do. I don't know your situation well enough and even if I did it's not mine to decide."*
She paused.

*"But I know someone. A woman who runs a support group two streets from here — Thursday evenings, same time as our rooftop gathering. She's been through something similar. She doesn't tell people what to do either. She just makes sure they're not doing it alone."*
The woman was quiet.
*"You don't have to go,"* Tali said. *"But I wanted you to know it exists. That you're not the only one."*
She gave her the address. She did not follow up. She had learned that following up in these situations could feel like pressure, and pressure was the last thing this woman needed more of.
She did not know if the woman went.
She did not know what happened with the father.
These were not hers to know.
Three weeks later the boy appeared at the top of the rooftop stairs. He sat in his usual corner. He said nothing all evening. On the way out he stopped beside Tali.
*"My mum said you came to see her."*
He was quiet for a moment. *"Things aren't fixed,"* he said. It was important to him that she know this. That she not think it had been solved by a visit.
*"I know,"* she said.
*"But she went somewhere. On Thursdays. She seems—"* He paused, searching for the word. *"Less like she's holding her breath."*
Tali nodded.
*"Is it different?"* he said. *"Being somewhere a long time?"*
*"Yes,"* she said. *"You know where things are. You know which people are safe. It's not always better. But it's different in ways that matter."*
He thought about this.
*"I'm going to stay,"* he said. Not to her — to himself. A decision out loud.
*"Good,"* she said.
He went downstairs.
The situation was not fixed. The father was still there. The mother was still in it. The boy was still carrying something too heavy for his age.
But she was less alone with it.
And he had said: I'm going to stay.
That was not nothing.
That was, in fact, the whole point.

title: What Tali's Mother Thought
paragraphs: Her mother had been on the rooftop for three months when she said:
*"You know what you're doing, don't you."*
It was not a question. Tali looked at her.

*"You're not fixing things,"* her mother said. *"You're teaching people to fix things. But you're not even doing that directly. You're showing them, by how you are with them, that it's possible. And they go away and show someone else."*
*"That's what you did,"* Tali said. *"In the war. Moving between buildings, knowing everyone, connecting the person with medicine to the person who needed it."*
Her mother was quiet for a moment. *"I didn't think of it that way. I was just trying to keep us alive."*
*"That's what I'm doing."*
*"We're not in a war."*
*"Aren't we?"*
Her mother looked at her sharply. Then at the city. Then back.
*"The war is different,"* she said.

*"The shape is different. The thing underneath is the same. People are afraid. They hurt each other because of the fear. The ones who want to keep power make sure the fear keeps moving. You either participate in that or you don't."*
*"And this is how you don't."*
*"This is how I try not to."*
Her mother was quiet for a long time.
*"I should have done more,"* she said finally. *"In the war. There were things I knew how to do that I didn't do because I was too tired or too scared."*
*"You kept us alive,"* Tali said. *"You kept moving when stopping would have been easier. You taught me everything I know about paying attention."* She paused. *"You did more than you think."*
Her mother looked at her with an expression Tali had seen before — the expression in the letter, the one with too many things in it to name.
*"When did you get so much older than me?"* her mother said.
*"I've been practicing,"* Tali said.
Her mother laughed. The real laugh — the one Tali remembered from before the hardest years, the one that came from somewhere unguarded.

They sat together on the rooftop as the sun went down over the city. Below them the evening was beginning — cooking smells and the sounds of children, a argument somewhere, music from a window, the particular music of people living.
*"What happens next?"* her mother asked.
*"The same thing that's been happening,"* Tali said. *"Work. Questions. Thursday evenings. Pipes that need fixing. People who need seeing."*
*"That's enough for you?"*
Tali thought about it honestly.
*"It's enough for now,"* she said. *"Ask me again in a year."*

title: The Last Thing
paragraphs: Not because the story ends — the story does not end, the work does not end, the questions keep travelling and Tali keeps asking them and the city keeps offering problems and the people on the rooftop keep trying to meet them.
But every story needs a place to pause. A breath before the next part. A moment to look at what has accumulated.
Here is what has accumulated:

A girl born in a war, raised in rubble, who crossed a border alone at eleven and lived on a rooftop in a city that didn't want her and spent four years paying attention to the people around her and asking three questions and drawing lines between what was broken and what could fix it.

A group of people who had nothing in common except the willingness to try. An old engineer with blueprints and a bad heart. A cynical plumber with good hands. A veteran with a radio and a dog. A grieving woman who brought food on Thursdays. A journalist who learned to stay longer. A boy who decided to stay.
A mother who crossed a border and climbed stairs and found her daughter on a rooftop surrounded by people she had gathered by simply asking what they needed.

Three questions that were travelling — city to city, language to language, hand to hand — not because anyone promoted them or sold them or put their name on them, but because they worked. Because they pointed at what was actually there instead of at what was easier to see.
That is what has accumulated.
It is not a revolution. It will not be on the news. It will not change the name of anything official or appear in any treaty or win any prize.

But somewhere tonight — in a kitchen that two women from opposite sides of a war are running together, in a classroom where a teacher makes tea on Friday mornings with boys who used to fight each other, in a hospital room where a woman carries messages between dying patients and the people they should have called years ago — somewhere tonight, something small and real is happening.

Because someone asked what was needed.
Because someone looked for who wasn't being seen.
Because someone acted with what they had.
Because a girl on a rooftop refused to stop asking.
You know what to do.
You have known since the first page.
The only question left is when you will start.
Start now.
*The questions are:*
*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*
*Ask them today.*
*Pass them on.*
*That is all.*
**THE END OF PART FIVE**
**THE END OF VOLUME ONE**

*This book belongs to no one.*
*It belongs to everyone who uses it.*
*Copy it. Translate it. Read it aloud.*
*Give it to someone who needs it.*
*The only condition is the one Tali always kept:*
*Use it to help.*
*Not to win.*
*Not to be right.*
*To help.*
*That is enough.*
*That has always been enough.*

*Volume One was Tali's story — how she came to be on a rooftop, how the questions formed, how the people gathered, how her mother arrived.*
*Volume Two is different.*
*The questions have left the rooftop. They are in other hands now. They are being asked badly and well and sideways and honestly and sometimes in the wrong order and sometimes not at all but almost.*
*Volume Two follows five people in five different parts of the world who have never met Tali and never will.*
*Each of them has the questions.*
*Each of them is trying.*
*That is the whole story.*

title: Marcus, Forty-One, Chicago
paragraphs: Marcus had been a police officer for nineteen years.

He was good at it — not in the way the films showed, not the brilliant detective or the fearless hero, but in the real way, the way that mattered in the daily work: he was consistent. He showed up. He remembered names. He treated people the same on the bad days as on the good ones, which sounds simple and is in fact the hardest thing about the job.
He had also, over nineteen years, shot two people.

Both were alive. One had been shooting at Marcus first. The other had not been — had been holding something that in the dark and the fear of the moment had looked like a weapon and was not. That man had spent four months in hospital and recovered and Marcus had spent the four years since trying to figure out what to do with what he had done and finding nothing satisfying.

He had taken a leave of absence three months ago. He had told his captain it was for his mental health, which was true, and he had not said the full truth, which was that he did not know if he could go back. He did not know if the job was the problem or if he was the problem or if the two had become so tangled that separating them was no longer possible.
His sister had given him the questions.

Not from Tali directly — his sister had gotten them from a colleague who had gotten them from a friend who had gotten them from a translated version of something she had read. The chain was long enough that by the time they reached Marcus they had no origin story attached, just the questions themselves, written on a card in his sister's handwriting:

*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*
He had put the card on his kitchen table and looked at it for two days without doing anything with it.
On the third day he applied the first question to himself.

It took him the better part of a week to get to the real pain, because the real pain was buried under layers of the easier pains — the guilt, the doubt, the anger at the situation, the grief for what the job had cost him.

The real pain, when he finally reached it, was this: he had become someone he did not recognise. Not because of the shooting — before the shooting. Gradually, across nineteen years, the job had taught him to see people as threats first and humans second, and he had accepted this as professional necessity, and it had leaked. Into his marriage, which had not survived it. Into his relationships with his children, who were ten and eight and slightly afraid of him in a way he had only recently admitted to himself. Into his view of the world, which had narrowed to the point where he walked into any room and immediately assessed the danger rather than the people.

He had not been seen either. The who is not being seen question, applied to his own life, produced an answer that surprised him: himself. He had not been seen as a person in years. He was a badge. A function. A problem to be managed by the department's wellness programme. Nobody had asked what he needed in so long that he had stopped being able to answer the question.
The third question was the hardest. What could he do right now, with what he had?

What he had: nineteen years of knowing how communities actually worked, at the ground level, in the real texture of streets and buildings and the informal systems that held neighbourhoods together beneath the official ones. He had names and faces and the particular knowledge of someone who had been present for the worst moments of many people's lives. He had, still, the ability to show up consistently and remember names.
He did not know yet what to do with these things.
But he had started asking.
He called the man he had shot.
This had seemed impossible for four years. He had been advised against it by lawyers, by his union representative, by the department's wellness officer. Too much liability. Too much risk.
He called him anyway.
The man's name was DeShawn. He was thirty-seven. He worked at a hardware store. He had a daughter.
He picked up the phone. There was a long silence.
Then Marcus said: *"I want to ask you something. You don't have to answer. What do you need? From me, from the situation, from any of it. What do you actually need?"*
Another long silence.
DeShawn said: *"Nobody ever asked me that."*
*"I know. I'm asking now."*

What DeShawn needed was not what Marcus had expected. He did not need an apology — he had made a kind of peace with what had happened, or enough of one to function. He did not need money or legal action or any of the formal remedies that had been offered and declined.
He needed someone to acknowledge that it had happened and that it had mattered and that the version of events that had been recorded officially was not the full truth of it.
He needed to be seen as someone the incident had happened to, not as a liability to be managed.
They talked for two hours.
They talked again the following week.

They did not become friends — Marcus was honest enough with himself to know that friendship was too much to ask for and too easy a resolution to a real thing. But they became something. Two people who had been connected by a terrible moment, learning to be connected by something else instead.
Marcus went back to work four months later.
He went back differently.

He still did the job. He still showed up and remembered names and treated people the same on bad days as good ones. But he had added something to this — a question he asked silently in every encounter, every call, every situation that threatened to simplify into danger and threat:
*Who is not being seen here?*
It did not make him perfect. It did not make the job safe or clean or without impossible moments. But it made him someone he recognised.
That was enough.

title: Priya, Twenty-Eight, Bangalore
paragraphs: Priya had built an app.

Not Tali's kind of building — not soldering irons and salvaged laptops and questions asked face to face. A startup, a pitch deck, a series A round, a team of eleven, an app that had two million users and was growing.

The app connected domestic workers — cleaners, cooks, caregivers — with households that needed them. It was well-designed. It was genuinely useful. It had improved the incomes of many of the workers who used it.

It had also, Priya had recently discovered, been used by several of the households on the platform to pay workers less than the agreed rate, to cancel bookings at the last minute without compensation, and in three documented cases to make accusations against workers that had led to the workers being removed from the platform without investigation.

Priya had found this out not through her company's systems — the systems had not been designed to surface this information — but because a cleaner named Amrita had found her personal email address and written to her directly.
The email was three sentences long:
*You built something that was supposed to help us. It is being used against us. I thought you should know.*
Priya had read the email six times. Then she had called a team meeting and presented the findings and asked what they were going to do about it.

The team had various responses. The legal counsel said the liability was manageable. The growth lead said the affected users were a small percentage. The investor relations person said this could be handled quietly.
Priya had listened to all of it.
Then she had said: *"What does Amrita need?"*
Silence.
*"Not what our legal exposure is. Not what the numbers say. What does the person who wrote me that email actually need?"*
More silence.

This was the first question. Priya had come across the three questions six months earlier, in a form she could not now trace — an article, a conversation, a thing someone had said at a conference that had lodged in her mind. She had been applying them haphazardly to her work and her life ever since.
She applied them now.

The real pain: not the incidents themselves, which were symptoms. The real pain was that the platform had been designed for the convenience of the households, who were the paying customers, and the workers had been treated as a resource to be efficiently allocated rather than as people with their own needs and vulnerabilities. The design reflected who the designers had been thinking about.

The forgotten person: Amrita. And the hundreds of other workers whose experiences had not made it to Priya's personal email because they did not have her address or the confidence to use it or the expectation that it would make any difference.
The third question: what could she do right now with what she had?
She had Amrita's email address.
She wrote back.

She asked if she could call. Amrita said yes. They talked for an hour — not Priya presenting the company's response, but Priya asking questions and Amrita answering them, and Priya listening to answers she had not anticipated and had not built the platform around.
Then Priya called five other workers from the platform who had flagged issues and had them flagged, resolved, and closed. She asked each of them the same question: *what do you need?*

What she heard, across all six conversations, was versions of the same thing: to be believed. To have complaints treated as information rather than as inconvenience. To have the platform's design start from their reality rather than from the households'.

She rebuilt the complaint system. She added worker advocates — experienced workers themselves, paid by the platform, whose job was to investigate and represent other workers in disputes. She changed the cancellation policy. She changed the payment system. She went back to the investors and told them what she was doing and why, and one of them said this would hurt margins and she said she knew that and she was doing it anyway.
The growth rate slowed for two quarters.

Then it increased — because workers who trusted the platform worked harder and stayed longer and recommended it to other workers, and households who used a platform that treated workers fairly found themselves getting better service, and it turned out that building something for everyone in the system rather than just the paying half was not idealistic but practical.
Amrita became the first worker advocate.
She was good at it.

title: Yusuf, Sixty-Seven, Istanbul
paragraphs: Yusuf had been a judge for thirty-one years.

He had seen the law from the inside for long enough to understand both its power and its limits. He had also seen it used — had participated in its use, he was honest enough to admit this — in ways that served the powerful better than the powerless, that processed the poor quickly and considered the wealthy carefully, that treated certain kinds of harm as criminal and other kinds, equally harmful, as simply the way things were.

He had retired eight months ago. He had retired because his back hurt and because he was sixty-seven and because he was tired in a way that sleep did not cure. He had not retired because he had made peace with what he had witnessed. He had retired with the account still open.
His granddaughter had given him the questions.

She was nineteen and studying political science and had the particular intellectual confidence of someone who has recently understood something important and is not yet old enough to know how long it takes to act on understanding. She had printed the three questions on a piece of paper and handed it to him at dinner without explanation.
He had looked at the paper and then at her.
*"A girl on a rooftop in a border city,"* she said. *"She asks these questions and things get better. I thought you might find them interesting."*
He had found them more than interesting.
He applied the first question to the thirty-one years.

The real pain — beneath the specific cases, beneath the systemic unfairness, beneath the exhaustion — was impotence. He had known, for most of those years, what the right outcome was in more cases than he had been able to produce. The system had its own logic and its own pressures and he had bent to them more often than he had resisted them, and the bending had accumulated into something he could not entirely look at.

He had not been seen either. Behind the robe and the title was a man who had entered the law because he believed in it and had spent thirty years watching his belief get worn smooth by friction. Nobody had asked Yusuf the judge what he needed. He was a function. A pillar. A man whose job was to hold things in place.
The third question took him longer.

What did he have? He had thirty-one years of knowing how the law worked and where it bent and which parts of it were flexible and which parts, properly applied, could do extraordinary things. He had a network of lawyers and legal scholars and judges and former colleagues. He had time. He had, still, the belief that had brought him into the law in the first place — battered, worn smooth, but not gone.
He started small.

There was a legal aid clinic two streets from his apartment that had been struggling for years — underfunded, overworked, trying to serve people who had no other access to legal representation. He had walked past it for years without going in.
He went in.
He offered to volunteer. The young lawyer running it looked at him with suspicion — former judges offering to volunteer for legal aid clinics was not a common occurrence.
*"What do you want from this?"* she asked directly.

He applied the second question to himself, in the moment, and answered honestly. *"To use what I know in a way that I can live with. I have skills that belong here more than anywhere else I can think of. I've been using them elsewhere for thirty years. I'd like to stop doing that."*
She was quiet for a moment.
*"Can you do Thursdays?"* she said.
He could do Thursdays.

He showed up the following Thursday and the one after and the one after that, wearing no robe, carrying no title, simply present with what he knew — which was, it turned out, a great deal, and which the people who came to the clinic needed in very immediate and practical ways.
He was, for the first time in thirty-one years, doing exactly what he had believed the law was for when he had entered it.
It did not fix the system. He was one man, one Thursday per week. The system was the system.
But the woman who came in on the third Thursday with a housing case that she had been trying to navigate alone for eight months left with a letter that solved it.
She was the real pain. She was the forgotten person. And Yusuf — retired, sixty-seven, with a bad back and an open account — was what she had needed.
*"Thank you,"* she said, at the door.
*"Come back if it doesn't work,"* he said. *"We'll try something else."*

title: Amara, Fifteen, Lagos
paragraphs: Amara was the youngest of four and the only one still in school.

Her three older brothers had left school at different points for different reasons — one to work, one because the fees had not been paid that term and by the time they could have been paid he had found work and seen no reason to return, one for a reason nobody in the family spoke about directly.

Amara stayed in school because her mother said she would stay in school and because her mother was not a person you argued with successfully. She was also, though she would not have said this aloud, staying in school because she was the kind of person who wanted to understand things, and school — imperfect, underfunded, with teachers who were overworked and textbooks that were out of date — was still the best available tool for understanding things that she had access to.

She came across the questions through her English teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, who had found them somewhere and had started using them in class — not as a lesson, just as a way of approaching discussions. Before any discussion about a text or a news story or a moral question, he asked three things: what is the real pain in this situation? Who is not being seen? What could someone do right now with what they have?
Amara had found this immediately useful in a way that most school activities were not.
She started applying the questions outside school.

Her neighbourhood had a problem that was not unique to her neighbourhood but felt very present in it: a stretch of road that flooded every rainy season, making it impassable for several weeks at a time, cutting off the market from the residential streets, destroying stock, preventing children from reaching school. This happened every year. It had been happening for at least twelve years.
The adults had complained. They had written letters to the local government. They had attended meetings where officials promised things that did not happen. The cycle continued.
Amara applied the three questions.

The real pain was not the flooding itself. The flooding was the symptom. The real pain was that the road existed in a part of the city that the local government considered low-priority — too poor to be worth maintaining, too poorly connected to put pressure on officials effectively. The flooding happened every year because the people it affected did not have sufficient power to make it stop.

The forgotten person: the market women. They were the ones most directly affected — their stock was destroyed, their income disappeared for weeks, their children missed school because the flooding meant the road was impassable. They were the most motivated to act. They had also never been asked what they thought should be done. Officials made promises to community leaders, who were all men. The market women were not in that conversation.
The third question: what could Amara do right now with what she had?
She was fifteen. She had no money, no connections, no power.
She had school. She had Mr. Adeyemi. She had the particular confidence that came from having applied the questions and found they worked.
She went to the market women.
She did not go with a plan. She went with the second question: *what do you see from where you are standing?*

They told her things that were not in any of the letters to the local government. They told her the exact mechanics of where the water came from and where it pooled and what had changed twenty years ago when a drainage channel had been partially blocked during a construction project and never properly cleared. They had been watching this for twenty years. Nobody had asked.

She took this information to her geography teacher, who confirmed that a blocked drainage channel would explain the flooding pattern exactly. She wrote a report — a school project, Mr. Adeyemi helped her frame it as a school project — documenting the problem and its cause and a proposed solution: clear the drainage channel, which required equipment and access but not the large-scale road reconstruction that had always been quoted as the necessary cost.

She presented it to the local government not through official channels, which had failed for twelve years, but through a journalist her older brother knew who covered infrastructure issues and was looking for a story.
The journalist published the report.
The drainage channel was cleared eight weeks later.
The following rainy season the road flooded for two days instead of six weeks.

The market women knew who had done it. They did not make a fuss about it publicly — they understood how these things worked, that credit would be taken by others and that was fine as long as the channel stayed clear. But on the first dry day after the flooding, Amara found a parcel outside her door. Inside: a quantity of groundnut oil, which was expensive, and a note in four different handwritings that said simply: *we see you.*
She read it several times.
She had been seen.
She kept the note.

title: Old Man Park, Seventy-Two, Seoul
paragraphs: He had not been called by his actual name in forty years.

His actual name was Park Joon-seo, but his children called him Abeoji, his grandchildren called him Harabeoji, his neighbours called him Ajeossi or just the old man from the fourth floor, and his wife had called him Joon for fifty-two years until she died and after that nobody called him anything that felt like him.

He was seventy-two. He lived alone. He was healthy enough to live alone. He did not particularly want to live alone but he understood that the people around him were busy and that being busy was the condition of life now in a way it had not always been, and he did not blame them.

He went to the park every morning at seven. He had gone to the park every morning at seven for eleven years. He sat on the same bench and watched the same stretch of path and drank from the same thermos his wife had bought him before she became too ill to leave the house.

On a Tuesday in November a young woman sat down on the other end of his bench. She was perhaps twenty-five, wearing a coat that was not warm enough for the weather, eating something from a container. She was crying quietly in the way of someone who does not want to be seen crying but cannot stop.
Park Joon-seo looked at her for a moment.
Then he said, in the flat, practical tone of a man who has been alive long enough to know that circling things takes too much time: *"What's wrong?"*

She looked at him, startled. People did not ask this directly. There were protocols. There was the careful Korean social architecture of approach and permission and the gradual building up to anything real.
He waited.
After a moment she said: *"I lost my job."*
*"When?"*
*"Yesterday."*
*"Is that what you're crying about?"*
She blinked. *"What else would I be crying about?"*
*"Losing a job is a thing that happens. People don't usually cry like that about a thing that happened. They cry like that about what the thing means."*
She stared at him.
*"What does it mean?"* he said.

She was quiet for a long time. Then, slowly, she told him. The job had been the proof — to herself and to her parents and to everyone who had expressed doubt — that she was capable, that she had made the right choices, that the years of difficulty had been worth it. Losing the job was not just unemployment. It was the thing that had been holding all the rest together.
He listened without interrupting.
When she finished he said: *"My wife died three years ago. For fifty-two years she was the proof that I had made the right choices. After she died I had to learn to be proof to myself."*
Silence.
*"That takes longer than you expect,"* he said. *"But it's possible."*
She wiped her face with her sleeve. *"How?"*
*"I come to this park every morning. I sit on this bench. I drink from this thermos. I watch the path. Eleven years. It doesn't fix anything. But it keeps me in practice."*
*"In practice for what?"*
*"Being present. It's easy to disappear when you're alone. I've found that coming to the same place every day makes it harder to disappear."*
She thought about this.
*"Can I come back tomorrow?"* she said.
*"I'll be here at seven,"* he said. *"I'm always here at seven."*
She came back the next day. And the day after.
After a week she brought her own thermos.
After a month she brought a friend who was also struggling.
The friend brought someone else.

Park Joon-seo had not asked for any of this. He had simply been present on a bench at seven in the morning, consistently, for eleven years, and had asked a direct question when a person was crying beside him.

The bench acquired a small informal reputation. Not large — this was not a movement or a programme, it had no name and no organiser. But in the way that useful things acquire reputations in communities: quietly, by word of mouth, in the spaces where people were actually talking to each other.
People came to the bench. He was there. He asked the direct question. He listened.
He had been doing this, without knowing it had a name, for his entire life.
He still did not know it had a name.
He did not need to.

title: What They Had in Common
paragraphs: Marcus in Chicago, Priya in Bangalore, Yusuf in Istanbul, Amara in Lagos, Park Joon-seo in Seoul.
They had never met. They shared no language, no religion, no culture, no political belief, no experience.
They had three questions.
And underneath the questions — underneath even the questions — they had one thing:
The willingness to look at the person in front of them and actually see them.

Not the category. Not the problem. Not the liability or the case number or the customer or the demographic. The person. With a real pain underneath the surface. With a perspective that nobody had thought to ask for. With a need that could be met, if someone was willing to meet it, with what was actually available.
This is not a complicated thing.
It is also not an easy thing.

Most people, most of the time, do not do it. Not because they are cruel but because they are busy and frightened and because the world has taught them, systematically and efficiently, that other people are dangerous or irrelevant or both.
These five were not extraordinary. They were not born different. They did not have gifts or talents or special access to anything that other people did not have.
They had started asking.
That is all.
That is everything.

title: Back on the Rooftop
paragraphs: Tali was eighteen when the letters from the five of them arrived.
Not at the same time — across the space of several months, through the chains of hands that things travelled through, each arriving with the particular quality of something that had come a long way.
She read them all on the rooftop, her mother nearby, the city below going about its business.

She did not respond to all of them — there were too many letters now, from too many places, and responding to all of them would have consumed every hour she had. She had made peace with this. The questions did not need her to tend them. They were moving on their own.
But she read every letter. She kept them in a box — an old shoebox that had come from somewhere she couldn't remember — under the edge of her mattress, beside her mother's book.
The box was getting full.

She sat on the rooftop and thought about the five letters and the hundreds of others and the people she would never meet who were asking the questions in places she would never go, in languages she did not speak, in situations she could not have imagined.
*What are you thinking?* her mother asked.
*"I'm thinking about how something you do alone on a rooftop can end up on the other side of the world,"* Tali said. *"And how strange that is."*
*"Is it strange?"*
*"It should be impossible. I'm seventeen. I live in a building nobody owns. I have no money and no position and no credentials."*
*"And yet,"* her mother said.
*"And yet."*
They sat with that.

*"You know what I think?"* her mother said. *"I think the questions were always there. People always needed to ask them. You didn't invent anything. You just — you made it simple enough that people could use it."*
*"Is that enough?"*
Her mother looked at her. *"You know the answer to that."*
Tali did know the answer.

Yes. It was enough. Not because it was sufficient — it was not sufficient, the world was still breaking in all the ways it had always been breaking and would keep breaking. But because something real was happening. Because a judge in Istanbul was spending his Thursdays on things that mattered to him. Because a girl in Lagos had cleared a drainage channel. Because a man in Seoul was sitting on a bench and asking the direct question. Because somewhere two women who had lost sons to the same war were running a kitchen together.
Not enough.
But real.
And real was what they had.
She picked up her tools.
Somewhere in the building a pipe was making a sound it shouldn't make. She had been meaning to look at it for three days.
She went downstairs.
The work was waiting.
It was always waiting.
That was fine.
**END OF PART SIX**
**END OF VOLUME TWO**
*Volume Three: What Breaks and What Holds — in which the questions meet their first serious opposition, and what has been built is tested in ways that matter.*
*The three questions:*

*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*

*They belong to no one.*
*They belong to everyone.*
*Use them.*
*Before Part Seven begins:*

*The questions have been travelling for two years.*
*Not everyone is pleased.*
*Some things that have been built are about to be tested.*
*This volume is about what survives the testing.*
*And what doesn't.*
*And why both of those things matter.*

title: The Article
paragraphs: It appeared on a Monday morning.

Not in a small publication — in one of the large ones, the kind that sets the conversation for the week, the kind whose pieces get shared across platforms and quoted in other pieces and referenced in meetings where decisions are made.
The headline was: *The Cult of the Rooftop: How a Teenage Girl's "Three Questions" Are Being Used to Undermine Community Institutions.*
Tali read it on her cracked screen in the bakery two streets away, where she still went most mornings to download content before the owner noticed her.
She read it twice.

The piece was well-written. That was the first thing she noticed. It was not the work of someone lazy or stupid. It was the work of someone who had done research — had found real examples of cases where the questions had been applied poorly, where well-meaning people had used them to justify ignoring professional expertise, where the emphasis on informal networks had been used as an excuse to defund formal services. These examples were real. Tali recognised some of them.

The piece was also dishonest. Not in the simple way — it did not lie about facts. It was dishonest in the way that selective truth is dishonest: it chose only the cases that supported its argument and arranged them to suggest a pattern that was not the whole pattern.

The author was a journalist named Brennan. He was forty-three, based in a city far from here, had written extensively about community organisations and their failures. His previous work was serious and mostly fair.
Tali looked at the piece for a long time.
Then she did something that surprised the people who knew her.
Nothing.

She closed the screen. She went back to the rooftop. She fixed the pipe on the third floor that had been making a sound for a week. She ate the meal Hana's daughter brought up at noon. She sat with her mother in the afternoon while her mother read.
She did not respond. She did not draft a reply. She did not ask anyone to defend her.
Carlos found out about the article by evening and came upstairs furious.
*"You've seen it?"*
*"And nothing. What would you have me do?"*
*"Respond. Correct the record. Tell people the truth."*
*"The people who need to know the truth already know it. They've seen the water. They've been on the rooftop. They've used the questions. An article won't change what they know."*
*"What about people who haven't? People who read this and think—"*

*"People who read this and decide the questions are dangerous without ever trying them were probably not going to try them anyway."* She looked at him. *"Responding turns it into an argument. Arguments are what the piece wants. Arguments generate engagement. Engagement validates the piece. The only thing I have that the piece doesn't is the actual work. I'm going to keep doing the work."*
Carlos stared at her. *"That's the most frustrating thing I've ever heard."*
*"You said that about the water too. And the water came back."*
He sat down heavily on the rooftop. Wallace, who had come up with him, lay across his feet.
*"What if people believe it?"* Carlos said.

*"Some will. That's how it works. Some people will read it and decide we're dangerous and that will be that. Some people will read it and be curious enough to find out for themselves. Some people won't read it at all."* She paused. *"The ones who find out for themselves are the only ones who matter to me. You can't convince people from a distance. You can only show them up close."*
Carlos was quiet for a long time.
*"I hate that you're right,"* he said.
*"I know,"* she said.

She did not tell him the other thing — the thing she had not fully admitted to herself until that moment. That her silence was not entirely non-attachment. That she had calculated, even slightly, that silence would serve her better than response. That she had chosen it partly because it was correct and partly because it was strategic.
Was that the same thing? Was choosing correctly for impure reasons still correct?

She had been on the rooftop at fourteen asking why it was hard to help strangers. She was on the rooftop now understanding that the difficulty was not only about strangers. It was about this: that the right action and the self-interested action were sometimes the same action, and you could not always tell whether you were doing the right thing or protecting yourself and calling it the right thing.
She filed this. She did not resolve it. Some things were not meant to be resolved cleanly. Some things were meant to stay in tension, pressing, reminding you to keep examining your own motives.

That was what the fourth question was for. Not just for situations involving others. For yourself. *Is this something I should handle alone — or does my own stake in the outcome mean I need someone else's eyes on it?*
She did not have an answer yet.
She kept watching.

The article was shared widely. It was quoted in three other pieces. A politician used it in a speech about the dangers of informal community organisations operating outside regulatory frameworks. Two organisations that had been using the questions quietly stopped mentioning them publicly.
Tali noted all of this. She kept doing the work.
Three weeks after the article appeared, a man came to the rooftop. He was in his fifties, well-dressed, with the careful manner of someone who had prepared what he was going to say.

His name was Dr. Mehmet. He was a sociologist at a university in the city. He had read the article and had then spent three weeks researching what the article had described and had concluded that the article was partially correct and substantially misleading.
He had come to say this in person rather than in writing because, he said, he had learned from his own work that these conversations were better face to face.
Tali offered him tea.

He sat. He told her what he had found. He was precise and specific and did not flatter her — he identified several cases where the approach had caused harm, where the emphasis on informal resolution had meant that people who needed professional intervention had not received it, where the three questions had been applied by people who had not understood their limits.
She listened to all of it.
*"You're right,"* she said. *"About those cases. I know about some of them. I think about them."*
*"What do you do with them?"*

*"I add them to what I know. I try to be clearer, when I teach the questions, about what they're not for. They're not a substitute for a doctor or a lawyer or a social worker. They're not an excuse to avoid calling for help when help is needed. They're a way of seeing more clearly — not a way of acting alone."*
He thought about this. *"That distinction doesn't come through in how people are using them."*
*"I know. That's a real problem."*
*"What are you going to do about it?"*
She looked at him. *"I'm going to add a fourth question."*
He raised an eyebrow.

*"Is this something I should be handling alone, or does someone with more knowledge or authority need to be involved?"* she said. *"That's the fourth question. It should have always been there. I left it out because I was thinking about the people who never ask for help at all. I forgot about the people who use it as an excuse not to."*
Dr. Mehmet looked at her for a long moment.
*"You're seventeen,"* he said.
*"That's remarkable."*
*"It's just paying attention,"* she said. *"Anyone can do it."*
He came back the following Thursday. He brought a colleague. The colleague brought questions of her own.
The fourth question began to travel alongside the other three.

title: What James Heard on the Radio
paragraphs: James had been running his radio network for four years.

It had grown from three frequencies and eleven contacts to nineteen frequencies and several hundred people across four cities — not a large number by any measure, but dense with the kind of information that official channels missed: what was actually happening on which street, who needed what, where the informal systems were working and where they were breaking down.
On a Wednesday evening in November he heard something that made him sit very still.

A conversation between two men he did not know, on a frequency that was not one of his. They were not trying to be covert — they were simply talking, the way people talk when they do not think anyone is listening, which meant they were talking plainly.
They were talking about the building.

Not abstractly. Specifically — the address, the rooftop, the water system, the people who came on Thursdays. One of them said: *the problem is it keeps growing.* The other said: *then we deal with it before it gets bigger.*
James sat with his headphones on for a long time after the conversation ended.
He did not panic. He had been in worse situations than this and had learned that panic consumed the time you needed for thinking.
He thought.
Then he went upstairs.
Tali was on the rooftop with her mother. He came up through the hatch and sat down and told them what he had heard, plainly, without embellishment.
Her mother's expression tightened. Tali watched her and recognised it — the specific recalibration of someone who has lived through situations where conversations like this had consequences.
*"Who are they?"* her mother asked.

*"I don't know yet. The frequency suggested someone with access to commercial communications equipment. Not government — the language was wrong for government. Someone with money and a reason to care."*
*"The water company,"* Tali said.
James looked at her.

*"We've been routing around them for two years. They've been losing customers in this district — people who used to pay for bottled water because the tap ran dry. Now the tap runs. They're losing money."* She paused. *"I should have thought about this earlier."*
*"What do we do?"* her mother said.
Tali thought about the three questions. Applied them to herself, which she did less often than she should.
The real pain — for the water company — was financial. They had a product that was losing market value because a problem they had benefited from had been fixed.
The forgotten person in this situation was the district's residents — the actual customers, the people both sides were, in different ways, fighting over.
The third question: what could she do right now?
*"Document everything,"* she said. *"The water system — every pipe, every valve, every modification. In enough detail that if the building disappeared tomorrow, someone else could rebuild it."*
*"That takes weeks,"* James said.
*"Then we start tonight."*
They spent three weeks documenting.

Fatima drew blueprints with the focused urgency of someone who understood that knowledge only survives if it is written down and distributed widely enough that no single point can destroy it. Carlos photographed every junction, every valve, every modification they had made to the original system. James compiled contact lists — every person in the network, every frequency, every informal connection that the rooftop had become the centre of.

Tali wrote. She wrote the history of the building — what they had done and how and why. She wrote the three questions in the simplest language she could find, with examples, with the fourth question included. She wrote it in three languages. She asked Nadia, who had contacts she no longer had, to help distribute it.
Nadia distributed it.

Within two weeks it existed in more places than could be simultaneously removed. Not published grandly — sent quietly to people who would keep it, teachers and community workers and the kind of people who print things out and put them in folders.

*"We've been behaving as if this place is permanent,"* Tali told the Thursday gathering. *"It's not permanent. Nothing is permanent. The question was never whether this building would last. It was whether what we've learned here would last. Now it will, regardless of what happens to the building."*
Fatima looked up from her blueprints. *"Good thinking,"* she said. *"Forty years too late for my water system. Not too late for yours."*
The threat, when it came, was not a raid or a confrontation or anything dramatic.

It was a letter. From a firm of lawyers, on behalf of a company whose name Tali did not recognise but which James identified within an hour as a subsidiary of the water company. The letter claimed that modifications to the building's water system had been made without authorisation and constituted illegal interference with licensed infrastructure.
The letter gave them thirty days to restore the system to its original condition.
Carlos read it and said several things that are not recorded here.

Fatima read it and said: *"They're not wrong about the legal position. What they're not saying is that the original condition was a system that hadn't provided water to this district in eleven years."*
Tali read it and said: *"Who is not being seen in this situation?"*
Nobody answered immediately.
*"The residents,"* James said eventually. *"Who have had water for two years and are about to be told they won't anymore. They're not party to this letter. They haven't been asked."*
*"No,"* Tali said. *"They haven't."*
She went downstairs and knocked on every door in the building.
Then she knocked on every door in the two buildings on either side.
She did not tell people what to do. She showed them the letter. She told them what it meant. She asked each of them the same question: *"What do you want to do about this?"*
What happened next was not Tali's plan. She had no plan beyond the question.

What happened was that thirty-seven residents — people who had been living alongside each other for years without necessarily knowing each other well — discovered that they had something in common that mattered enough to act on.

They contacted the local housing authority. They contacted a legal aid organisation — Yusuf's Thursday legal aid clinic, as it happened, which had by now developed a reputation for taking cases that other firms found inconvenient. They contacted Dr. Mehmet, who had become a careful ally and who knew which university departments had been studying informal water systems in exactly this kind of district.

They contacted a journalist. Not Brennan — a different one. A local one who knew the district and had been watching what had been built here with the specific attention of someone who understood its significance.
She wrote a story. Not about Tali — about the thirty-seven residents and the water and the lawyer's letter and the subsidiary company and the eleven years before the water came back.
The letter was quietly withdrawn six weeks later.
No announcement. No apology. The threat simply stopped.
The water kept running.

title: What Carlos Said When He Left
paragraphs: Carlos left on a Thursday.

Not dramatically — he told Tali the week before, gave her time to absorb it, showed up on the last Thursday to eat Mira's food and argue with James one more time about something nobody else could follow.
On the way out he stopped beside Tali on the rooftop.
*"I got a real job,"* he said. *"Good money. Benefits. Work I'm actually trained to do."*
*"I know,"* she said. *"You told me."*
*"I'm not abandoning this."*
*"I know that too."*
He was quiet for a moment. *"I used to think all of this was naive. Girl on a rooftop with three questions. I thought it would last six months."*
*"You told me that."*
*"You didn't argue."*
*"You weren't wrong to think it. Most things like this do last six months."*
*"What made this different?"*

She thought about it. *"Nothing was owned. Nobody was in charge. There was no centre that could be removed. It was just people who knew each other, helping each other, asking the questions. That's hard to stop because there's nothing to stop. You can't arrest a question."*
Carlos looked at the city for a while.
*"I'm going to use the questions at the new job,"* he said. *"The people I'm working with — they're good but they don't ask. They just fix. I'm going to ask."*
*"That's the whole point,"* Tali said.
*"I know."* He picked up his bag. *"You're going to be fine."*
*"I know."*
*"I'm going to come back for Thursdays."*
*"I know that too."*
He went downstairs.

He did come back for Thursdays. Not every Thursday — he was busy, the job was demanding, he had a life that had expanded beyond the building now. But most Thursdays. And when he came he brought his questions and his bad jokes and his particular talent for turning a wrench at exactly the right moment, and the rooftop was better for it.
The work continued.
It always continued.

title: Tali at Eighteen
paragraphs: On the morning of her eighteenth birthday — still only approximately known, still marked by the month rather than the exact day — Tali sat on the rooftop and did what she had done at sixteen and before that at fourteen: she looked at the city and tried to see it clearly.
Two years had passed since her mother had climbed the stairs.
Her mother was here now, had been here for five years, and the adjustment — which had been harder than Tali had expected or admitted to anyone — had settled into something real.

The first months had been the particular difficulty of two people who had each built a self in the other's absence and now had to find out whether those selves could share a space. Her mother arranged things in ways that were not wrong but were not Tali's ways. She asked questions about where Tali had been and what she had eaten and whether she was sleeping, and Tali heard these questions as surveillance rather than love, and said so, and her mother went quiet in the specific way of someone who has been hurt and is deciding whether to show it.

There was a fight in the fourth month. A real one — raised voices, the kind that leave something in the air afterward. Her mother had said: *"I spent five years not knowing if you were alive. Can you not tell me when you will be home?"* And Tali had said: *"I have been making my own decisions since I was eleven years old. I don't know how to be a person who checks in."* And her mother had said: *"I know. I know that. And I know whose fault that is."*
The silence after that had lasted three days.
On the fourth day Tali had applied the questions to the situation, slowly and painfully, in the privacy of her own mind.

The real pain: not the argument about coming home. Her mother had spent five years believing her daughter might be dead. The need to know Tali was safe was not control — it was the residue of five years of not knowing, and it was not going to disappear simply because Tali had arrived on the rooftop intact.

Who was not being seen: her mother. Tali had been so focused on the difficulty of adjusting to being known again, to having someone whose first thought in the morning was of her, that she had failed to see what her mother was carrying into every question, every request, every moment of ordinary maternal attention.
What could she do?

She went downstairs. She knocked on her mother's door. She said: *"I understand why you ask. I'm going to try to tell you when I'm coming home. Not because I need to, but because you do. And what you need is as real as what I need."*
Her mother had looked at her for a long moment.
Then she said: *"You used the questions on us."*
*"Did it work?"*
*"Ask me in a year."*
It had worked. Not immediately, not perfectly, but in the slow way that real things work — by being applied consistently, with honesty, over time.

It had also reminded Tali of something she had known intellectually for years but had not felt until now: the questions were hardest to ask about the people you loved most. Because the answers required the most change.
Her mother was downstairs making tea. She would bring it up in a few minutes without asking if Tali wanted it, because she had learned that Tali always wanted it but rarely asked.
Tali looked at the city.

The water ran. The Thursday gatherings continued. The questions were somewhere she could not track or contain — in cities she had never visited, in languages she could not read, in situations she would never know about. Dr. Mehmet had written a paper about informal community resilience that referenced the three questions — and now the four questions — and the paper had been read by people who would use it and people who would argue with it and people who would do nothing with it at all, and that was fine.

James was still on the radio. Fatima was still drawing blueprints, slower now, the sessions shorter, but still drawing. Mira cooked on Thursdays. Nadia wrote carefully and stayed longer and went back. The boy from next door — he had told her his name eventually, Karim — came every week and sometimes brought other people and sometimes came alone and sat in the corner and that was fine too.
The threat from the water company had not returned. Perhaps it would. Perhaps something else would come instead. The work had never been safe and she had never expected it to be.
What she had expected — what she had learned to expect — was that the work would continue regardless. Not because she would always be here. Because the work did not belong to her.
It belonged to anyone who picked it up.
Her mother came up the stairs with two cups of tea and sat beside her.
They looked at the city together.
*"What are you thinking?"* her mother asked. She always asked this.
*"I'm thinking about what comes next,"* Tali said.
*"I don't know. That's new. For a long time I always knew what came next — the next pipe, the next person, the next question. Now I can see further and I'm not sure what I'm looking at."*
*"That's called growing up,"* her mother said.
*"Is it always this uncomfortable?"*
*"Good to know."*
They drank their tea.
Below them a child was crying and then stopped crying and then, after a moment, laughed. Somewhere a door opened and closed. The smell of cooking drifted up from one of the floors below.
*"What do you want?"* her mother said. *"Not what needs doing. What do you want?"*
Tali had been asked this before. She had given the same answer she always gave — enough to eat, enough sleep, someone who would notice if she disappeared.
She gave a different answer now.
*"I want to go somewhere,"* she said. *"Somewhere I've never been. I want to see if the questions work somewhere completely different. Somewhere I don't know anyone and nobody knows me."*
Her mother was quiet.
*"Not forever,"* Tali said. *"But for a while."*
*"Where?"*
*"I don't know yet."*

Her mother looked at her. Tali felt the layer underneath — the worry, which was real, and the recognition, which was older than the worry. The recognition of a person who had spent her own life moving toward difficult things rather than away from them.
*"When?"* her mother said.
*"Not yet. There are things here that need finishing first."*
*"There will always be things that need finishing,"* her mother said. *"You know that."*
*"I know. But these specific things. Fatima's heart. Karim's situation. The fourth question — I want to see it travelling properly before I go."*
Her mother nodded slowly.
*"And then?"*
*"And then I go,"* Tali said. *"And I come back. And I go again. That's what this is, isn't it? You move. You pay attention. You ask the questions. You come back when you can."*
Her mother looked at the city for a long time.
*"Yes,"* she said. *"That's what it is."*
She put her arm around Tali.

They sat like that as the morning opened up below them — the city beginning its day, indifferent and enormous and full of people trying, the same as it had always been, the same as it would always be.
The tea went cold. Neither of them moved.
**END OF PART SEVEN**
**END OF VOLUME THREE**
*Volume Four: Tali Moves — in which she goes somewhere she has never been, knowing nobody, with three questions and a fourth, and discovers what the questions look like when you are the stranger.*
*The four questions:*

*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*
*Is this something I should handle alone, or does someone with more knowledge or authority need to be involved?*

*Ask them anywhere.*
*They work anywhere.*
*That is the point.*

*She is eighteen.*
*She has never been anywhere except the places she was forced to go.*
*Now she chooses.*
*This volume is about what happens when you take the questions somewhere new.*
*And what they show you about yourself.*

title: The Decision
paragraphs: She did not leave immediately.
There were, as she had told her mother, things that needed finishing first.

Fatima's heart procedure was scheduled for March. Tali wanted to be there before and after. Not because Fatima needed her specifically — Fatima was the kind of person who needed nobody specifically and had said so repeatedly and was also, underneath this, deeply glad to have people around her, which she would never say directly but which was visible if you paid attention.

Karim's situation at home had shifted — the father had left, not dramatically, simply one morning he was not there and did not come back, and the mother had entered the specific complicated relief of a woman who has escaped something and is not yet sure what she is allowed to feel. Tali had been sitting with her on Tuesday mornings, asking the questions, watching the slowly changing quality of the answers. She wanted to see that through to something stable before she left.

The fourth question needed more time to travel properly. Dr. Mehmet had been incorporating it into his teaching and had identified several cases where it had prevented harm — where people had used it to recognise that a situation needed professional intervention rather than informal support. But it was still new and people were still learning its edges and she wanted to be reachable while that happened.
She spent three months finishing.
Fatima's procedure went well. She came home thinner and slower and with a look in her eyes that Tali recognised as someone who has been reminded, very directly, that the time is finite.
She drew blueprints the afternoon she came home. Not for long — an hour, maybe less. But she drew.
*"Don't fuss,"* she told Tali, who was not fussing but was sitting nearby in the way that constituted fussing.
*"I'm just sitting here,"* Tali said.
*"That's fussing."*
*"Then I'm fussing."*
Fatima made a sound that might have been a laugh. She drew for another twenty minutes. Then she put her pencil down and looked at Tali.
*"Where are you going?"* she said. She had known Tali was going. Nobody had told her. She simply knew.
*"I don't know yet. Somewhere I've never been."*
*"Go somewhere with a complicated water system,"* Fatima said. *"You'll learn something useful."*
*"I'll try."*
*"And come back."*
*"I'll come back."*
Fatima picked up her pencil.
*"Good,"* she said. *"Now stop fussing and let me work."*
She left on a Tuesday in May.

Her mother walked with her to the edge of the district — not to a bus station, not to an airport, just to the point where the familiar streets gave way to the less familiar ones, which was how these journeys began.
At the corner her mother stopped.
*"I did this,"* her mother said. *"When I was twenty-three. Left everything and walked into something I didn't know."*
*"I know,"* Tali said. *"You've told me."*
*"I'm telling you again because it's different when you're the one leaving."* Her mother looked at her. *"It was the best thing I ever did. Until you."*
Tali stood with that for a moment.
Then she hugged her mother. Her mother held on — the same way she had held on when she climbed the stairs two years ago, the same grip, the same weight of everything in it.
*"Go,"* her mother said finally.
Tali went.

title: The First Place
paragraphs: The city she arrived in was large and indifferent in the way that large cities are indifferent — not hostile, just vast, with no particular interest in one more person arriving with a bag and nowhere specific to be.

She had money — not much, but enough. She had saved it over two years from the repair work, from the alterations woman who still gave her sewing work when it came, from small jobs that had accumulated into something she could travel on for a few months if she was careful.

She found a room in a building that rented to people like her — the transient, the undocumented, the between-things. The woman who ran it was sixty, suspicious, fair. She charged what the room was worth and expected it paid on time and did not ask about the rest.
Tali paid on time. She did not explain the rest.

The neighbourhood was dense and layered — multiple languages on every block, shops that sold things she had never seen, a market that ran from five in the morning until the smell of it told you it was time to leave. She spent the first week walking. Just walking. Paying attention.

She did not ask the questions yet. She was still learning the texture of the place — which streets felt safe at which hours, which faces were permanent and which were passing through, where the informal systems ran and where the official ones stopped.
Her mother had taught her this. You read a place before you act in it.
She read.
On the eighth day she found the thing that needed fixing.
It was not water this time. It was a school.

A primary school two streets from her room, serving the children of the neighbourhood. It was underfunded and overcrowded and the teachers were doing their best in the way that teachers doing their best in impossible conditions do their best — with a kind of determined exhaustion that Tali recognised from her own childhood.
But that was not the thing.
The thing was the children who were not in the school.

She noticed them because she was paying attention. Children of the right age, on the streets during school hours, not in any distress — just present, in doorways and alleys and the edges of the market. Not truant exactly. Simply not there.

She found out why by asking. Not the questions yet — just ordinary questions, the kind that any stranger might ask. She asked a market stallholder. She asked a woman hanging washing. She asked a man fixing a bicycle outside a building.
The answers, across three days of asking, assembled into a picture.

The school required a registration document. The registration document required a proof of address. The proof of address required a utility bill. The utility bills for this neighbourhood came in the landlord's name, not the tenants' names. The tenants — many of them in the same position as Tali, between things, undocumented, transient — could not get a utility bill. Could not get a proof of address. Could not register their children.
The children were not in school because a piece of paper was missing.
Not a significant piece of paper. Not an insurmountable barrier. Just a piece of paper that nobody had thought to find a way around.
Tali sat on the step outside her room and thought about this.
Then she applied the questions.
The real pain: not administrative — human. Children not learning. Parents who wanted their children educated and had no way to make it happen. Teachers who saw empty seats and could not fill them.

The forgotten person: the school's head teacher. Who had probably been dealing with this problem for years and had tried various things and had possibly found partial solutions that nobody knew about.
What could she do right now?
She went to the school.

The head teacher was a woman named Marta. She was fifty-one, had been running the school for twelve years, and had the specific weariness of someone who has been fighting the same bureaucratic wall for a long time without making a dent.
Tali asked if she could sit with her for twenty minutes.
Marta looked at her with the expression of someone who had learned to be careful about who she gave her time to.
*"Who are you?"* she said.
*"Someone who noticed the children who aren't here. I wanted to ask what you see from where you are standing."*
Marta stared at her for a moment.
Then she said: *"Come in."*

Marta had, it turned out, been fighting this problem for nine years. She had found partial solutions — a sympathetic housing officer who would occasionally write letters, a community organisation that had helped in two cases, a workaround involving a local councillor that had worked three times and then stopped working when the councillor changed.
She had never had anyone come in and ask what she saw.
She talked for forty minutes. Tali listened.

What emerged from the listening: the problem was not the regulation itself, which had exceptions built into it for exactly this kind of situation. The problem was that nobody in the school's administration had time to research the exceptions, apply for them individually for each child, and chase the responses. The process existed. The capacity to use it did not.
*"What would you need,"* Tali said, *"to clear the backlog? How many children are we talking about?"*
*"Fourteen currently. There have been more. Some families move on."*
*"If someone helped you with the paperwork — researched the exceptions, prepared the applications — could you submit them?"*
Marta looked at her carefully. *"Who is this someone?"*
*"Me. For now. While I'm here."*
*"You know how to do this?"*
*"I know how to research things and how to write clearly and how to be persistent with bureaucracies. That's most of what paperwork requires."*
Marta was quiet for a moment.
*"Why?"* she said. Not suspiciously — genuinely. She had learned to ask why.
