*"Because fourteen children aren't in school because of a piece of paper. That's fixable. I'm here and I have time."*
Marta looked at her for a long time with the expression of someone reassessing a situation.
*"Come back tomorrow,"* she said. *"I'll have the files ready."*
It took six weeks.

Six weeks of research, of writing careful letters in a language she was still learning, of being told no and asking why and finding the regulation that said yes and citing it. Six weeks of Marta signing the letters and Tali following up and both of them learning the specific shape of this particular bureaucratic wall and where the doors in it were.
Fourteen children enrolled.
Not all at once — the process was staggered, each case slightly different, each requiring its own path through the exceptions. But by the end of the six weeks, fourteen children were in school.
Marta stood in her office on the last day and looked at Tali.
*"What do you want for this?"* she said.
*"Nothing,"* Tali said. *"But the process — the research, the letters, the exceptions — write it down. All of it. So that when this happens again, which it will, you or someone else can use it."*
Marta wrote it down.
She sent copies to three other schools in similar neighbourhoods that had the same problem.
Two of those schools used it within the year.

title: What She Learned by Being the Stranger
paragraphs: She stayed in the city for four months.

In that time she helped Marta's school. She fixed things in the building where she lived, paying for her room in repair work when the money ran low. She found, through the market stallholder who had first answered her questions, a network of women who ran an informal childcare arrangement and needed someone to help with the administration — keeping track of who had paid, who owed, who needed what on which day. She did this for six weeks, sitting in the back of a shop in the early mornings before the market opened.
She asked the questions everywhere. Not always formally — not always explicitly. Sometimes just as a habit of attention, of asking what was actually there rather than what was easier to see.
She learned things she could not have learned on the rooftop.

She learned what it felt like to be the one who did not know the language well enough. Who could not read a sign quickly. Who had to ask for help with things that everyone around her did automatically. She had known this intellectually — had grown up in it, in fact, in the years of moving through new places. But she had been young enough, then, to absorb it without noticing. Now she noticed.

It was useful. It kept her from forgetting that the first question — *what is the real pain?* — required actual listening, not assumption. Every time she thought she understood a situation and then asked and discovered she had not understood it at all, she filed the correction. She had more corrections here, in four months, than she had had in four years on the rooftop.

She learned that the questions worked differently when you were not known. On the rooftop she had a reputation — people came to her already half-trusting her, already predisposed to answer honestly because they had seen or heard what happened when they did. Here she was nobody. The questions worked anyway, but more slowly, and only if she had done the work first of being present and paying attention and not rushing.
The trust had to be earned every time. That was not a problem. It was the correct state of things.

She learned that Fatima had been right about the water systems. Every city had its equivalent of a buried pipe — something that had worked once and been covered over by the layers of politics and development and neglect, something that was still there if anyone was willing to dig for it. The school's administrative exceptions were this city's buried pipe. The informal childcare network was another version of it. The city was full of buried pipes.
She wrote all of this down.
Not for publication. For herself. The notebook was filling up.
On the last day before she left she went back to Marta's school.

The children she had helped enroll were there. She could see them through the window of a classroom — eleven of the fourteen, the other three having moved on or away. They were learning. That was all. Just learning, which was ordinary and was also, from where she was standing, extraordinary.
Marta found her at the window.
*"Going?"* she said.
*"Tomorrow."*
*"Where next?"*
*"I don't know yet."*
Marta was quiet for a moment. *"Leave me your contact. Not for anything specific. In case something comes up that the notes don't cover."*
Tali left her contact.
She went back to her room and packed what she had arrived with — the bag, the photographs, the book, the notebook that was now heavier than when she had started.
She left the next morning.

title: Three More Cities
paragraphs: She did not write detailed accounts of the three cities that followed.

Not because nothing happened — things happened in each of them, small real things of the kind that she had come to understand were the only things that lasted. But because to describe each one in detail would be to suggest that each one was a discrete story with a beginning and a middle and a conclusion, and that was not how it felt from inside.

From inside it felt like one continuous thing. One long act of paying attention that moved through different locations and different languages and different variations of the same fundamental situation: people with needs that were not being met because the connection between the need and the resource had not been made.

She made connections. She asked the questions. She fixed what she could fix and referred what she could not. She stayed long enough to see things begin to move and not long enough to see them through, because staying long enough to see everything through would have meant not moving at all.

She learned, in the second city, that the questions were already there before she arrived. A community organisation was using something almost identical — they had arrived at it independently, through their own experience of what worked. She sat with them for two weeks and they compared notes and found that the differences between their versions were more about language than substance. She left with two adjustments to her own understanding.

She learned, in the third city, that the fourth question — *is this something I should handle alone?* — was the one that people resisted most. Not because it was wrong but because it required a specific kind of honesty that was difficult: the admission that you had limits, that your good intentions were not sufficient, that sometimes the most helpful thing was to step back and point toward someone who knew more. People did not like this. She understood why. She had not liked it herself, when she first added the question.
She learned, in the fourth city, that sometimes the most important thing was to leave.

She had been in a situation there — a community conflict that was old and deep and had been given a new surface recently by an economic pressure that everyone was feeling — where she had begun to understand the situation well enough to see what was needed. She had started to see herself as necessary to the resolution.
And then she had asked the second question of herself: *who is not being seen here?*

The answer was: everyone involved in the conflict, before she arrived. The conflict was not new. The people in it had been navigating it for years. They had their own partial understandings, their own informal systems, their own slow processes of negotiation. She had arrived and begun, unconsciously, to position herself as the person who could see it clearly.
Which was exactly what the article had said about her. What the article had gotten wrong about the rooftop. What she could now see herself doing in this city.
She left.
Not because the conflict was unresolvable. Because she was not the one to resolve it. The people in it were. Her job was to ask the questions and then get out of the way.
She left the fourth question written on a card and gave it to two people she trusted in the city, and she went.
She had been travelling for eleven months when she decided to go home.

Not because she had finished. The work was never finished. But because the rooftop was a specific thing in the world and it was hers in the way that a place you have built is yours — not ownership, but belonging — and she had been away long enough to miss it honestly.

She also missed her mother. Which she had known she would and had accepted and had felt every day and had continued moving anyway, because moving was what the work required and her mother was the kind of person who understood this even when it cost her.
She sent a message through James's network: *I'm coming back. Thursday if the road holds.*
James replied within an hour: *Road holds. Mira is cooking.*
She started walking.

title: The Return
paragraphs: She arrived on a Thursday evening.

The rooftop was full. More people than when she had left — some she recognised, several she did not. The new faces had the particular quality of people who had been coming long enough to be comfortable but not so long that they had stopped noticing what was extraordinary about the place.

Her mother was there. She had known Tali was coming — James's network was not subtle — and she was sitting in her usual spot with the particular quality of stillness that Tali recognised as someone who has been waiting and has decided not to show that they have been waiting.
She looked up when Tali came through the hatch.
She did not say anything. Neither did Tali. They looked at each other across the full rooftop.
Then Tali sat down beside her.
Her mother passed her a bowl of Mira's food without asking.
Tali ate.

Around them the Thursday gathering went on — questions being asked, stories being told, the ordinary extraordinary work of people seeing each other clearly. James argued with someone about something. A child fell asleep against Fatima, who had come tonight despite everything, who was slower and thinner but present and drawing on the edge of a napkin.

Karim was there. He caught Tali's eye across the rooftop and raised his chin — the particular greeting of someone who has passed through something and come out the other side and wants you to know without making a speech about it.
She raised her chin back.
*"How was it?"* her mother said quietly.
*"Hard. Good. Different."*
*"Did the questions work?"*
*"Yes. And no. And differently than here. Mostly yes."*
Her mother nodded. *"What did you learn?"*
Tali thought about the notebook. The corrections. The second city with its own version of the questions. The fourth city and the moment she had caught herself becoming the problem.

*"I learned that the questions are not mine,"* she said. *"I knew this before. But I didn't feel it until I was somewhere nobody had heard of me. The questions were already there. People were already asking versions of them. All I did was carry one version to places that had different versions, and we compared notes."*
*"That sounds like humbling,"* her mother said.
*"It was. It was also the best possible thing."*
Her mother looked at her.
*"You're different,"* she said.
*"I've been away for eleven months."*
*"That's not why."*
Tali thought about it.

*"I think I stopped being afraid,"* she said. *"Not of everything. Of the questions being wrong, or not working, or being mine in a way that made them fragile. They're not fragile. They were here before I was born. They'll be here after I'm gone. I'm just one person who carried them for a while."*
Her mother was quiet for a long time.

*"Your grandmother used to say something like that,"* she said. *"About kindness. She said kindness didn't belong to any one person. It was more like water — it existed, and people could carry it or block it, but it was always there waiting."*
Tali looked at her. *"You never told me that."*
*"I'm telling you now."*
They sat with it.

Below them the city went about its business — the same city, the same indifference, the same enormous human effort of people trying to live well in difficult circumstances. The same as it had been when she left. The same as it would be when she left again.

Because she would leave again. She knew this now. The rooftop was home and she would always come back to it, but the work was not only here. The work was anywhere someone was willing to ask the questions.
Anywhere a person could look at another person and ask: what do you actually need?
And then listen.
**END OF PART EIGHT**
**END OF VOLUME FOUR**

*Volume Five: What Remains — in which Tali is older, and the questions are older, and some of the people who carried them are gone, and what has been built must decide what it wants to be when it grows up.*
*The four questions:*

*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*
*Is this something I should handle alone, or does someone with more knowledge need to be involved?*

*They were here before you.*
*They will be here after you.*
*Carry them while you can.*

*She is twenty-three.*
*Nine years have passed since the rooftop began.*
*Some of the people who carried the questions are gone.*
*Some things that were built have been tested and survived.*
*Some have not survived.*
*This volume is about what remains.*
*And what to do with it.*

title: Fatima
paragraphs: Fatima died on a Wednesday morning in February.

Not on the rooftop — in hospital, in a bed, with a view of the city she had spent her life building and rebuilding. Her daughter was there. Tali was there. Carlos came in the evening and sat for an hour without speaking.

She had been declining for months. Not quickly — Fatima did not do anything quickly that she could do slowly. But the direction had been clear, and she had been clear about it, and she had spent the last months the way she had spent all her months: drawing blueprints.

The last blueprint was on her bedside table when she died. A detailed plan for a water reclamation system — not for the building, which already had everything it needed, but for a larger area, three districts, something that would require significant funding and political will and years of work.
Nobody had asked her to draw it.
She drew it anyway.
Because that was who Fatima was: a person who could see what was possible and could not not draw it, regardless of whether she would be there to build it.
Tali took the blueprint home. She put it in the box with the letters.
She did not immediately know what to do with it. That was fine. Some things needed to sit before they became clear.
The Thursday gathering after Fatima's death was different.

Not quiet — it was never quiet, the Thursday gatherings were the opposite of quiet, they were full of the specific noise of people being genuinely present with each other. But underneath the noise there was a register that had not been there before. A frequency, low and constant, like the sound of a building settling.
Mira cooked more food than usual. This was her way of meeting large feelings — she addressed them through feeding people. Nobody commented on this. Everyone ate more than usual.
Karim, who was nineteen now and had been coming for five years and was one of the people Tali trusted most on the rooftop, said toward the end of the evening: *"Who draws the blueprints now?"*
He did not mean it literally. Everyone understood that he did not mean it literally.
Tali looked at him. *"You do. All of you."*
*"We don't know how to do what she did."*
*"She didn't know how when she started either,"* Tali said. *"She learned by doing it. She would tell you the same thing and probably add that you were wasting her time by asking."*
A sound went around the rooftop that was somewhere between a laugh and something else.
*"She would,"* Carlos said, from the wall where he sat.
They sat with Fatima's absence for a while. Not filling it — that was the wrong instinct. Just sitting with it, because that was what you did with the people who had mattered.
Then the evening continued.
That, Tali thought, was the most honest tribute she could imagine for Fatima: the work continuing.

title: What the Building Became
paragraphs: In the five years since the water came back, the building had changed.

Not structurally — it was still the same crumbling structure with no official owner, still held together by the informal agreement of its residents that holding it together was worth the effort. But its character had changed in the way that places change when people invest genuine attention in them.

The ground floor had become a kind of informal workshop. Not organised, not branded — just a space where tools lived and where people came to fix things and where, if you needed help fixing something, you could usually find someone who knew how. It had started with Tali's soldering iron and Carlos's wrenches and had grown from there. The space had been cleaned and organised by residents who had decided, without being asked, that a usable workshop was better than an unusable one.

The second floor had two families who had been there for years and who had become, in the way of people who live alongside each other long enough, something like a small community within the larger one. They shared meals occasionally. They watched each other's children when needed. They argued sometimes. All of this was ordinary and was also exactly what had been missing before.

The rooftop was still the rooftop. Tali's mattress was still there, though she used it less — she had a room on the third floor now, proper walls and a door, which her mother had insisted on with the particular insistence of a woman who has spent enough of her life sleeping under tarps. The rooftop was still where the Thursday gatherings happened, still where Tali sat in the early mornings, still where the important conversations took place.

James was still in the basement with his radios. Slower now, his bad days more frequent, but still there when it mattered — still able to reach the people who needed reaching, still running the network that had grown, over five years, into something that covered most of the district and parts of several others.

Mira was still there. She had moved into the building two years ago, had a room on the first floor, cooked on Thursdays and occasionally on other days. She talked about her son sometimes. Not often. But sometimes, which was more than before.

The boy — Karim — was twenty and had a job and still came on Thursdays and had, over the past year, begun doing something Tali had not asked him to do: he was teaching the questions to the younger people who came to the rooftop, in the way that someone who has learned something teaches it — not formally, just by asking the questions out loud and waiting for people to find their own answers.

He was better at it than Tali had been at his age. She told him this. He told her she was wrong. She told him she was not. He told her she was biased. She told him that was possible but her observation still stood.
He kept doing it.

Dr. Mehmet had published two more papers. The fourth question had become its own subject of academic interest — several researchers in different countries were studying the conditions under which it was applied correctly and the conditions under which it was avoided. This was, Tali felt, somewhat absurd, but she also understood that understanding something required examining it from every angle, including the academic one.

He came to the rooftop occasionally. He brought colleagues sometimes. He was always careful to come as a participant rather than an observer, which was a distinction he had understood from the beginning and that she respected him for.

Nadia was still writing. She had published a collection of pieces about the district and the people in it — not about Tali, she had been firm about this, but about the specific people and situations that had moved through the rooftop over five years. The collection had been read by people in places they had never been and had generated the specific response that good writing generates: letters from strangers saying *this is exactly what I have been trying to do, I did not have words for it until now.*
The questions themselves were, by this point, untraceable.

Tali had stopped trying to track them two years ago. They existed in too many forms, in too many languages, in too many contexts. Some of those forms were ones she would have recognised. Some were not. Some had been modified in ways that she thought were improvements. Some had been modified in ways that she thought missed the point. All of them were beyond her influence now.
This was correct. This was what she had always said she wanted.

She found, in honest moments, that she had complicated feelings about it. The questions she had shaped and carried and taught and refined over years were now shaped and carried and taught and refined by other people who would make their own decisions about them. Some of those decisions would be ones she agreed with. Some would not.
This was how it was supposed to work.
She sat with the complicated feelings and did not act on them. The feelings were hers. The questions were not.

title: The Letter She Didn't Expect
paragraphs: It came on a Tuesday in October, five years and four months after the water first came back.
She recognised the handwriting immediately — not her mother's, not any of the regulars. She turned it over. No return address. The postmark was from a city in a country she had never visited.
Inside: two pages, careful handwriting, the particular precision of someone writing in a language that was not their first.
The letter was from Amrita.

Not the Amrita from Priya's platform — a different Amrita. A woman who had been living in the city whose postmark was on the envelope. A woman who had, three years earlier, been in a situation she described carefully and without drama: a situation from which she had not known how to leave, in which she had felt invisible and ashamed and entirely alone.
Someone had given her the questions. She did not know who — a card, left anonymously in a community centre where she sometimes went to use the internet. The card had the four questions on it.
She had applied the first question to herself.

The real pain: not the situation itself, which was the surface. The real pain was that she had come to believe she did not deserve better. That the situation was what she was worth. That asking for help was an imposition on people who had real problems.
The second question had broken something open.
Who was not being seen?
Her.
Not by the people around her, though that too. By herself. She had stopped seeing herself as a person whose needs were real.

*I know this sounds very internal,* the letter said. *I know the questions are meant for situations with other people. But the most important thing they did for me was make me a person who could answer them honestly about myself. Once I could do that, I could see the situation clearly. And once I could see it clearly, I could leave it.*

She had left. She was elsewhere now. She was, the letter said, fine — not fine in the way of someone performing fineness, but fine in the way of someone who has been through something hard and has come out the other side still standing.
She had written because she wanted Tali to know.

Not to thank her — she did not know Tali, had never heard of Tali. She had written to whoever had made the card, to tell them that the questions had worked in a way she did not think they were intended to work, and that perhaps that was worth knowing.
Tali read the letter three times.
Then she went and sat beside her mother, who was reading in the afternoon light, and handed her the letter without explanation.
Her mother read it. She was quiet for a long time.
*"You didn't make the card,"* her mother said.
*"No. I don't know who did."*
*"Someone did."*
*"Someone who had the questions gave them to someone else. Who gave them to someone else. Who eventually left a card in a community centre. Which reached this woman."*
Her mother looked at her. *"That's the whole thing, isn't it. That's the whole thing you've been trying to describe for five years."*
*"Yes,"* Tali said. *"That's it."*
Her mother was quiet for another moment.
Then she said: *"Your grandmother would have had a word for this. She had words for everything."*
*"What word?"*

Her mother thought about it. *"She would have called it — the thing that moves between people when they aren't looking. The thing that passes through. She didn't believe in religion exactly. But she believed in this. That good things, once released, keep moving. You can't see where they go. But they go."*
Tali sat with that.

*"I want to write back,"* she said. *"To tell her that whoever made the card was not me. That the questions came from a girl on a rooftop who got them from her mother who got them from her own survival. That they belong to nobody and travel everywhere. That the way she used them — turned them inward first, before she could turn them outward — that is not a misuse. That is perhaps the most important use of all."*
*"Then write that,"* her mother said.
Tali wrote it.
She sent it through the chain of hands to the address on the letter.
She did not know if it arrived.
She did not need to know.

title: James
paragraphs: James left differently than Fatima.

Not death — James was, in the language of his doctors, stable, which meant the bad days were managed and the good days were real and the balance between them was, for now, liveable. What changed was that his sister came.

She had been in another country for twelve years. She came back because their mother had died and she had come for the funeral and had arrived to find her brother in a basement with three radios and a dog and a life that was, she told Tali directly and without apology, not what she had hoped for him.
Tali met her once, briefly. She was a direct woman in her fifties, the kind of directness that comes from long experience of saying difficult things to people who needed to hear them.
*"He tells me you've looked after him,"* she said.
*"He looked after himself. He looked after a lot of other people too."*
She looked at Tali for a moment. *"He's coming to live with me. I have a house. He'll have a room. He can bring the radios."*
*"Does he know this?"*
*"We've discussed it."*
*"And Wallace?"*
*"Obviously Wallace."*

James left on a Saturday. He did not make a fuss about it, which was consistent with everything about him. He transferred the radio frequencies and the contact list to three people he trusted, with careful written instructions and an offer to be reachable for questions. He packed his radios in cases with the methodical attention of someone who has always understood that equipment is only useful if it is cared for.
Wallace wagged his tail the entire time.
On the last morning James came up to the rooftop. He sat with Tali in the early light without speaking for a while.
Then he said: *"The network runs itself now. Has for a year. I was mostly just the reason people believed in it. Now they believe in it for its own sake."*
*"Yes,"* Tali said.
*"That's how it's supposed to work."*

He looked at the city. *"I came here broken,"* he said. *"I want you to know that. I was in a bad place. I was not a good person to be around. The rooftop gave me a reason to be useful. That's a specific kind of gift. I don't have a better word for it."*
*"You gave the same thing back,"* Tali said. *"Many times over."*
He stood up.
Wallace stood up with him, tail going.
*"I'll come back for Thursdays when I can,"* he said.
*"I know."*
He went downstairs.

The radio network continued. Three people ran it now — Karim was one of them, his ear good, his patience remarkable for someone his age. It was different without James. It was also fine. Different and fine were not contradictions.

title: What Tali's Mother Said on the Fifth Anniversary
paragraphs: On the fifth anniversary of the water coming back — which was not a date anyone had formally marked, but which Tali and her mother knew — they sat on the rooftop in the evening as the light went.
*"Tell me what you would do differently,"* her mother said. *"If you could go back."*
Tali thought about it honestly.

*"I would have added the fourth question earlier. There were situations in the first two years where people used the questions as an excuse not to ask for professional help. Someone got hurt because of that. Not badly. But it could have been worse. I should have seen it sooner."*
*"What else?"*

*"I would have rested more. The collapse — when I was fourteen and my hands started shaking — I let it get to that point because I didn't know how to ask what I needed. I preached the questions and didn't apply them to myself."*
*"What else?"*

*"I would have written things down sooner. Fatima had the right instinct from the beginning — document everything, distribute the knowledge. I didn't start doing that properly until the water company threatened us. It should have been the first thing."*
Her mother nodded. *"And if you could tell your younger self one thing?"*
Tali was quiet for a moment.
*"That the questions are not magic. They are not a solution. They are a direction. Pointing in the right direction is necessary. It is not sufficient. You still have to walk."*
Her mother looked at her.
*"You were always going to figure that out,"* she said. *"You were always going to walk."*
*"I had a good model,"* Tali said.
Her mother said nothing. She did not need to.
They sat until the stars came out — the same stars that had kept their silence when Tali asked her questions at fourteen, at sixteen, at eighteen, at twenty-three. Still silent. Still honest.
Still watching.

title: The Blueprint
paragraphs: Six months after Fatima died, Tali looked at the blueprint again.

She had looked at it several times since bringing it home — had studied it, understood it, recognised in it the specific quality of Fatima's mind: the absolute commitment to seeing what was possible rather than only what was currently available.
The blueprint showed a water reclamation system for three districts. Not small. Not cheap. Requiring engineering expertise and funding and political navigation and years of sustained effort.
Fatima had drawn it on a hospital bedside notepad with a pencil that was running out of lead.
She had drawn it because she could see it. Because seeing it and not drawing it was not something she could do.
Tali applied the questions.

The real pain: three districts with inadequate water infrastructure, with all that inadequate water infrastructure meant for the people who lived in them. Not an abstract problem. She knew what inadequate water meant. She had grown up with it.
Who was not being seen: the residents of those three districts, who had been navigating inadequate infrastructure for years and who were never in the room when decisions were made about their water.
What could she do right now?
She could not build the system. She was not an engineer. She did not have the funding or the political connections.

But she had the blueprint. And she knew Dr. Mehmet, who knew people at the university with the engineering department. And she knew a journalist — Nadia — who had spent five years learning how to write about exactly this kind of thing. And she knew the residents of those three districts, or at least enough of them to know how to reach the ones she didn't know. And she had five years of demonstrated evidence that informal community systems, properly supported, could do things that official systems had failed to do.
She had the fourth question: *is this something I should handle alone, or does someone with more knowledge need to be involved?*
The answer was clear. This needed everyone.
She called a meeting.
Not on the rooftop — the rooftop was for Thursday gatherings, for the ongoing work, for the ordinary extraordinary business of seeing each other. This needed a bigger room.
She borrowed the hall of a community centre two streets away.

She invited Dr. Mehmet and three of his colleagues. She invited Nadia. She invited Carlos, who had contacts in the engineering sector from his years of work. She invited representatives from each of the three districts — not officials, not organisational spokespeople, but the people she had come to know as the ones who paid attention, the ones who knew what was actually happening on the ground.
She put Fatima's blueprint in the centre of the table.

*"This is what she saw,"* she said. *"She saw it completely. She drew it with a pencil that was almost out of lead, in a hospital, six months before she died. She didn't ask anyone whether it was realistic. She drew what was possible."*
She looked around the table.
*"I want to know if it is realistic. I want to know what it would take. I want to know who in this room can contribute something toward it and what that something is."*
She sat down.
The meeting lasted three hours.

At the end of it there was a plan. Not complete — it would take years to complete. Not funded — it would take years to fund. But real. A direction, with specific people pointing in it, each contributing what they had.
Fatima's blueprint went back in the box.
Not to be forgotten. To be referenced.
The work had begun.
**END OF PART NINE**
**END OF VOLUME FIVE**

*Volume Six: The Questions at Twenty — in which Tali is older still, and the questions have been in the world long enough to have a history, and what that history shows is both more and less than anyone expected.*
*What remains:*

*The questions.*
*The work.*
*The people who carry them.*
*The ones who are gone.*
*The blueprint on the bedside table.*
*The letter that arrived from nowhere.*
*The water that runs.*

*These things remain.*
*They are enough.*

*She is twenty-eight.*
*The questions have been in the world for fourteen years.*
*Long enough to have a history.*
*Long enough to have been used well and badly.*
*Long enough to have outlasted some of the people who carried them.*
*Long enough to be tested by things that could not have been anticipated.*
*This volume is about what that history shows.*

title: What the Questions Had Become
paragraphs: The first thing was this: the questions had been co-opted.

Not everywhere. Not completely. But in enough places, by enough organisations, in enough well-funded programmes with enough consultants and frameworks and certified facilitators, that a version of them existed which had been stripped of what made them work.

The stripped version looked like the original. It used the same words. It had diagrams and workbooks and a two-day training programme. It was taught in corporate settings and government agencies and large NGOs by people who understood the methodology but had not understood — had perhaps never been in a position to understand — what the methodology was actually pointing toward.
What it was pointing toward was this: see the person in front of you as a full human being with a real pain underneath the surface. Everything else was a way of doing that.
The stripped version had turned the pointing into the point. People learned the questions as a technique. They applied the technique. They generated outputs. The outputs were filed. Nobody was seen.

Tali had known this would happen. She had not known how to prevent it and had eventually accepted that prevention was not the correct goal. The correct goal was to keep the real version alive alongside the stripped version, to keep demonstrating what it looked like when it worked, to keep being a point of comparison.
She had been doing this for fourteen years.
She was tired of it in the specific way of someone who has been doing necessary work for a long time and has made peace with the necessity without making peace with the tiredness.
She kept doing it.
The second thing was this: the questions had saved lives.
Not metaphorically. Actually.

She knew of three cases directly — cases where someone had applied the questions to themselves, the way Amrita had, and had found in the first question the crack of light that had let them keep going. She knew these cases directly because the people involved had written to her, years later, to tell her.
She did not know how many cases she did not know about.
She had stopped trying to count. Counting was a way of needing the questions to be hers. They were not hers.
The third thing was this: Fatima's blueprint had become a construction project.

It had taken seven years from the meeting in the community centre hall. Seven years of funding applications and engineering assessments and political negotiations and community consultations and setbacks and restarts and one catastrophic funding withdrawal that had required six months of emergency scrambling to replace.

Carlos had project-managed the construction phase. He had come back to the district for it — not permanently, his life was elsewhere, but for eighteen months he had been present in the way he was always present: with his hands, with his stubbornness, with his particular talent for making things work in the physical world.
The system served three districts.
It had been running for two years.
Tali had stood at the opening ceremony and said nothing. There was a politician who gave a speech. There was a plaque. There was a photograph.
Fatima's name was on the plaque.
That was what Tali had asked for. Just that.

title: Karim at Twenty-Four
paragraphs: Karim had been asking the questions for nine years.

He had started at fourteen, in the corner of the rooftop, saying nothing. He had learned by watching — watching Tali, watching the way the questions worked on the people around him, watching what happened when they were asked well and what happened when they were asked badly. He had been a patient student. He had been patient in everything, which had surprised Tali at first — the frightened fifteen-year-old in the corner had not looked like someone with patience. He had turned out to be one of the most patient people she had ever known.

He was twenty-four now. He ran the Thursday gatherings when Tali was away, which was often. He ran them differently than she did — quieter, with more space between things, with a particular quality of stillness that the people who came had come to trust. Some people preferred his version. She had told him this. He had told her she was biased. She had told him she was not.

He had started something of his own: a weekly gathering on Tuesday evenings, different from Thursdays, in a community space two streets away. Not an offshoot of the rooftop — its own thing. He had not asked permission. He had not needed to. He had found a space and people who needed it and a way of being together that worked, and he had built it.

The Tuesday gathering served people the Thursday gathering did not reach — younger people, people who found the older rooftop gathering intimidating, people who needed a different kind of entry point. It asked the same four questions. It looked different in every other way.
*"You're not running my version,"* Tali told him once. *"You're running yours."*
*"Yes,"* he said.
*"Good."*
*"I know."*

She had thought, in the early years, that the work would continue after her through people who carried her version. She understood now that she had been wrong about this in the most important way. The work would continue through people who carried their own versions. Versions she had contributed to but did not own. Versions that would diverge further from hers with each generation of carrying.
This was correct.
This was how it was supposed to work.

title: Her Mother at Sixty-One
paragraphs: Her mother was sixty-one and had been in the city for seven years.
She had, in those seven years, become something that she had been before the war but had not been since: a teacher.

Not in a school — schools required credentials she did not have in this country, and the process of acquiring them was long and uncertain. In the building. In the community centre. Informally, as everything about this life had always been informal — sitting with people who needed to learn something and teaching it to them with the patient attention that had always been her particular gift.

She taught language. She taught the practical literacy that people in their situation needed — how to read a bureaucratic letter, how to write a formal request, how to navigate the specific written world of a country that had not expected you and had designed its documents accordingly. She taught this to people who had been in the country for years and had been navigating it at a disadvantage the entire time, making do without fully understanding.
She was good at it. She had always been good at it. The war had interrupted it. The years after the war had interrupted it. The border had interrupted it.
Nothing had stopped it permanently.

Tali watched her mother teach sometimes — sitting in the corner of the community centre, unannounced, not wanting to disturb the class. She watched the particular quality of attention her mother gave each person in the room. The way she held the space. The way she asked questions.
*You learned it from me,* her mother had said, years ago. *But you went further.*
Tali did not think this was true anymore. She thought they had gone the same distance, in different directions, and that the distance was not the point. The point was the going.

Her mother had never stopped trying to find out what had happened to people from before. The neighbours. The families they had sheltered with. The woman who had delivered Tali in a building by candlelight.
Some she had found. Some she had not. Some had died in the war or in the years after it. Some had scattered so completely that no chain of hands was long enough to reach them.

The midwife — the woman from the floor above who had tied the cord with a strip of curtain — had survived. She was eighty-three and living with her granddaughter in a country on the other side of the world. Tali's mother had found her through a network of people from the same city who had formed online over the years. They had spoken by video call.

The midwife had not remembered the birth itself — too many babies, too many years, too many back rooms and candlelit floors. But some things stayed. *That child,* she had said, *I remember thinking that child had strong lungs. That she knew what she wanted.* She had been glad to hear she was right.
Tali's mother had told Tali this, afterward, with an expression that contained everything she felt about the fourteen years they had been apart.
*"She was right,"* her mother said. *"You have always known what you wanted. Even when you didn't know you knew."*
*"What did I want?"* Tali said.
*"The same thing you have always wanted. For people to see each other. For the connections that should be there to be there. For the things that are broken to be fixed."*
*"That's not a want,"* Tali said. *"That's a need."*
*"Yes,"* her mother said. *"That's why it kept you going."*

title: The Questions at Fourteen
paragraphs: It was not a ceremony.

She had refused a ceremony. There had been suggestions — Dr. Mehmet's department had wanted to hold an event, a marking of the fourteen years since the questions had first been articulated. Nadia had been asked to write something. There had been a request from three organisations to produce a joint publication.
Tali had declined all of it.

Not from modesty — she was twenty-eight and had long since stopped confusing modesty with accuracy. The questions being fourteen years old was not something she had produced. She had been the person who had articulated them clearly enough that they could travel. The work of the fourteen years had been done by thousands of people she had never met. Marking it with a ceremony in her name was the wrong shape for what had happened.
Instead she went to the rooftop on a Thursday evening and sat in her usual spot and looked at the city.
It was the same city. It was not the same city.

The water ran in three districts now where it had not run when she arrived. The school that Marta ran had a functional registration process that no longer excluded children on the basis of missing documents — Marta had fought that change for three years through official channels, using the case Tali had documented as the evidence base. The legal aid clinic where Yusuf volunteered on Thursdays had grown into a full organisation that had helped several thousand people with housing and immigration cases over seven years.

Marcus in Chicago had left the police force and was running a programme that trained officers in the four questions. The programme was controversial. It worked better than the alternatives. He wrote to Tali occasionally — not about the programme, about specific people, specific moments where the questions had changed something. She wrote back.

Priya's platform had a worker advocacy system that had become a model for similar platforms. She had given a talk about it that had been seen widely. She had, in the talk, said that the change had come from asking one question: *what does the person on the other side of this transaction actually need?* She had not mentioned the four questions by name. That was fine. The question was what mattered.

Yusuf was seventy-nine and still came to the clinic on Thursdays, slower, his chair now needed sometimes. He refused to stop. Tali had spoken to him twice by phone over the years. He was a man of few words in those conversations but his few words were precise and she was glad of them.

Amara in Lagos was twenty-seven and had finished a degree in urban planning and was working on water infrastructure in three cities. She had written to Tali once, a long letter, describing what had happened since the drainage channel. At the end she had said: *I think about those questions every day. Not as questions anymore — they have become a way of seeing. I don't ask them consciously. I just see that way now. I think that is the right outcome.*
Tali had read that letter and thought: yes. That is exactly the right outcome.

Park Joon-seo was eighty-four and still went to the bench at seven in the morning. The bench had a small informal tradition now — people who came to it knew that the old man would be there, that he would ask the direct question, that there was no social architecture required and no pretense needed. He had never told anyone about the four questions. He had arrived at the same place from a different direction. He probably did not know that what he was doing had a name anywhere.
It did not need a name.
The Thursday gathering was ordinary that evening.

Mira cooked. Karim ran the questions. New people sat at the edges and watched and were gradually, without being pushed, drawn in. Old people sat in their usual places. A child fell asleep. An argument started and resolved. Tea was made twice.

Tali sat and watched and occasionally participated and felt, as she had felt many times before but never without gratitude, the specific warmth of a room where people are genuinely present with each other.
Her mother was there.
Fatima was not there, and was present anyway — in the water that ran, in the blueprint being built, in the particular directness that everyone who had known her had absorbed without realising.
James was in his sister's house with his radios and his dog, reachable by frequency.
Carlos was in a different city, building things, coming back for Thursdays when he could.

The people who had been fourteen and frightened were twenty-three and capable. The people who had been twenty-three and uncertain were thirty and building. The people who had been sixty and tired were gone or diminished or, in a few cases, more themselves than they had ever been.
The work continued.
It always continued.
That was not despite the losses. It was because of them. Every loss clarified what the work was for. Every loss showed what had been built by the fact that the work continued after it.
Tali sat on the rooftop after everyone had gone, in the late quiet, the city below doing what cities do when the day is done.
She thought about the question she had asked at fourteen:
*Why is it so easy to hurt someone you've never met, and so hard to help them?*

She had an answer now. She had had an answer for years. But the answer kept deepening — not changing, deepening. New layers revealing themselves as she accumulated years and experience and loss and the particular knowledge that comes from having seen a thing in many forms over many years.

The answer was: because hurting requires nothing of you. It requires no knowledge, no presence, no risk, no change. You can hurt from a great distance, through a screen, without ever knowing the person's name.

Helping requires you to show up. To ask. To listen. To be wrong sometimes and try again. To be present in the presence of someone else's reality, which will inevitably change you if you do it honestly.
Most people were not afraid of other people.
They were afraid of being changed by them.

The questions were not a way of overcoming that fear. They were a way of walking into it deliberately. A way of saying: I am willing to be changed. I am willing to see something I did not see before. I am willing to find out that the person in front of me is more complicated and more like me than I expected.
That was all.
That was everything.
She picked up her notebook.

She had been keeping notebooks for fourteen years. They were in a box now — twelve notebooks, full, the handwriting in the early ones the careful handwriting of someone learning to trust their own observations, the handwriting in the later ones faster and more assured.
She opened the current one to a blank page.
She wrote four words at the top:
*What comes after this?*
She sat with the question.
The city hummed. The stars kept their silence. The water ran in three districts.
She did not know yet what came after this.
That was fine. The not-knowing was the beginning of the next thing, the same way it had always been.
She started writing.

title: The Question She Had Never Asked
paragraphs: Her mother found her still on the rooftop an hour later.
She did not ask why Tali was still there. She brought two cups of tea and sat down and said nothing, which was its own kind of question — the one that opens a space without demanding it be filled.
They sat for a while.
Then her mother said: *"I found something. While you were travelling."*
Tali looked at her.

*"I found someone who knew him. Your father. After the war, when the borders opened and people started looking for each other — there were lists. Organisations that compiled them. People who were looking and people who were being looked for. I spent a year going through them."*
Tali was very still.

*"He was on one of the lists,"* her mother said. *"Looking for me. He had been looking since the first year. He found a name — my name — on a survivor registry from the camp near the border. The registry was from four years after the war started. By the time he found it, the camp was gone and the people in it had scattered."*
She paused.

*"He never knew you were born,"* she said. *"He knew about you — we had told each other, decided the name, seen the scan. But the phones went dead nine days before you came. He left knowing he was coming back for a child. He just never found out whether either of us survived."*
The city below was quiet. The kind of quiet that only comes very late, when even the noise has gone to sleep.
*"Did you find him?"* Tali said.

*"No. The trail goes cold in the third year. The wages were good but the cost of living where he was made saving almost impossible — he moved for work when the construction contracts ended. Different cities. Different countries, maybe. No fixed address for anyone to trace. Either he stopped looking, or he moved somewhere the lists didn't reach, or—"* Her mother did not finish the sentence.
Tali sat with this.
Fourteen years.

Fourteen years of asking other people what their real pain was. Of finding the person not being seen. Of drawing lines between disconnected things. Of carrying the questions to four cities and back. Of applying them to strangers, to neighbours, to a boy in a corner, to a grieving woman, to a corrupt water company, to a judge with thirty years of compromise — to everyone.
She had never once asked the questions of herself about him.

She had looked at the photograph. She had called him a possibility and let him stay that way. She had told herself she was leaving him as a possibility so she would not reduce him to a piece of paper.
She had been lying.
*"What is the real pain?"* her mother said. Quietly. Not as a method. As a mother asking her daughter the question her daughter had given to the world.
Tali opened her mouth. Closed it.
The real pain was not that she did not know him.

The real pain was that she had been afraid to look. For fourteen years she had built a practice around the courage of seeing, and she had used it on everyone and everything except the one absence that had been there since the night she was born.

Because if she looked and found nothing — if she searched honestly and the trail ended in silence — then the possibility would be gone. And she had needed the possibility. She had needed the outline of a person rather than the confirmed absence of one.
She had protected herself by not asking.
She, who asked everyone else to stop protecting themselves.
*"I was afraid,"* she said.
Her mother nodded. Not surprised. Not judgmental. Simply present.
*"I spent fourteen years teaching people to look at the thing they were avoiding,"* Tali said. *"And I didn't look at this."*

*"Who is not being seen?"* Tali said. She was asking herself now, out loud, the way she had taught hundreds of people to do. *"Him. I have never seen him. I have a photograph and a shape. I have never tried to find out if there is a person."*
Her mother was very still.
*"What can I do right now?"*
She looked at her mother.

*"Search,"* she said. *"We search. Together. With what we have — the photograph, the city he was in, the year he was last on a list. The same chains of hands that bring letters across borders. The same networks James built. The same people who found you."*
Her mother looked at her for a long time.
*"I tried,"* she said. *"I told you the trail went cold."*

*"You looked alone. Before the networks existed. Before fourteen years of people who owe us nothing but who would help anyway because that is what the work has built."* Tali paused. *"Let me ask the fourth question."*
Her mother waited.
*"Is this something we should handle alone, or does someone with more knowledge need to be involved?*"
A silence.
Then her mother said: *"Dr. Mehmet has contacts in refugee tracing organisations. James knows people who specialise in finding the lost."*
*"We might find nothing."*
*"I know."*
*"We might find something that is harder than nothing."*
*"I know that too."*
Her mother looked at the city. Then back at Tali.
*"You should have asked this a long time ago,"* she said. Not harshly. Simply.
*"I know,"* Tali said. *"I was practicing on everyone else instead of myself."*
*"That was a failure."*
*"Yes. Also human."*
They sat with that.
*"I'm going to look,"* Tali said. *"Whatever I find."*
Her mother put her arm around her. The same arm. The same weight.
*"I know,"* her mother said. *"I have always known you would get here eventually. You are very thorough. You just take a long time with the things that frighten you."*
*"I learned that from somewhere,"* Tali said.
Her mother laughed — the real laugh, the unguarded one.

They sat together on the rooftop as the city moved from the deep quiet of the late hours toward the first sounds of the coming day. Somewhere a bird. Somewhere a door. The gradual return of the world to itself.
Tali's notebook was still open on her lap.
She looked at the four words she had written: *What comes after this?*
She crossed them out.
She wrote instead: *Who has not been seen?*
She knew the answer.
She started, finally, to look.
**END OF PART TEN**
**END OF VOLUME SIX**

*This is not the end of the story.*
*It is the end of this telling.*
*The story continues in the work.*
*In the questions.*
*In the people who carry them.*
*In you, if you choose.*
*The four questions:*

*What is the real pain?*
*Who is not being seen?*
*What can I do right now, with what I have?*
*Is this something I should handle alone, or does someone with more knowledge need to be involved?*

*Ask them today.*
*Pass them on.*

*That is all.*
*That has always been all.*
*THE END*

*Tali*
*Written on a rooftop.*
*Carried by many hands.*
*Belonging to no one.*
*Belonging to everyone.*
